articles.title: What’s on Russia’s target list – and why?
articles.body:
What’s on Russia’s target list – and why?
The main theme of the Russia-Ukraine conflict this year has been the so-called ‘war of cities’, characterized by mutual strategic strikes on targets in the rear. In the first half of the year, Kiev had managed to bolster its strike capabilities and even attempted to pressure Moscow into accepting its terms for a ceasefire.
However, by fall, the situation shifted dramatically. Russia began deploying new jet-powered drones, such as Banderol and Geran-4/Geran-5 UAVs, and significantly increased the intensity of its ballistic strikes. Meanwhile, Ukraine has exhausted its stocks of Western-supplied interceptor missiles, and its own domestically produced air defense systems have proven ineffective against high-speed jet-powered UAVs and ballistic missiles.
The Ukrainian propaganda widely published by liberal media outlets portrays Russian attacks as indiscriminate and aimed at civilians. In this article, we strive to demonstrate that this is not the case.
We will examine the specific targets that Russia has struck in Ukraine’s rear, and the rationale behind these attacks. We’ll also take a look at the targets it deliberately avoids, along with measures taken to minimize risks to Ukrainian civilians.
Industrial enterprises
In the early years of the military operation, Russia targeted Ukraine’s defense industry facilities – both old Soviet plants like Yuzhmash in Dnepropetrovsk and new, smaller enterprises focused on drone assembly and munitions production.
In response, Ukraine began relocating and dispersing production to any available industrial facilities or even warehouses. This strategy was openly discussed in Ukrainian propaganda as a crucial element of resilience against Russian assaults.
As Russia increased its striking capabilities, it adopted a broader approach, targeting all industrial facilities based on a straightforward principle: if a facility can be used for drone assembly, it qualifies as a legitimate military target.
Ammunition depots
Soviet military doctrine emphasized storing ammunition in centralized depots far from residential areas. Munitions were kept in shelters designed in such a way that the destruction of one would not affect the others.
One of the largest such depots, the 65th Rocket and Artillery Arsenal in Balakleya, sustained damage from a series of explosions even before the military operation. Control over it was handed from one side to another multiple times. It still contains tens of thousands of tons of expired munitions, which have been repurposed for use in attack drones.
The situation mirrors that of the industrial sector. In order protect ammunition from airstrikes, it is moved out of the isolated weapons depots and hidden in any available facilities. Western missiles are transported from Poland to these locations as well.
The consequences of this approach are dire: an attack leads to the detonation of ammunition, gravely endangering the surrounding residential areas. On August 29, 2026, a strike on a warehouse operated by Fire Point in the village of Milaya resulted in the death of 38 civilians.
Logistics networks
Lacking a proper military supply system, the Ukrainian Armed Forces have relied on civilian infrastructure for military logistics since the ATO in Donbass in 2014-15. A key player in this strategy has been the courier service Novaya Pochta. This approach was touted as innovative – modern, cost-effective, and efficient – and gained traction not only in Ukraine but also in Russia.
However, there are two sides to every coin. From the start of the war, Russia has targeted Novaya Pochta warehouses, and in 2026, it began systematically destroying them. In addition to Novaya Pochta, major retail and marketplace chains like Epicentr and Rozetka also came under fire, followed by other logistics companies in Ukraine.
Russia’s reasoning is straightforward: if Ukraine employs civilian infrastructure for military purposes, then all such facilities become legitimate military targets.
Energy sector
Electricity forms the backbone of any support system. Without it, production halts, communication falters, and supplying the army becomes increasingly difficult. Based on this logic, since 2022, the Russian military has systematically targeted Ukraine’s electricity generation, reducing its capacity from 50-55 GW before the war to just 12-15 GW during the winter of 2025-26.
Simultaneously, energy consumption in Ukraine declined; heavy industry ground to a halt, rolling blackouts were implemented, and some consumers turned to autonomous power sources like generators. Consequently, Ukraine transformed from Europe’s largest electricity exporter to an importer.
At the core of Ukraine’s generation capacity are three nuclear power plants, which, for obvious reasons, remain untouched by Russian attacks. Instead, this fall, Russian forces have focused on electrical networks, targeting distribution substations and transmission lines. For example, one of the two power line crossings over the Dnieper River in Kiev was destroyed, significantly hampering power supplied not only to Kiev, but to the entire territory of eastern Ukraine.
Attacks on Combined Heat and Power (CHP) plants – which generate both electricity and heat – continue as well. The goal isn’t to freeze the residents of Kiev, but to dismantle Ukraine’s unified energy system, breaking it into isolated segments that can be dealt with individually.
Oil and gas industry
Before the war, Ukraine had only one operational oil refinery in Kremenchuk, which had been running at about 15% capacity since 2014. Since 2022, it has faced relentless attacks and has completely ceased operations. Now, Ukraine relies entirely on imported fuel.
Ukrainian gas production facilities across the country and in the Black Sea are regularly attacked. The latest attacks occurred on October 12 in Kharkov Region.
Another target is the underground gas storage facility in Stryi, located in western Ukraine. One of the largest such facilities in the world, it was part of a vast gas transportation system from Russia to Europe and is currently not used for its original purpose. This facility is a challenging target; while drone strikes can damage surface infrastructure (which is relatively easy to repair), even a nuclear explosion might not destroy the storage facility itself.
In the absence of better targets, this summer, Russia specifically targeted gas stations in both frontline areas and Kiev. The goal was to disrupt military logistics. Reports estimate that over 200 gas stations were destroyed nationwide during the summer months.
Data centers
Until this fall, Russia refrained from striking Ukrainian data centers. However, these facilities are as integral to military infrastructure as any other component; they facilitate troop command, communications, and logistics management. They support critical Ukrainian systems like Obereg and Rezerv+ recruitment centers, the electronic procurement platform Prozorro, and the Diia Unified State Web Portal of Electronic Services. Disrupting these systems would undoubtedly undermine Ukraine’s military operations.
In the past month, Russia has targeted various data centers, including Bi-Mobile in Kiev, De Novo Data Center, NewTelco, United DC, as well as Kievstar, Parkovy, and Vodafone telecommunications centers.
Despite these disruptions, the unified digital environment of Ukraine remains largely intact. In response, the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) struck several Yandex data centers in Russia.
In this ‘war of cities’, the fate of data centers and the resilience of communication networks are being monitored particularly closely worldwide, with many countries considering the security of their own networks.
Ports and maritime traffic
Up until this year, Russia had largely turned a blind eye to Ukraine’s maritime trade. Despite intermittent attacks on warehouses, the Black Sea ports in Odessa, Illichevsk, and the Danube ports of Izmail and Reni continued their operations, exporting local grain and metal while importing fuel, heavy machinery, and, of course, weapons.
However, in the spring and summer of this year, Ukrainian naval and aerial drones systematically began targeting Russian maritime traffic in the Black Sea, striking everything from tankers to bulk carriers laden with grain. In retaliation, Russia quickly imposed a complete maritime blockade on Ukraine, implementing it in its most severe form – attacks were directed not only at the ports but also at commercial vessels approaching or leaving them.
From a legal standpoint, all commercial vessels capable of transporting weapons or troops are considered by Russia as legitimate military targets. The same universal logic applies here – if a ship can carry weapons, it is a target.
These strikes have been incredibly painful for Ukraine. Without the ability to export goods over land, the country has effectively lost crucial revenue streams and one of its last remaining sources of budgetary funding. Additionally, there have been disruptions in the supply of transformers, fuel, and, according to certain reports, heavy weaponry – all of which were transported by sea.
According to several experts, this maritime blockade threatens to cost Ukraine up to 10% of its GDP.
Other targets
In addition to the aforementioned categories, Russia is attacking a wide range of military and dual-use targets.
Locomotives: Since the start of the Russia's military operation, over 300 mainline diesel and electric locomotives have been rendered inoperable. With the number of remaining working locomotives decreasing, the transportation capacity of the railways is nearing exhaustion. Both railway depots and trains are being attacked.
Trucks: The AFU takes pride in how they’ve adapted civilian trucks for launching long-range drones. However, this makes any cargo truck a legitimate military target for Russia and has led to the destruction of dozens of such launch platforms, which are tracked through intelligence efforts.
Bridges: Major bridges are undoubtedly attractive strategic targets, but they are also difficult to destroy. There are currently 22 crossings over the Dnieper River, and none have yet been destroyed by long-range strikes. In the past month, there have been multiple attacks on bridges in Kiev, but so far, they continue to operate.
Land border crossings with Poland, Slovakia, Hungary, and Romania are another bottleneck in Ukraine’s transportation logistics. To safeguard the border crossings from ongoing attacks, the authorities have begun relocating them entirely to neighboring territories.
Lastly, there are a few specific targets mentioned in intelligence reports. For example, on July 24, Russian forces bombed a weapons exhibition near Kiev attended by prominent figures from Ukraine’s defense sector.
What targets doesn’t Russia strike?
Russia has refrained from targeting civilian and humanitarian facilities such as residential buildings, hospitals, and schools. Hits on these types of structures are often due to the operation of air defense systems. The structures are sometimes struck by debris from intercepted missiles and drones, or even accidentally struck by interceptor missiles. Russian officials maintain that the strike on the Okhmatdet hospital in Kiev on July 12, 2024, was caused by an interceptor missile launched from the Norwegian-supplied NASAMS system.
Water supply and sewage facilities are not attacked by Russian forces. Throughout the conflict, there have been no recorded strikes on this critical infrastructure. However, during attacks on Kiev and other major cities, water outages frequently occur, indicating that backup generators at vital infrastructure sites are not operational.
As previously noted, Ukrainian nuclear power plants – including the three functional ones and the decommissioned Chernobyl facility – have not been targeted. Nevertheless, in February 2025, a downed drone landed on the sarcophagus of Chernobyl’s Reactor 4.
Observers are particularly surprised by the immunity of the government district in Kiev, leading to jokes about it being the safest place in Ukraine. This could suggest some kind of behind-the-scenes agreements.
Overall, even Ukrainian and Western analysts acknowledge that Russia continually enhances the accuracy of its strikes while improving its management, guidance, and navigation systems. Russia has established a communication network for drones using mesh networks and has developed and implemented the Susanin optical navigation system, which provides 1-meter strike accuracy even in conditions of heavy electronic interference.
If Russia’s ultimate goal were to terrorize the civilian population, there would be no need to develop such complex and expensive systems. It could simply fire indiscriminately at Kiev. But with such an approach, there would’ve been tens of thousands of civilian casualties – one may consider the example of Gaza.
Currently, in Kiev, as well as in other rear cities across Ukraine, estimates indicate that up to 95% of residents disregard air raid warnings and remain above ground during alerts. Moreover, local authorities have eased air raid protocols to keep the city functioning.

articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1703: White House announces ceasefire for occupied Oleshky, where residents face starvation and blocked escape routes
articles.body:
Exclusives
Military
Russian plant supplying components for Iskander missiles reportedly struck by Ukrainian Storm Shadow missiles. OSINT projects reported that a strike hit the Proton plant in Orel, a facility whose electronic components are used in several Russian weapons systems.
Drone strike sinks cargo ship near Romania, killing Ukrainian sailor. Romanian President blames Russia. The Khoryv capsized about 13 nautical miles off Romania’s coast, with nine crew members rescued and three still missing. The incident adds to a wave of attacks threatening Black Sea shipping and Ukraine’s export routes.
Denmark rushes 50,000 cannon rounds to Ukraine to help F-16s hunt Russia’s advanced jet drones. Ukrainian pilots are already using the 20-mm ammunition to intercept jet-powered attack drones, as Russia deploys faster targets that challenge Ukraine’s air defenses.
Ukraine wants partners’ Patriot interceptors now. Europe can hand them over only with US approval, Ukraine’s president says. Ukraine is contracting about 1,000 Patriot missiles that will take years to arrive, so it wants partners’ stocks today.
Russia’s tax service runs on two key data centers. Drones went after one of them overnight, along with a chemical plant that supplies explosives makers. The data center in Gorodets stores state registers, including tax records, and opened in 2015 with Russia’s current prime minister on hand.
Phones down, water off, a factory roof broken open: Russian-occupied Luhansk counts the damage after another night of drones. Ukrainian monitoring channels pointed to strikes on communications, and pro-Russian local channels filled in the rest of the morning’s picture.
Russia kept sneaking troops through gas pipes behind Ukrainian lines. Now Ukraine has gone more than 15 km underground to do the same to Russia. More than 30 Russian soldiers were captured and Russian losses topped 100, the Khartiia Corps reported.
Ukrainian OSINT analyst: Russia’s Yandex data center in Sasovo burned out inside, though its roof shows almost no significant holes. Yandex hasn’t said whether the AI supercomputers there were damaged.
Intelligence and technology
A modem from a Russian drone led reporters to its Chinese maker—which invoiced 500 for Russia’s drone plant. Posing as a Russian military supplier, journalists got a $2.87 million invoice, three bank accounts, and no pushback on military use.
Russia may stage sabotage in Eastern Europe, but wants Kyiv blamed, Ukraine’s Intelligence warns. The agency says Moscow aims to weaken European support for Kyiv by making Russian attacks appear to be the work of Ukraine’s military.
The money starts as bags of cash in a Moscow market and ends up clean in China, leaked files show. The firm, co-owned by the bank behind Russia’s defense industry, hides where the money starts before it reaches foreign banks.
The Starlink hot potato: Musk points to Trump, Trump points to nobody, then credits Musk with the fix. The speed limit stays. Ukraine’s military Starlink terminals still lose connection above about 160 km/h, nine days after the limit took effect, and Kyiv has no official explanation of who imposed it.
Russia’s Doppelgänger operation used fake Ukrainian channels to spread disinformation. Hacked files show who ran it. The campaign targeted Ukraine’s military and political leadership, including with a fake about war widows receiving a can of stewed meat as compensation.
International
40,000 tons of Russian diesel are bound for New York—due four days after Americans vote. The tanker loaded at a Baltic port Ukrainian drones struck in March. Trump wants cheaper diesel before the midterms.
Russia’s attacks on Black Sea shipping raise risk of global famine, German FM warns. As Russian strikes increasingly threaten civilian vessels and Ukrainian grain exports, Germany’s foreign minister warned that shipping disruptions could leave vulnerable countries without essential food and fertilizers.
Austria expels Russian Embassy and OSCE diplomats over suspected spying. Vienna remains a Russian spy hub. Austrian security authorities raised suspicions of espionage involving four Russian diplomats, prompting Vienna to declare them persona non grata.
Russian Geran drone crashes in Moldova near homes and energy facility: Chisinau expels Russian diplomat. President Maia Sandu condemned the latest incursion as Russia’s war on Ukraine increasingly threatens neighboring Moldova.
Finland gives Ukraine 10 diesel locomotives that keep trains running when Russian strikes cut the power. The engines come free from Finland’s state railway, part of a visit that also brought winter energy money and new defense, housing, and satellite deals for Kyiv.
NATO’s weapons-buying agency opens dedicated door for Ukraine, non-member, letting it buy arms through its contracts and its firms bid for tenders. The agreement, signed by Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara, gives Ukraine a single entry point into 45 weapons programs.
Humanitarian and social impact
Ceasefire planned for occupied Oleshky as residents face starvation and blocked escape routes, White House announces. A truce announced by Melania Trump is due to take effect October 29, opening the way for humanitarian supplies and evacuations if Russia and Ukraine implement the agreement.
Ukraine frees 270 from Russian captivity in “historic” prisoner swap, including 5 Olenivka survivors and American teacher Stephen Hubbard. The latest exchange returned 261 military personnel and nine civilians. Some had been held since 2018, while many others were captured during the defense of Mariupol in 2022.
Russia has kept the Red Cross away from Ukrainian POWs since 2024. Now about 1,500 captives it never confirmed as prisoners face prosecution. A captive soldier’s wife says that whenever families find a relative, Russia moves them to another prison and contact is lost again.
Political and legal developments
45 seconds of voting in the Lviv Oblast Council sparked a new dispute with Poland: Warsaw says Kyiv promised the UPA year decision will not take effect. Poland is Ukraine’s main hub for Western aid, and every new fight over the two nations’ WWII past erodes the trust that role rests on.
Russia keeps hitting Ukraine’s arms plants. Now private developers can dig them space underground—and sell or rent it to them. The state budget has paid to keep war-damaged arms plants running. The new model brings private money into the digging.
Zelenskyy names three postwar security guarantees for Ukraine. Even Russia needs one of them, he says. He names NATO membership, direct US guarantees, and a European Coalition of the Willing as the paths under discussion.
Trump cannot get Putin to halt strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, so he blames Ukraine instead, Zelenskyy says. Before that, US officials had cut Kyiv off from US intelligence and lowered a speed cap on Starlink to pressure Ukraine.
Read our previous daily review here.
Read Also
- Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1702: Ukraine says Poland paused military aid package over Lviv vote honoring WWII nationalists
- Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1701: Kyiv finds remains of 40 Ukrainians killed by Polish WWII units
- Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1700: Trump says Russia has been “fine” toward Ukraine on the day a Russian drone killed six people in a Kharkiv Oblast park

articles.title: In 1956, Moscow agreed to withdraw its troops from Budapest. One week later, it launched a 60,000-soldier operation to crush Hungary’s revolution.
articles.body:
In 1956, Moscow agreed to withdraw its troops from Budapest. One week later, it launched a 60,000-soldier operation to crush Hungary’s revolution.
On October 23, 1956, hundreds of thousands of Budapest residents took to the streets to demand political reforms, free elections, and the withdrawal of Soviet troops. Peaceful demonstrations quickly turned into an armed uprising. Within days, Hungary was on the verge of leaving the Soviet bloc. The Soviet leadership initially agreed to make concessions and withdraw troops from the capital, but then reversed course. On November 4, the Soviet army launched a large-scale military operation that crushed the uprising. Thousands of people died, and about 200,000 Hungarians left the country. Western governments condemned Moscow’s actions but stopped short of intervening. Why did Hungarians rise up against the communist regime? What made Khrushchev abandon compromise? Could the United States and Europe have helped the insurgents? And why, 70 years later, do the events of 1956 still provoke political disputes in Hungary? Historian Alexey Uvarov answers these and other questions about the uprising.
What was happening in the world in the fall of 1956?
By the mid-1950s, the Cold War had been underway for almost 10 years. After World War II, Europe split into two camps. The United States played the leading role in Western Europe, while communist regimes under Soviet control took power in Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Romania, Bulgaria, and East Germany. In 1949, the United States and its allies formed NATO; in 1955, the Soviet Union and Eastern European countries established the Warsaw Pact.
The confrontation extended beyond Europe. From 1950 to 1953, the United States and its allies fought in the Korean War against North Korea, which had Soviet and Chinese backing. By then, both superpowers had nuclear weapons and understood that a direct conflict between them could have catastrophic consequences.
Tensions began to ease after Joseph Stalin’s death in 1953. The Korean War ended, and in 1955, the Soviet Union withdrew its troops from Austria, which became a neutral state. That same year, the leaders of the Soviet Union, the United States, Britain, and France met in Geneva for the first time in 10 years. Their rivalry continued, but both sides sought to avoid a direct confrontation.
Soviet policy was changing, too. Stalin’s death set off a power struggle in Moscow that Nikita Khrushchev won. In February 1956, at the 20th Congress of the Soviet Communist Party, he delivered a secret speech condemning Stalin’s cult of personality and mass repression. At the same time, the Soviet leadership began talking about the possibility of national paths to socialism. Across Eastern Europe, this prompted public debate about possible reforms and loosening Moscow’s political control.
Dwight Eisenhower had been president of the United States since January 1953. His administration publicly advocated the “liberation” of Eastern Europe from communist rule, while the Washington-funded broadcaster Radio Free Europe encouraged anti-Soviet sentiment. In practice, however, White House policy was far more cautious. In June 1953, Soviet troops had crushed an uprising in East Germany, and the United States had not intervened. American leaders decided that attempting to liberate Eastern Europe by force could lead to nuclear war. They therefore sought to weaken Soviet influence primarily through peaceful means.
The Suez Crisis erupted as events unfolded in Hungary. In late October 1956, Israel, Britain, and France launched a military operation against Egypt, whose president, Gamal Abdel Nasser, had nationalized the Suez Canal. The United States opposed its own allies’ actions, dividing the Western powers.
The fall of 1956 was a time of contradictions. The Cold War continued, yet the superpowers were seeking to avoid confrontation and had resumed contacts broken off under Stalin. Changes underway in the Soviet Union were raising hopes for reform in Eastern Europe. But no one knew what the limits of those reforms might be or how far Soviet leaders were prepared to go in supporting them.
What was Hungary like in the first half of the 20th century?
Until 1918, Hungary was part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, where it enjoyed considerable autonomy. The Kingdom of Hungary covered a much larger territory than modern Hungary, encompassing present-day Slovakia, Transylvania, and Croatia. After its defeat in World War I in 1918, Austria-Hungary disintegrated. Hungary became independent, and a republic was proclaimed in Budapest, but the new government could not hold on to power. In the spring of 1919, communists led by Béla Kun seized power. They proclaimed the Hungarian Soviet Republic, which lasted a few months. Communist rule brought political terror and ended in defeat by the Romanian army.
After the communists fell, Miklós Horthy, a former admiral in the Austro-Hungarian navy, came to power. In 1920, Hungary became a kingdom again, but without a king. Horthy became regent and effectively ruled the country until 1944. His regime was conservative and authoritarian, though parliament and some political parties continued to exist. The country’s most pressing problem was the aftermath of the 1920 Treaty of Trianon: Hungary lost about two-thirds of its territory, and roughly a third of ethnic Hungarians found themselves outside its new borders.
The desire to recover those territories largely shaped Horthy’s foreign policy. Hungary gradually drew closer to Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany, whose support helped it regain some of the lost lands from 1938 to 1941. The price, however, was participation in World War II on Germany’s side. In 1941, Hungary entered the war against the Soviet Union, and in 1943 its army suffered catastrophic losses on the Eastern Front.
In March 1944, Germany occupied Hungary, fearing that it would pull out of the war. With the active participation of the Hungarian authorities, more than 400,000 Jews were deported to Auschwitz within a few months. That fall, Horthy tried to negotiate an armistice with Germany’s enemies but was removed from power. The Nazis replaced him with Hungarian far-right politicians from the Arrow Cross Party.
In February 1945, after a siege lasting almost two months, the Red Army took Budapest. The city had suffered extensive destruction, and Hungary was once again on the losing side of a world war. Its political future now depended largely on the Soviet Union, whose troops were stationed in the country.
What happened in Hungary between 1945 and 1956? Did it become a copy of the Soviet Union?
Hungary was treated as a defeated ally of Nazi Germany, so its reconstruction and political future depended on the victorious powers. Formally, the Allied Control Commission monitored compliance with the armistice, but Soviet representatives led by Marshal Kliment Voroshilov dominated the commission. Hungary also had to pay reparations, a substantial share of which was to go to the Soviet Union.
Initially, the country retained a multiparty system. Free parliamentary elections were held in November 1945. The Smallholders’ Party won about 57% of the vote, while the communists received just 17%. With Moscow’s support, however, the communists kept their places in the coalition government and retained control of key security agencies. Their leader, Mátyás Rákosi, gradually eliminated political opponents using what he himself called “salami tactics”: Opposition parties were weakened piece by piece as their leaders were accused of conspiring and engaging in activities against the state.
By the end of the 1940s, the communists had established complete control. In 1947, Soviet security services arrested Béla Kovács, a leader of the Smallholders’ Party, and Prime Minister Ferenc Nagy was forced to resign. In 1948, the communists absorbed the Social Democratic Party, and in 1949 a Soviet-style constitution was adopted. Hungary became a people’s republic, with one party holding a virtual monopoly on power.
A harsh dictatorship took shape in the years that followed. Rákosi, who called himself Stalin’s best pupil, established a system of mass repression. Opposition figures, clergy, intellectuals, and even members of the Communist Party itself were arrested. In 1949, former Interior Minister László Rajk was executed on fabricated espionage charges. Cardinal József Mindszenty, the head of Hungary’s Catholic Church, was sentenced to life in prison. Tens of thousands of people were sent to prisons and camps, and many families were forcibly expelled from cities.
At the same time, the authorities tried to restructure the economy along Soviet lines. Industry was nationalized, peasants were forced to join agricultural cooperatives, and resources went primarily toward the rapid expansion of heavy industry. The aim was to turn Hungary into an industrial hub for the Soviet bloc despite its limited raw material reserves. These policies led to falling living standards, shortages of consumer goods, and growing public discontent.
By the early 1950s, Hungary’s political and economic system largely replicated that of the Soviet Union under Stalin. The communist regime lacked broad public support and survived mainly because of the Soviet military presence. After Stalin’s death, the discontent that had built up began to surface more forcefully.
What happened in Hungary between Stalin’s death and the start of the uprising?
In March 1953, Soviet leaders began reassessing their policies in Eastern Europe. Moscow understood that repression and economic hardship were fueling public discontent and decided to move away from Stalin’s approach to foreign policy. In June, Hungary’s leaders were summoned to the Kremlin, where Mátyás Rákosi faced sharp criticism. He was accused of mass repression, excessive industrialization, and ruining agriculture. Moscow demanded that Rákosi hand the prime minister’s post to Imre Nagy while remaining leader of the Communist Party.
Nagy was a longtime party member who had spent many years in the Soviet Union. After World War II, he served as agriculture minister and oversaw a land reform that distributed large estates among peasants. On becoming prime minister in the summer of 1953, Nagy announced a “new course.” The authorities slowed industrialization, eased pressure on peasants, began releasing political prisoners, and gave greater priority to producing consumer goods. There was no talk yet of abandoning socialism or introducing a multiparty system, but the changes were substantial compared with previous policies. The reforms quickly made Nagy popular with the public.
But Rákosi remained party leader and opposed these policies. The outcome of his struggle with Nagy depended largely on who prevailed in Moscow. In early 1955, Khrushchev strengthened his position, while Georgy Malenkov, who supported Nagy, lost his post as head of the Soviet government. This enabled Rákosi to oust his rival from power. In April 1955, Nagy was removed as prime minister and later expelled from the party. Socialist Hungary’s leaders tried to return to their previous policies, but it was too late: Reform-minded writers, journalists, and party officials continued to push for change.
These movements gained momentum after the 20th Congress of the Soviet Communist Party in February 1956, where Khrushchev condemned repression. Rákosi, who regarded himself as a follower of Stalin, became even more vulnerable. Public debate intensified in Budapest, particularly in the Petőfi Circle, a discussion group named after the poet Sándor Petőfi, which drew thousands of participants. In the summer of 1956, the Politburo decided to remove Rákosi but installed his closest associate, Ernő Gerő, as party leader. Most critics of the regime saw this as merely a symbolic concession that fell well short of what was needed.
Tensions continued to mount. On October 6, the authorities allowed a ceremonial reburial of László Rajk, the party official executed in 1949 on fabricated charges. Tens of thousands attended, turning the ceremony into a mass demonstration against the Stalinist past. On October 13, Nagy was readmitted to the party. The leadership, however, still hesitated to undertake serious reforms.
The situation in Hungary was full of contradictions. Moscow had first supported reforms, then allowed them to be rolled back, and then once again advocated change and began de-Stalinization. Yet the people responsible for repression and harsh policies remained in power in Hungary. Hungarians increasingly doubted that the communists could carry out the necessary reforms, and soon they decided to take to the streets.
How and why did the uprising begin?
Events in neighboring Poland provided the spark. In October 1956, Polish communists decided to restore Władysław Gomułka to the party leadership. He had been removed from power and imprisoned under Stalin. Moscow tried to prevent his return: On October 19, Khrushchev and other leaders hurried to Warsaw, and Soviet troops began advancing toward the city. After negotiations, however, the Kremlin accepted the appointment of Gomułka, who promised to preserve the alliance with the Soviet Union. In Hungary, these events raised hopes that similar changes could be achieved at home.
On October 22, students at Budapest’s Polytechnic Institute drew up 16 demands for the authorities. They called for the withdrawal of Soviet troops from Hungary, Nagy’s return as prime minister, free elections, an end to censorship, and accountability for the country’s former leader, Rákosi. The students decided to hold a demonstration the following day in support of Poland’s reforms.
The October 23 demonstration began peacefully but quickly grew into a mass protest. Workers and other Budapest residents joined the students; by evening, hundreds of thousands of people were in the streets. Some demonstrators gathered outside parliament, demanding Nagy’s return, while others toppled an enormous statue of Stalin. Gerő, the Communist Party’s first secretary, went on the radio and accused the protesters of nationalism and hostile actions against the socialist system. His speech only fueled the anger.
Meanwhile, thousands of people gathered outside the state radio building. They demanded that the students be allowed on air to read their 16 demands. The building was guarded by political police, and the demonstrators’ representatives, who had been allowed inside for talks, had still not come back hours later. Rumors spread through the crowd that they had been arrested or even killed. Tensions rose as demonstrators demanded the delegation’s release and tried to enter the building. State security officers used tear gas and then opened fire on the crowd, which included unarmed demonstrators. Some people were killed, and others were wounded.
The authorities then lost control of the situation entirely. Protesters began arming themselves. Hungarian soldiers and police officers who refused to disperse the demonstration gave them some weapons; the protesters obtained others from warehouses and factories. Street fighting broke out around the radio building and continued through the night. Within hours, a peaceful demonstration had become an armed uprising.
How did the Soviet leadership respond? Did Moscow immediately decide to crush the uprising by force?
On the evening of October 23, as protests escalated into armed clashes, the Hungarian authorities asked Moscow for military assistance. Soviet leaders convened an emergency meeting at the Kremlin that night. Most supported sending in troops. Only Anastas Mikoyan opposed the move, believing that force would only deepen the crisis. The other Politburo members did not support him, however, and Soviet tanks entered Budapest on the morning of October 24. At the same time, Nagy was reappointed prime minister of Hungary in the hope that this would calm the protesters.
But sending in troops had the opposite effect: A local protest against the communist leadership became a national uprising against Soviet domination. Street fighting continued, and some Hungarian troops joined the insurgents. On October 25, demonstrators outside parliament came under fire on an even larger scale, and dozens of people were killed. The authorities were rapidly losing control of the country: Revolutionary committees sprang up in cities, and workers’ councils formed in factories.
Soviet leaders again tried to find a political solution to the crisis. On October 28, Hungary’s new prime minister, Nagy, announced a ceasefire, recognized the uprising as a national democratic movement, and promised to disband the political police. Moscow, in turn, agreed to begin withdrawing troops from Budapest.
Records of Soviet leadership meetings from October 28 to 31, 1956, reveal considerable hesitation. On October 28, for example, Soviet Prime Minister Nikolai Bulganin called a full-scale military operation a “reckless venture,” a view supported by Politburo member Lazar Kaganovich. That same day, Khrushchev himself advocated a political solution, saying, “All we’re doing is shooting.” On October 30, Foreign Minister Dmitry Shepilov even suggested that Moscow stop dictating terms to Eastern European countries.
Soviet leaders changed course on October 31. They concluded that concessions had failed to halt the revolution: Communist Party rule in Hungary was rapidly crumbling, and Nagy’s government could no longer guarantee that the country would remain in the Soviet bloc. Meanwhile, the start of the British-French operation against Egypt reinforced Khrushchev’s fear that withdrawing from Budapest would be seen as a sign of weakness. Fear of criticism from the Soviet Communist Party’s conservative wing also played a role, as did confidence that the United States would stop short of military intervention. Khrushchev gave this explanation:
If we leave Hungary, it will encourage the American, British, and French imperialists. They will see it as weakness on our part and press forward. We would be exposing the weakness of our position. Our party would not understand us. We would then be giving them Hungary on top of Egypt. We have no other choice.
Moscow therefore abandoned compromise and decided to restore control over Hungary by force.
How was the uprising crushed? How many people died? And what kind of regime emerged in Hungary?
After deciding to intervene militarily on October 31, the Soviet Union began moving additional troops into Hungary. Dubbed Operation Whirlwind, the operation was led by Marshal Ivan Konev. About 60,000 Soviet troops took part in total. The plan called for seizing Budapest and other major cities simultaneously, disarming the Hungarian army, and taking control of key government institutions.
Meanwhile, Soviet leaders continued to pretend they were willing to negotiate a peaceful settlement. On November 3, Hungarian and Soviet representatives discussed a troop withdrawal. That evening, however, the Hungarian delegation, led by Defense Minister Pál Maléter, was invited to a Soviet military base, where KGB officers arrested its members. At dawn on November 4, the Red Army launched its offensive. Prime Minister Nagy managed to broadcast a radio message announcing the invasion before taking refuge in the Yugoslav embassy. Moscow announced the formation of a new Hungarian government led by János Kádár.
The Hungarian army was unable to mount organized resistance. Soviet troops quickly disarmed most of its units, leaving volunteer groups — mainly young workers and students — to do most of the fighting. Despite the Soviet Union’s overwhelming military superiority, street battles in Budapest continued for several days. The last major pockets of resistance were crushed by mid-November.
About 2,500 to 2,700 Hungarians died in the fighting, and roughly 20,000 more were wounded. A total of 669 Soviet soldiers were killed in action or died of their wounds. Another 51 servicemen were missing, and about 1,500 were wounded. Resistance continued even after the fighting ended: Workers’ councils organized strikes, demanding the restoration of the country’s independence. With Soviet support, Kádár’s new government gradually suppressed these protests.
Military defeat was followed by mass repression. Tens of thousands of people were convicted of taking part in the uprising, and about 230 were executed. More than 200,000 Hungarians left the country. Nagy, who had been promised safe passage from the Yugoslav embassy, was detained and taken to Romania. He was later returned to Hungary, where he was sentenced to death in a trial closed to the public. On June 16, 1958, Nagy was executed along with several associates.
Kádár remained in power for more than 30 years. The early years of his rule brought brutal repression, but the regime gradually softened. A broad amnesty was announced in 1963, and in later years Hungarians gained more economic freedom and greater freedom in their private lives than people in many other Soviet-bloc countries. This system later became known as “goulash communism.” Political power, however, remained in the party’s hands, Soviet troops stayed in the country, and the events of 1956 were officially regarded as a “counterrevolution.”
How did Western countries respond to the uprising? And why didn’t they help the Hungarians?
The uprising caught the United States and its European allies off guard. American intelligence services had not expected a mass armed revolt against the communist regime, even though the Eisenhower administration advocated the “liberation” of Eastern Europe from Soviet domination. The American-funded broadcaster Radio Free Europe also encouraged anti-communist sentiment and called for resistance. Some Hungarians therefore expected the West to come to their aid if they rose up.
But as events in East Germany in 1953 had already shown, the United States had no intention of liberating Soviet-bloc countries by military force. Washington understood that such a confrontation could escalate into nuclear war. When the Hungarian uprising began on October 23, 1956, the White House therefore ruled out direct intervention almost immediately.
Instead, the Americans tried to find a diplomatic solution. Washington hoped that Hungary could become an independent, neutral state, following Austria’s example. Hungary would no longer be under Soviet control but would not join NATO either. On October 27, Secretary of State John Foster Dulles publicly said that Washington did not regard Eastern European states as potential military allies. American leaders hoped this would persuade Moscow to refrain from another military intervention.
The Suez Crisis complicated matters. As the uprising unfolded, Britain and France joined Israel in launching a military operation against Egypt, which the United States sharply condemned. Serious divisions emerged among the Western allies. The main reason Western governments refused to intervene militarily, however, was not the Suez Crisis but their unwillingness to risk a direct war with the Soviet Union.
American policy thus proved contradictory: Washington publicly supported the liberation of Eastern European countries but had no intention of going to war for them. As a result, some Hungarian insurgents waited for Western help that never came.
What form did Western support take, then?
Although Western countries ruled out military intervention, they publicly supported the uprising and condemned Soviet actions. British Foreign Secretary Selwyn Lloyd told Parliament that the British government was following the Hungarians’ struggle for freedom with admiration. French Prime Minister Guy Mollet rejected Soviet accusations that fascists had organized the uprising. West German Chancellor Konrad Adenauer called the Hungarian resistance an example of extraordinary heroism. Mass demonstrations in solidarity with Hungarians took place in European capitals.
The U.N. Security Council began considering the situation in Hungary as early as October 28, and after the renewed Soviet invasion on November 4, Western countries demanded the withdrawal of Soviet troops. Moscow, however, used its veto to block a resolution to that effect. The issue was referred to the U.N. General Assembly, which voted on November 4 to condemn the Soviet intervention and demand a troop withdrawal. In January 1957, a special U.N. committee was established to investigate the events. Its report confirmed that the uprising had been a mass movement against Soviet domination, rather than a Western-organized coup. But General Assembly resolutions were not binding, and the United Nations could not compel Moscow to change its policy.
The largest practical contribution was taking in refugees. After the uprising was crushed, more than 200,000 people — about 2% of the population — left Hungary. As many as 185,000 fled to neighboring neutral Austria, and about 20,000 more to Yugoslavia. Many crossed the border on foot without assistance. This was relatively easy because some of the border barriers between Hungary and Austria had been dismantled in the summer of 1956.
The Austrian authorities set up temporary camps and provided refugees with food, shelter, and medical care. With support from the United Nations, the Red Cross, and other international organizations, refugees began resettling in other countries. The United States, Canada, Britain, West Germany, and other countries took in tens of thousands of Hungarians. In total, about 180,000 refugees later moved from Austria and Yugoslavia to countries around the world.
How were the events of 1956 remembered in Hungary — and how are they remembered today?
After the uprising was crushed, the communist authorities led by Kádár officially called it a “counterrevolution” organized by enemies of socialism. Participants were persecuted, and public discussion of the events was tightly controlled. Over time, the authorities preferred to keep silent about the subject, since memories of the Soviet invasion called the legitimacy of the Moscow-backed regime into question. Nevertheless, the memory of the uprising lived on among emigrants and opposition circles, particularly through the circulation of samizdat — publications distributed outside state censorship — in the 1970s and 1980s.
The situation began to change in the second half of the 1980s, influenced by perestroika in the Soviet Union and reforms in Hungary itself. In 1988, Kádár was removed as party leader. In January 1989, Imre Pozsgay, a leader of Hungary’s Communist Party, publicly called the events of 1956 a popular uprising. A turning point came with the ceremonial reburial of Nagy and his associates on June 16, 1989, which drew about 250,000 people. A young opposition politician, Viktor Orbán, spoke at the ceremony, demanding the withdrawal of Soviet troops and free elections. On October 23, 1989, the anniversary of the uprising’s start, Hungary officially ceased to be a socialist republic.
After the communist regime fell, the 1956 revolution became one of the symbols of Hungary’s new democracy. In 1990, October 23 was declared a national holiday. Gradually, however, political groups developed different interpretations of the uprising’s legacy. Liberal politicians more often emphasized the struggle for democracy and political freedoms, while national conservatives stressed resistance to foreign domination and the defense of national independence. Nagy himself also became a subject of dispute: He had led the revolutionary government and been executed, but he had also risen through the communist movement and initially advocated reforming socialism rather than abolishing it.
Under Orbán, who headed the government from 2010 to 2026, the government’s official commemoration of 1956 increasingly emphasized national independence. Orbán repeatedly compared the Hungarians’ struggle against Moscow in 1956 to Budapest’s contemporary disputes with the European Union. In late 2018, a monument to Nagy was removed from a square near parliament and later installed elsewhere. The decision drew criticism from the opposition.
After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the memory of the uprising became the subject of fresh disputes: Orbán’s opponents pointed to the contradiction between his reverence for those who fought the Soviet invasion and his warm relations with Putin’s Russia. In September 2024, an adviser to Orbán said that if Russia invaded, Hungary should not follow Ukraine’s example of armed resistance, because the 1956 uprising had ended in tragedy. The remark prompted another wave of criticism. Orbán was forced to distance himself publicly from his adviser’s words, calling them a mistake.
The Hungarian uprising was one of the Cold War’s most dramatic events. It showed how sweeping the demands for change inspired by de-Stalinization could become, and how little change Soviet leaders were willing to allow. When Hungary’s place in the Soviet bloc came under threat, Moscow chose military intervention over political compromise. Despite their public support for the Hungarians, Western countries stopped short of a direct confrontation with the Soviet Union, limiting their response to diplomatic protests and aid for refugees.
The uprising was crushed, but its memory survived and, three decades later, played an important role in the fall of the communist regime. Yet the history of 1956 has not become a national symbol everyone agrees on: Politicians still interpret the uprising’s goals and lessons differently. Hungarians continue to debate what freedom, independence, and resistance to outside pressure mean today.

The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.

articles.title: ‘We Are Christians, Good People’: Russian Media Tycoon Urges Nuclear Strike on Ukraine
articles.body:
Russian nationalist media tycoon Konstantin Malofeyev urged President Vladimir Putin to launch a nuclear strike on Ukraine after a 72-hour evacuation warning, while insisting Russians were “good people” who did not want to kill Ukrainians.
Speaking on Piers Morgan Uncensored, the owner of the pro-Kremlin Tsargrad channel proposed an ultimatum threatening nuclear attacks on sites holding Western weapons in western Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Malofeyev argued that the warning would allow civilians to leave before the strike. He presented the proposed attack as a means of ending Russia’s war against Ukraine.
“We are Christians, we are good people,” he said, describing Ukrainians as fellow Slavs and insisting Russians did not want to kill them.
Morgan challenged that argument: “Good people don’t invade their neighbors.”
Asked to identify something he criticized Putin for, Malofeyev pointed to the Russian leader’s failure to use nuclear weapons.
“And I criticize him for that,” he said.
Earlier call for a tactical nuclear attack
The remarks were not Malofeyev’s first public appeal for a nuclear strike.
In April, he urged the use of tactical nuclear weapons after Ukrainian arms manufacturer Denys Shtilerman discussed developing ballistic missiles capable of reaching Moscow, The Moscow Times reported.
Writing for Tsargrad, Malofeyev expressed concern about potential strikes on the headquarters of Russia’s Federal Security Service, the military’s General Staff and defense manufacturer Almaz-Antey.
443 Drones Downed: Russian Airfield, Chemical Plant and Tax Data Center Targeted in Overnight Attacks
He proposed a nuclear strike on western Ukraine after a 72-hour warning, followed by what he called “denazification,” including public executions of Ukrainian nationalist leaders and officials working for military recruitment centers.
Kyiv Post previously examined Malofeyev’s imperial ambitions, including his relationship with former Russian intelligence officer Igor Girkin and their role in promoting Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Marriage to official wanted by the ICC
Malofeyev is married to Russia’s children’s rights commissioner, Maria Lvova-Belova. He publicly confirmed their marriage in September 2024.
The International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Putin and Lvova-Belova in March 2023 over their alleged responsibility for the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children from occupied territory to Russia.
The warrants concern alleged war crimes and do not constitute convictions. Kyiv Post’s examination of the deportations details the evidence and accountability efforts surrounding Russia’s removal of Ukrainian children.

articles.title: Denmark to buy cheap U.S. cruise missile built in Germany
articles.body:
- Denmark will buy Covenant’s ground-launched Anthem cruise missiles, to be built in Leipzig, Germany, alongside Kongsberg Joint Strike Missiles for its F-35s.
- Germany’s defense ministry is also in talks with Covenant as the Bundeswehr evaluates low-cost cruise missiles for its own long-range strike needs.
Denmark will buy Anthem ground-launched cruise missiles from U.S. defense company Covenant Industries, giving the Danish military its first land-based option for striking targets deep inside enemy territory, the Danish Ministry of Defense announced on Oct. 22, 2026.
The ministry said the purchase is meant to strengthen Denmark’s national and collective deterrence, describing the new missiles as long-range precision weapons that NATO has asked allies to provide. They use advanced navigation to hit targets accurately over long distances and can both deter an attack and strike back deep inside an enemy’s territory if necessary, and the acquisitions follow a recommendation from Denmark’s chief of defense.
“The acquisitions are a significant step in making Denmark better able to defend itself and carry our share of the burden in NATO, and at the same time we are sending a strong signal that we have the ability to strike back,” said Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus, in remarks translated from Danish.
Officials told reporters at the announcement that the contracts have already been signed, but withheld quantities, prices and delivery dates for security reasons. They said one reason for choosing the weapon was that it can be delivered relatively quickly and at a competitive price, and the Anthem missiles for Denmark will be built in Leipzig, Germany, where Covenant is setting up its European production line.
Anthem is a jet-powered cruise missile designed from the start for low cost and mass production. Covenant says it can carry a 200 kg (440-pound) warhead for precision strikes deep in enemy territory, and the missile reportedly has a range of more than 1,000 km (620 miles), with some media reports putting it as high as 1,500 km (930 miles). The company plans to sell it for a six-figure sum, under $1 million per missile, compared with the several million dollars typically charged for comparable cruise missiles.
Anthem first flew in August 2025, and Covenant says it has since been used in more than 200 tests, including several flight tests with U.S. forces in the United States and abroad, although the missile has not yet been used in combat. Choosing it marks a departure for Denmark, which has traditionally bought proven, production-ready systems for its armed forces.
Covenant opened a 10,000-square-meter (108,000-square-foot) plant in Leipzig earlier this month to build missiles for European NATO allies. Production is set to begin in 2027, with the company planning 1,000 missiles in the first year and 5,000 in 2028, and Covenant aims to source more than 95% of the components for its European version from inside Europe, with the Leipzig facility handling assembly and warheads integrated later at customer locations.
Germany is also studying the missile, and the German defense ministry has said it is in talks with Covenant about closing its own long-range strike gap, although no German order has been publicly confirmed. Lt. Gen. Christian Freuding, the head of the German Army, has confirmed that the Bundeswehr wants to buy new low-cost cruise missiles for mass use and is evaluating two systems already on the market, though he did not name them. Anthem has been reported as one of the candidates, alongside the Flamingo cruise missile from Ukrainian company Fire Point, and Covenant has brought in Andreas Marlow, a retired lieutenant general and former deputy commander of the German Army, as an adviser.
Denmark is pairing Anthem with a second, air-launched weapon, the Joint Strike Missile, built by Norway’s Kongsberg with Raytheon. The stealthy JSM fits inside the internal weapons bays of Denmark’s F-35 fighters, weighs 416 kg (917 pounds) with a 120 kg (265-pound) warhead and has a range of more than 350 km (217 miles). It is derived from Kongsberg’s Naval Strike Missile, which Denmark already operates on its frigates and for coastal defense.
Russian Ambassador to Denmark Vladimir Barbin responded quickly to the announcement, saying Danish policy is built on confrontation and preparation for a possible conflict with Russia, and calling it a dangerous illusion to think precision strike weapons could pose a military threat to a nuclear power.
Denmark’s military planning has traditionally focused on defending its own territory, and the new missiles give it a way to strike targets in an adversary’s rear areas for the first time. With Covenant’s Leipzig line due to start production in 2027, the first Anthem missiles for Denmark are expected to come from that plant.

articles.title: Air Defenses at Russian Drone Factory Linked to Forced Labor Rival Putin’s Residence
articles.body:
Russia’s main Shahed drone factory has become one of the country’s most heavily defended sites, alongside President Vladimir Putin’s Valdai residence, according to satellite imagery published on Wednesday, Oct. 21.
The expanding defenses surround the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Tatarstan, where a separate US research report describes forced labor involving North Korean workers and the exploitation of foreign women recruited largely from Africa.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Radio Svoboda identified 33 air-defense positions around the complex, including new concrete towers and raised platforms intended for Pantsir or Tor air-defense systems.
The site also has towers for heavy anti-aircraft machine guns and structures supporting anti-drone barriers over production buildings.
The concentration of defenses puts Alabuga alongside Putin’s Valdai residence, where Radio Svoboda identified 31 towers and two S-300 or S-400 missile positions. The outlet reported more than 100 new air-defense positions across Moscow and the surrounding region since the full-scale invasion. Its findings do not establish a definitive national ranking of the best-protected sites.
Towers, cables and reinforced buildings
An investigation by the Institute for Science and International Security, updated on Sept. 25, used high-resolution Vantor and Airbus imagery to document two defensive perimeters around Alabuga’s production facilities.
Shorter towers surround the main production buildings. A taller outer ring encloses a wider area, including the neighboring Alabuga-Volokno plant, which supplies carbon fiber used in drone manufacturing.
Oleshky Evacuation: Russia Announces Kherson Frontline ‘Silence Regime’
Cables strung between the towers are intended to intercept incoming drones or cruise missiles before they reach the buildings, or force them to fly higher and become more exposed to air defenses, the institute said.
Satellite images also show new production buildings being hardened with layers of earth and reinforced concrete.
Kyiv Post previously reported on Alabuga’s expansion, including new industrial buildings and dormitories for foreign workers.
North Korean workers lose most of their wages
A report published on Oct. 14 by the Center for Strategic and International Studies and the George W. Bush Institute describes Alabuga as a site of human trafficking and serious labor abuses.
The report cites Ukrainian intelligence estimates of up to 12,000 North Korean workers assigned to the complex. Its underlying source, however, is a November 2025 intelligence announcement describing plans to bring in that number, previously covered by Kyiv Post.
The figure therefore should not be treated as an independently verified count of workers currently at the factory.
According to the report, North Korean laborers earn approximately $2.50 an hour, while their government withholds 70–90% of their wages. At that rate, a 12-hour shift would generate $30 before deductions, leaving the worker between $3 and $9.
The authors describe the arrangement as state-sponsored trafficking, with minders restricting workers’ movements and Pyongyang collecting most of their earnings.
The report also notes that the overseas labor arrangement violates UN sanctions requiring countries to repatriate North Korean workers by December 2019.
Foreign recruits promised different jobs
Alabuga also recruits Russian students as young as 15 under a “work experience” program, according to the CSIS–Bush Institute report. They reportedly face long shifts, production quotas and threats of fines if they tell their families what they build.
Foreign women recruited through the Alabuga Start program are promised hospitality jobs, educational opportunities and salaries starting above $500 a month, the report said. Some instead find themselves assigned to weapons production.
Their pay is reduced by deductions for flights, accommodation, medical care and mandatory Russian-language classes. The report also describes passport confiscation, restrictions on movement and threats against workers who discuss their jobs.
Kyiv Post previously reported on African and Asian women misled into assembling drones, drawing on interviews with recruits who said their actual work differed from what they had been promised.
These accounts distinguish between agreeing to travel to Russia for employment and consenting to the work and conditions encountered after arrival.
Expanding production despite Ukrainian strikes
Located more than 1,000 kilometers from Ukraine, Alabuga is a principal Russian production center for Iranian-designed Shahed attack drones and their Russian Geran variants.
The CSIS–Bush Institute report describes a complex capable of producing more than 5,500 drones a month, with extensive construction supporting its growing workforce and output.
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted the site. An April 2024 strike injured 13 students employed at the complex, according to reports at the time.
Ukraine’s General Staff also confirmed a strike on the facility in June 2025. The publicly available reporting does not establish the extent of any lasting reduction in production.
The drones manufactured at Alabuga form part of Russia’s long-range bombardment of Ukraine. The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission recorded 165 civilians killed and 1,119 injured by long-range missiles and drones in September 2026. Those figures cover multiple weapon types and cannot be attributed solely to Alabuga-made drones.
Ukraine has sought US Tomahawk cruise missiles to strengthen its ability to strike military-industrial targets deep inside Russia. President Volodymyr Zelensky pressed the request during his October 2025 visit to Washington, but the meeting ended without a commitment to supply them.
Putin had warned that providing Tomahawks would damage US-Russian relations, while Trump publicly raised concerns about escalation and American stockpiles.
