270 Ukrainian POWs return home in latest swap with Russia
Ukraine and Russia exchanged prisoners of war on Oct. 23, with 270 Ukrainian service members returning home, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced.
The exchange, the first in two months, also saw 270 Russian prisoners of war returned to Russia from Ukrainian captivity.
According to Zelensky, most of the Ukrainians returning home had been captured during the Siege of Mariupol in spring 2022. They included service members from the Ground Forces, Navy, and Air Assault Forces, as well as border guards and fighters from the Azov regiment, which led the city's defense.
Five of the released POWs survived the Olenivka prison massacre in July 2022, when a thermobaric munition was detonated inside a prison barracks housing Ukrainian prisoners of war.
According to Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, a "significant portion" of the released prisoners had been found guilty on sham criminal charges while in Russian captivity.
Seven Ukrainian civilians were also brought back from Russia with the help of Ukrainian authorities on Oct. 23, Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said in a Facebook post. Lubinets added that another seven civilians had traveled to Russia as part of family reunification efforts supported by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).
Zelensky, as well as the Coordination Headquarters later said that nine civilians had been released.
Lubinets called the prisoner exchange "historic," saying it brought home the largest number of convicted Ukrainian service members since 2022: 86 convicted soldiers and one person who had been facing criminal prosecution.
Ukraine, international human rights organizations, and the U.N. have described such trials in Russia as war crimes. The Third Geneva Convention grants POWs protected status under international humanitarian law and prohibits prosecuting them solely for their participation in hostilities, subject to the rules governing lawful combatant conduct.
Lubinets added that the exchange marked the return of Azov Regiment service members for the first time "in a long while."
Two of those released had been held in Russian captivity since 2018 and 2020, spending eight and six years in captivity, respectively, Lubinets said.
The youngest released POW was 24, while the oldest was 63, he added.
While intermittent U.S.-mediated "peace talks" between Russia and Ukraine have failed to secure even a partial ceasefire, prisoner exchanges remain one of the few channels of regular cooperation between Moscow and Kyiv.
The latest swap was the 11th reported prisoner exchange of 2026. The previous two exchanges took place in August.

articles.title: Turkey says renewed attack on Iran would expand conflict, diplomacy only way
articles.body:
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan cautioned on Friday against any renewed attack on Iran, saying such a move would exacerbate tensions and further expand the conflict there, adding that diplomacy and dialogue were the only way to end the war.
Fidan met his counterparts from Egypt, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Germany, France, Britain, and Italy in Istanbul to discuss developments in the Iran war, attacks on Saudi Arabia by Iran-backed Houthis, and Russia's war in Ukraine.
It was the first collective meeting between the countries, comprising the Regional Four (R4) and EU 3 (E3), alongside Italy.
"We are all in agreement that a new attack on Iran would expand the war in the region," Fidan told a press conference after the meeting. "A military intervention on Iran is not in any way a solution. Nobody approves this at the moment," he added.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said after Friday's meetings that renewed escalation between Iran and the United States would only have losers and raise oil prices.
The comments followed a New York Times report on Wednesday that the US and Israeli militaries had drawn up specific plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the US midterm congressional election next month. Citing US officials, it said likely targets would include Iran's energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and its missile and drone arsenal.
Trump says US would not launch attack before midterms
US President Donald Trump said earlier this month that the US would not launch an attack on Iran before the midterms, as Washington and Tehran were having "productive" talks about ending their six-month-old war. On Friday, he said the US could end the war quickly but questioned whether Washington should seek a swift conclusion or allow the conflict to gradually wind down.
NATO member Turkey has been in close contact with Washington, Tehran and regional mediators to seek an end to the war. It has repeatedly called for attacks to stop and warned against the regional expansion of the conflict.
Fidan also said the countries meeting on Friday had discussed possible parameters to ensure the war in Iran does not expand further, but did not elaborate.
Following Friday's meetings, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Germany, France, and Britain were ready to negotiate with Iran to rule out its acquisition of nuclear weapons, while calling for support for Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

articles.title: Peace talks, Zelensky, the EU, ‘political schizophrenia’ and a new Cold War: RT stories that shaped the week
articles.body:
Peace talks, Zelensky, the EU, ‘political schizophrenia’ and a new Cold War: RT stories that shaped the week
Witkoff returns to Russia
US envoy Steve Witkoff arrived in St. Petersburg on Wednesday to present a new set of peace proposals to Russian President Vladimir Putin. As was the case in every round of talks so far, Moscow found little to agree with in the terms put forward by Kiev and its European backers, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov told reporters afterwards.
Although the key issues of the conflict – territory and Ukraine’s neutrality – remain unresolved, Witkoff and Putin pressed ahead with striking their own deals. Russia released US Air Force veteran Stephen Hubbard, who had been convicted on charges of fighting for Ukraine, Putin confirmed his willingness to hold trilateral talks with Washington and Kiev, and within two days of the meeting, the first tanker of diesel fuel left Russia for the US since the so-called “diesel deal” was struck last week.
That the US would even consider meeting with Putin rubbed the Europeans the wrong way. Speaking after Witkoff met Zelensky in Oslo on Tuesday, EU chief diplomat Kaja Kallas accused US President Donald Trump and his envoys of “trying to push Ukraine into surrender.”
Kallas is in an unenviable position. Trump has proven able and willing to negotiate with Putin above the Europeans’ heads, as he did when he waived sanctions on Russian diesel. Faced with the prospect of being cut out of an eventual peace deal, the EU is reportedly searching for an envoy to represent Brussels’ interests at the negotiating table. As anti-Russia hardliners, Kallas and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen have essentially ruled themselves out; French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz are drowning in domestic turmoil and watching their legitimacy collapse in real time; and the supposed ‘compromise candidate’ trumpeted by EU media, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, is a potentially toxic choice.
EU leaders, Putin remarked on Thursday, suffer from “a kind of political schizophrenia.” The Europeans “now go so far as to constantly speak of a ‘Russian threat’ and even discuss preparations for a war with Russia” against the will of their citizens, he explained. “They will hopefully realize that it is better to live in harmony with Russia – a path that truly serves the interests of their own peoples.”
The only European official present at the St. Petersburg meeting was von der Leyen’s chief of staff, Bjorn Seibert.
Zelensky scorned again
Zelensky signaled his disapproval with the Witkoff-Putin meeting in as clear a manner as possible; firing drones at St. Petersburg and the surrounding Leningrad Region. His own meeting with Witkoff in Oslo didn’t go so well either. The New York Times reported that the US envoy “reproached Zelensky for his sharp responses” to Trump’s recent assertion that Zelensky “doesn’t know what he’s talking about,” and “should have this war settled a long time ago.” Zelensky spent the rest of the week trying to dress up a ceasefire as a new idea that hadn’t been discounted dozens of times already by Moscow.
The deepening rift between Kiev and Washington is one of multiple diplomatic crises facing Zelensky.
South Korea pulled diplomats from the Ukrainian capital over Ukraine’s refusal to apologize for exposing the secret transfer of North Korean POWs to Seoul, a move that the South Koreans warned could endanger the POWs’ relatives in North Korea and undermine stability on the Korean Peninsula.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk slammed the Ukrainian government for allowing the city of Lviv to dedicate 2027 to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) and its leader, Nazi collaborator Roman Shukhevich. Tusk, one of Ukraine’s most loyal sponsors, called the move a “suicidal tactic.” The city, a hotbed of nationalism and neo-Nazism, has since reportedly backtracked.
Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) confirmed on Wednesday that it is investigating National Bank of Ukraine chief Andrey Pyshny in a graft probe reportedly aimed at Zelensky’s inner circle. One day earlier, NABU accused Ukraine’s cybersecurity agency of stealing $5 million by purchasing drones at inflated prices.
RT has covered the rampant graft in Kiev extensively in our ‘State of Corruption’ series, which you can read here.
France fails
Just as corruption has come to define Zelensky’s Ukraine, the fiery collapse of the social contract now defines the closing stages of Emmanuel Macron’s presidency in France. After mass protests over rising prices and deteriorating social conditions degenerated into riots last week, almost 3,000 people were arrested this week as violent unrest continued to plague the streets of French cities.
Macron has refused to accept that his migration policies may be to blame for the riots, which Trump claimed are being led by “migrants, jihadists, and communists.” His government has also refused to change course on an austerity budget that will do little to alleviate the protesters’ economic concerns.
Instead, the French president has ordered military personnel into the streets, banned “illegitimate” protests, and imposed localized curfews. Whether he can count on the police to enforce these measures for much longer is unclear: France’s largest police union said on Thursday that it intends to sue the French state for creating the conditions that led to the riots, and leaving officers “betrayed and abandoned” to handle the violence without adequate training or protection.
The EU’s Cold War in the Arctic
The EU updated its Arctic Strategy, insisting the region is “Europe’s Northern Neighborhood” and announced its plan to redraw the map of the northern hemisphere completely. In an ominous document assessed here by RT, the bloc set out plans to build military logistics corridors above the Arctic Circle, develop polar-capable weapons systems, increase surveillance of Russian shipping in the Arctic Ocean, and encourage its member states to hold more military exercises in the frozen north.
The Starlink wars return
The EU and its member states may be Ukraine’s leading backers, but the US provides Zelensky with something that the Europeans don’t have: access to SpaceX’s Starlink satellite constellation. Ukraine depends on Starshield, SpaceX’s military-grade version, to guide its drones, connect to NATO headquarters, and receive real-time updates from Palantir’s battlefield management software.
As long as this dependence exists, the US holds a powerful instrument of leverage over Zelensky. While nobody in SpaceX or the US government has taken responsibility for throttling Ukraine’s access to the network earlier this month, the Wall Street Journal claimed this week that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk – who has condemned Ukraine’s drone strikes on Russian oil refineries – personally ordered that the Ukrainian military’s access to the network be restricted.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied that the government played any role in the slowdown, saying that “it sort of happened” accidentally. However, a turn of phrase by Rubio suggested that the connection problems may have been deliberate, and intended as a warning to Zelensky: “Ukraine,” he said on Wednesday, “would not exist as a sovereign state” without US support.
Moscow is well aware that Kiev uses Starlink to strike civilian targets as well as military ones. Russia’s Investigative Committee confirmed this week that two of the seven drones that struck a female dormitory at a college in Starobelsk in May – killing 21 people – were guided by SpaceX’s network. As long as Kiev continues to use this system, it remains a potential source of escalation between Russia and the US.
What we’re watching
We’re keeping a close eye on three consequential elections over the coming days, starting on Sunday with a presidential election in Brazil and parliamentary elections in Serbia. The showdown between Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro is an intensely personal battle between two bitter rivals, with the potential to pull another Latin American nation into the orbit of the US and reshape the future of the BRICS group.
RT looked at the candidates, the issues, and the competing accusations of corruption and foul play here, and we’ll be analyzing the results by Sunday night.
In Serbia, former President Aleksandar Vucic is now running for prime minister, in a snap election pitting his ruling coalition against a new political faction put together by the organizers of anti-government protests raging in Serbia since 2024. Vucic’s coalition has a narrow lead, but accusations of foreign interference are flying, and we’ll know by Monday whether Vucic’s gambit paid off.
Few world leaders have been as consequential as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Perennially on the verge of prosecution over multiple corruption scandals and facing mass protests, Netanyahu’s political fortunes changed with Hamas’ October 7 attack on Israel in 2023. Three years later, Netanyahu has managed to achieve almost all of his war aims – leveling Gaza, diminishing Hezbollah in Lebanon, neutering Syria, and leading the US into war with Iran.
However, with the Iran war stalled and Netanyahu offering no plan for a post-conflict Gaza, dissent has returned, and polls suggest that his right-wing coalition will fall up to 10 seats short of the 61 needed to govern. The closing of polls on Tuesday night may signal the start of a lengthy process of political horse-trading, with Netanyahu’s future no clearer than it is now.
For more on these stories as they develop, stick with RT.

articles.title: Saudi missile plant expansion may produce more powerful missiles, study says
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia expanding missile plant to build bigger weapons, satellite image researchers believe
- Saudi Arabia appears to be expanding its al-Duwadimi missile plant, with satellite images showing new casting pits and storage buildings for larger solid-fuel missiles.
- US researchers said the work could help Riyadh build longer-range or heavier weapons, boost defence against Iran, and widen its role in the Yemen conflict.
- The move may deepen fears of missile proliferation and increase US political opposition to a Saudi nuclear deal, while the plant could be ready by year-end.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - Saudi Arabia appears to be expanding its ballistic missile factory to build larger solid-fuel missiles that could fly farther or carry heavier payloads, according to two US researchers who analysed more than a year of commercial satellite images.
More capable missiles could help Saudi Arabia to deter attacks by Iran and make its military more self-reliant, while possibly strengthening its position in a deadly conflict with Yemen’s Tehran-backed Houthi fighters.
But they risk fuelling a regional missile race and could deepen opposition in the US Congress to a US-Saudi civilian nuclear agreement that has already raised concerns about proliferation.
Satellite company Planet Labs, based in the US, took images of the al-Duwadimi complex about 200km west of Riyadh between April 2025 and September 2026.
The two researchers, Sam Lair and Michael Duitsman of the Foreign Policy Research Institute, assessed that those images show a new building that houses casting pits - wells in which a mixture of fuel ingredients is poured into missile motor casings and allowed to harden.
The Saudi embassy and Information Ministry did not respond to requests for comment.
The building, flanked by what appear to be walls to protect nearby structures from accidental explosions, is at least twice as large as the one believed to house the plant’s existing casting pits, Lair and Duitsman said in their assessment.
The Foreign Policy Research Institute (FPRI) is a non-partisan research organisation in Philadelphia.
A second new building could be used to store fuel ingredients or finished missile components, they said.
The imagery “suggests that Saudi Arabia is expanding the infrastructure at the missile production complex, likely to produce larger missiles which could deliver larger payloads or reach longer ranges,” they wrote.
Militaries favour solid-fuel missiles because they can be stored for long periods and launched more quickly than liquid-fuel systems.
Lair and Duitsman and experts from the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) and the CNA research and analysis organisation told Reuters that the makeup of Saudi Arabia’s missile force suggests that the al-Duwadimi complex relies on Chinese technology.
Lair and Duitsman said that its characteristics also are similar to Chinese missile plants.
Saudi Arabia secretly acquired about 40 liquid-fuel DF-3 ballistic missiles from China in 1987, according to a 1991 declassified CIA estimate. It displayed two of them for the first time in an April 2014 military parade, according to a Youtube video and photographs of the event.
The FPRI team also recently identified from social media videos and photos what they assessed was the wreckage in Yemen of a Saudi-fired Chinese-designed DF-15 missile.
Lair said the kingdom may now be producing the solid-fuel DF-15, and that the expansion of a1-Dumadimi is likely for the production of the longer-range DF-21 or a similar missile.
Riyadh is believed to have turned to Beijing because Washington has long restricted exports of longer-range missile systems.
The Chinese embassy and defence ministry did not respond to requests for comment.
The CIA declined to comment.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
Missiles would alter balance of power
Sascha Bruchmann, a research fellow at IISS, said longer-range missiles would allow Saudi Arabia to strike Iran without risking its US-supplied F-15 jet fighters against Iranian air defences.
“You’d want a system to threaten whatever is holy to Tehran... if you don’t have the political will to send an F-15 with JDAMs over Tehran,” said Bruchmann, referring to US-made satellite-guided bombs.
“Iran has a lead because its missiles and drones can strike Saudi wherever it wants. The Saudis could close that capability gap a bit.”
Bruchmann, who reviewed the FPRI analysis at Reuters request, concurred that the expansion of al-Duwadimi could be for producing more powerful solid-fuel missiles.
Janes, the defence intelligence company, also reviewed it and said the buildings “may suggest an effort to expand production capability or support the development of longer-range missiles.”
Saudi Arabia’s apparent pursuit of more powerful missiles comes as other Gulf powers are also seeking to expand their offensive and defensive arsenals, said Decker Eveleth, a CNA analyst who has been tracking the al-Duwadimi construction with commercial satellite imagery and concurred with the FPRI assessment.
“This is being replicated across the Middle East,” he said.
“You see exactly the same thing happening in the UAE. You see the exact same thing happening in Turkey. Everybody is doing this now.”
The expansion of al-Duwadimi could have political consequences in the US by stiffening bipartisan congressional opposition to a US-Saudi agreement under which the US would help Riyadh establish uranium enrichment for power generation.
Opponents say that the deal lacks sufficient safeguards to prevent Riyadh from secretly building a nuclear weapon. The kingdom has denied any such plan.
Work on the plant began in 2025
The FPRI assessment said the Planet Labs imagery showed that the expansion at al-Duwadimi began in April 2025 with ground-clearing and digging for the suspected storage building. Work on the suspected casting-pit building began later that month or in early May, it said.
A Dec 12, 2025, photo showed what researchers assessed were two deep pits inside the building that had no roof yet.
A Sept 18, 2026, photo shows the roof still partly missing and “heavy duty blast diverting walls” on either side to prevent accidental explosions from damaging adjacent structures.
The walls, the researchers said, are somewhat similar to those depicted in imagery of US and Iranian missile plants and “further evidence the building is for casting solid propellant motors.”
Finishing the roofs would not take long, the FPRI said, but installing casting equipment may take several months. The facility could be ready to start producing missiles as early as the end of the year. REUTERS

articles.title: Regional powers, European heavyweights meet in Istanbul for 1st joint talks
articles.body:
The R4 meeting was attended by Pakistani Foreign Minister Muhammad Ishaq Dar (2nd L), Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty (L), and Saudi Arabian Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan (R). (AA Photo)
Istanbul hosted high-level diplomatic talks on Oct. 23, bringing together foreign ministers from regional and European powers to discuss the Iran conflict, maritime security, the Palestinian issue and the Russia-Ukraine war. 
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan chaired the inaugural joint meeting of the R4 and E3 diplomatic groups, bringing together Türkiye, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia under the R4 framework, alongside Britain, France and Germany, which constitute the E3.
The Oct. 23 meeting marked the first joint gathering of the two mechanisms, reflecting efforts to expand cooperation between European powers and key regional actors amid mounting geopolitical tensions.
Italian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani was also expected to attend the talks, bringing the number of participating countries to eight.
Fidan held separate meetings in Istanbul with British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Pakistani Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar.
The discussions were scheduled to begin in the R4 format before being expanded to include top diplomats from the E3 group and Italy.
According to Turkish diplomatic sources, Fidan was expected to emphasize that regional security requires countries in the region to assume primary responsibility for addressing their own challenges.
Within this framework, he was expected to highlight Türkiye's commitment to strengthening cooperation mechanisms founded on regional ownership.
Fidan was also expected to stress that existing disputes must not exacerbate one another, conflicts must not spread to new fronts, and regional tensions must not escalate into wider instability.
The Turkish foreign minister was expected to identify Israel's policies toward the Palestinian territories, which he considers an obstacle to peace efforts, and its expanding military actions across the region as major drivers of instability in the Middle East.
Fidan was also expected to underline that tensions between the United States and Iran could be resolved only through diplomacy and dialogue, warning that military approaches fail to deliver lasting solutions and instead deepen regional vulnerabilities.
Ensuring freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on a lasting basis was another key priority on the agenda, given the waterways' significance for regional and global stability.
The discussions were also expected to cover Houthi attacks targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia. Fidan was expected to reaffirm Türkiye's support for Saudi Arabia's security and highlight the principle of collective security and solidarity underpinning the Mecca Defense Agreement.
Ahead of the talks, Miliband's office said the discussions would focus particularly on the Strait of Hormuz and the security situation in Saudi Arabia.
He was also set to warn that Iranian tactics were being replicated elsewhere in the region, with attacks on Saudi Arabia further destabilizing the Middle East and placing additional pressure on strategic maritime routes, including Bab el-Mandeb and the Suez Canal.
The meeting was also expected to address the security implications of the Russia-Ukraine war, particularly the risk of the conflict spreading into the Black Sea.
Fidan was expected to reiterate that Türkiye, as a Black Sea littoral state, would continue presenting proposals to the parties to prevent further escalation and contain the conflict's impact on regional security.
Attacks on commercial vessels, frequently involving drones, have increased in recent months as the conflict has extended its reach across the Black Sea, placing Turkish shipping at growing risk.
Türkiye submitted a proposal to Russia and Ukraine last month aimed at halting attacks on maritime targets. However, strikes have continued in recent weeks, particularly in waters near Romania and Bulgaria.
NATO announced on Oct. 20 that it was deploying additional aircraft, drones and radar systems to the Black Sea to improve regional surveillance and situational awareness through enhanced sensor coverage and greater information-sharing.
The R4 mechanism, established this year by Türkiye, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, is intended to promote lasting regional stability and strengthen dialogue on shared challenges through an approach based on regional ownership.
The four countries have held six foreign ministers' meetings, beginning in Riyadh on March 18, with the most recent taking place in New York on Sept. 21 on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly's high-level week.
The E3, comprising Britain, France and Germany, emerged from diplomatic coordination on Iran's nuclear program launched in 2003. Initially focused on the nuclear issue, the grouping has gradually developed into a platform for joint diplomatic initiatives on a broader range of regional and international matters.

articles.title: Pentagon Bets Big on Drone-Killing APKWS Laser-Guided Rockets
articles.body:
The Pentagon has concluded a new agreement to buy laser-guidance kits that turn rockets into drone-killing weapons.
BAE Systems and the Defense Department announced a framework deal of up to seven years for 25,000 Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System guidance kits annually for the U.S. military.
Another 10,000 kits could be produced each year for international customers, who are increasingly interested in the system.
APKWS is a laser-guidance kit that converts 2.75-inch unguided rockets into precision munitions. It is currently fielded by the U.S. Air Force, Army, Marine Corps, and Navy, as well as U.S. allies.
APKWS has become the preferred method for U.S. warplanes to down drones fired by Iran and Iranian-backed militias in the Middle East over the past few years. But it is not just an air-to-air weapon. APKWS munitions can also be fitted to various platforms for air-to-surface, surface-to-surface, and surface-to-air use.
APKWS is an attractive capability for the Pentagon because of its low cost—roughly $35,000, according to officials. That gives the Air Force a way to shoot down drones without expending costly air-to-air missiles.
For compraison, Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missiles cost roughly $1 million each, and AIM-9s cost hundreds of thousands of dollars depending on the variant. The most capable model is the AIM-9X, which costs around $500,000. APKWS was first tested in an air-to-air role in 2019. The Air Force did not pursue the idea heavily until a few years later, before fielding it in combat in 2024.
“We were on the wrong side of the cost curve in our munitions employment,” former Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. David Allvin said in an interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine.
“The great thing about it is that there wasn’t a formal requirement set out for this. This was sort of organic. People started figuring it out without it being a big program of record,” Allvin added. “Good thing they did.”
Now, just a few years later, the Pentagon is betting big on APKWS’ future.
APKWS scored its first combat air-to-air kill in the fall of 2024 in the Middle East by F-16 from the 510th Fighter Squadron at Aviano Air Base, Italy, current and former officials told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
When the 480th Fighter Squadron from Spangdahlem Air Base, Germany, deployed to the Middle East soon after, they scored dozens more aerial kills—108 in total using all weapons during their deployment.
By the spring of 2025, the Air Force began flight testing APKWS on F-15E Strike Eagles, and fielded the capability in the Middle East within roughly a week. Around the same time, U.S. Air Forces in Europe also fielded APKWS for its air-to-air training. The system has also been on A-10s to shoot down drones.
The APKWS has its origins in the decades-old Hydra rocket system and was first used as precision air-to-ground weapon during the Global War on Terror, deploying in 2012.
It was adapted to serve in an air-to-air role when Air Forces Central, commanded by then-Lt. Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich from 2022-2024, began looking for an alternative to using costly air-to-air missiles against drones. CENTCOM and the Air Force supported the effort.
The framework agreement is intended as a signal of what the Pentagon plans to buy, subject to specific contracts and the congressional funding needs for those deals.
BAE says the new agreement will help expand production at its facilities in Hudson, N.H., and Austin, Texas.
“This agreement highlights the importance of sustained investment in critical munitions to strengthen readiness and equip forces for evolving operational needs,” BAE Systems president and CEO Tom Arseneault said in a statement.
“By securing multiyear demand, this agreement keeps production lines running at capacity, provides our forces with interceptor inventory, and flips the cost calculus in the taxpayer’s favor,” Michael Duffey, undersecretary of defense for acquisition and sustainment, added.
APKWS can also be used in a ground-to-air role, as the modifications needed to hit aerial targets are largery limited to software and the use of a proximity fuse. It can be fitted to anti-air systems such as Sierra Nevada Corporation’s BRAWLR, which is deployed overseas by the U.S. military, and L3Harris’ VAMPIRE, which is used by Ukraine and is being supplied to the U.S. It has been fitted to other nations’ fighter platforms and has been tested on the MQ-9 Reaper as well.
“This drone problem is not going away,” retired Lt. Gen. Derek C. France, who led Air Forces Central from April 2024-August 2026, said in a recent interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine. “It’s accelerating in tactics, speed, advancements, and the numbers. That’s the direction that we’re going.”

articles.title: Finland May Have Quietly Handed Ukraine Its Rare ItO 90M Air Defense Fleet
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Finland May Have Quietly Handed Ukraine Its Rare ItO 90M Air Defense Fleet
A previously undisclosed Finnish air-defense system has appeared in Ukrainian service, revealing that Helsinki quietly transferred rare ItO 90M launchers. These are now being used to defend the country from cruise missiles, aircraft, and Russia’s increasingly fast jet-powered drones.
Ukraine has now publicly confirmed the presence of Finland’s rare ItO 90M systems, showing that the launchers had been transferred without prior announcement and are already integrated into the country’s air-defense network against cruise missiles, aircraft, and jet-powered drones.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Finnish ItO 90M short-range surface-to-air missile system appeared for the first time in footage released by Ukraine’s 1039th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment, according to Defense Express on October 23.
Until now, there had been no public indication that Ukraine had received the system. Finland never announced a transfer, and it remains unclear when the launchers arrived or how many were supplied.
The footage nevertheless indicates that the systems are already operational and being used in Ukraine’s air-defense network.
Finland’s Crotale on wheels
The ItO 90M is essentially Finland’s version of the French Crotale NG air-defense system, mounted on the Sisu XA-181 armored personnel carrier chassis.
Ukraine has already operated French Crotale NG systems since 2022, but the French military uses them primarily in a towed configuration. Finland’s version gives the system significantly greater mobility by integrating it onto an armored vehicle.
Both versions fire the VT-1 interceptor missile.
The missile can engage targets at ranges of up to 15 kilometers and altitudes of around 9 kilometers. It can accelerate to approximately 1,250 meters per second—about Mach 3.6, or roughly 2,800 mph—and carries a 13-kilogram warhead.
Those characteristics make the system suitable for engaging aircraft and helicopters, but Defense Express notes that its capabilities are particularly relevant for Ukraine because it can also intercept cruise missiles and high-speed UAVs, including Russia’s newer jet-powered drones.
Secret transfer of a rare system
The biggest unanswered question is how many ItO 90Ms Finland may have supplied.
Finland acquired just one prototype and 20 production systems during the 1990s, meaning its entire original inventory amounted to only 21 launchers.
Even if all the systems survived and remained serviceable, the fleet was tiny from the outset.
Defense Express therefore raises the possibility that Finland may have chosen to transfer a significant portion—or potentially even its entire remaining ItO 90M inventory—to Ukraine rather than retain a handful of systems requiring their own maintenance, training, and logistical support.
There is currently no confirmation that all 21 were transferred, however, and neither Helsinki nor Kyiv has disclosed the number delivered.
Already defending Ukrainian skies
Whatever the size of the transfer, the first public footage confirms that at least some Finnish ItO 90Ms are no longer sitting in storage or training units—they are already being used by Ukrainian air-defense troops.
Their appearance comes as Ukraine faces a rapidly evolving Russian aerial threat, including faster jet-powered drones that place greater demands on short-range air defenses.
With VT-1 missiles capable of speeds well above Mach 3, the Finnish systems provide another layer between Ukraine’s cheaper interceptor drones and its more expensive long-range air-defense systems.
Previously, reports emerged that Finland is already preparing its 36th military aid package for Ukraine, with a decision on its approval expected before the end of 2026.

articles.title: Europe faces threat of organised sabotage, terrorist attacks: Estonian FM Tsahkna
articles.body:
Europe faces threat of organised sabotage, terrorist attacks: Estonian FM Tsahkna
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
Estonia's counterintelligence service has recently warned that sabotage operations orchestrated by Russian special services have reached a new and dangerous phase in Europe, with targets no longer being purely symbolic. Talking Europe sits down with the country's foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, to discuss the security situation in Estonia and the European Union in general.
Speaking of undercover operations against Estonia attributed to Russian special services, Tsahkna says: "We have witnessed terrorist attacks, sabotage attacks, against the defence industry companies. We just attributed, three weeks ago, one serious attack against our defence industry company organised by the Russian secret services. We caught these three guys. They are in prison now. We see an increase in the number of these attacks. But we also see that they are not against the Baltic States as much as against Europe as a whole. We (in the Baltics) are not at the top of this list. Russia is increasing the pressure on Europe. This is about terror attacks, sabotage attacks, cyberattacks, and any kind of disinformation to divide our unity and to divide our societies as well."
Tsahkna distinguishes between this hybrid war and Russia’s actual military capabilities, which he implies have been degraded by its involvement in Ukraine.
"When I served as a defence minister in 2016-2017, we had permanently 120,000 Russian troops on the other side of our borders, very close, ready to go within 48 hours. These troops were literally sent to Ukraine; they are not existing anymore. They are dead," he says.
Tsahkna goes on: "We know exactly what to do on the military level. We have NATO troops. Actually, French troops are located in Estonia. They are 100 percent integrated with our troops. We have very solid NATO regional defence plans. So this is not the main concern. The main concern now is to keep all of us in Europe united. And we need to understand that [Russian President Vladimir] Putin is testing all of us. He's very carefully watching how we are acting, how united we are, how we are responding."
On diplomatic moves to try to reach a ceasefire in Ukraine, Tsahkna warns that Europe cannot, and should not, become a kind of neutral arbiter.
"Europe is taking part in initiatives, and we just had a meeting in Oslo, together with the US representative and President Zelensky and also the Nordic presidents, prime ministers and the Norwegian prime minister, " Tsahkna says. "So it's not about whether Europe is connected. Of course, we must be there. But we must also understand the position. We cannot let ourselves be dragged into the mediating position that Putin really wants: appointing a special envoy and then trying to mediate between Ukraine and Russia. So we are part of the process, of course, but we are not in the mediating position, a so-called neutral position, in which we would somehow stop our sanctions or give the frozen assets back to Russia. So this is important to understand. "
Tsahkna also has a few observations about the recent protests, violence and unrest in France.
"Elections are coming next year in France that are so important for Europe," he notes. "Of course, using violence is not a solution. And in Estonia we have been paying a lot of attention to keeping our society united, not divided. How to not go to the way of radicalisation. Because divisions in society are making you weaker as a country and as a nation. But of course, it's a matter for France and for the French how to have this dialogue about the future. You know, I'm coming from [the] north. We are very calm people!"
Programme prepared by Oihana Almandoz, Isabelle Romero, Perrine Desplats and Ahmed Hassaine

articles.title: Russian plant supplying components for Iskander missiles reportedly struck by Ukrainian Storm Shadow missiles
articles.body:
Ukrainian missiles reportedly struck a factory in the city of Oryol on 23 October, with OSINT projects reporting that the target was the Proton electronics plant, which produces components used in Russian weapons systems.
The strike comes amid Ukraine’s broader campaign to target Russian military production facilities and other infrastructure supporting Moscow’s war against Ukraine. Ukrainian strikes on such facilities aim to weaken Russia’s ability to manufacture and maintain the weapons it uses in its invasion.
The plant reportedly supplies electronic components for Iskander-M ballistic missiles, which Russia regularly uses to attack Ukrainian cities, as well as other weapons systems, including the Pantsir-S1 air defense system.
The strike could disrupt production supporting Russia’s war effort. Photos show extensive damage to the building. Information about casualties remains unclear.
Plant reportedly produces components for Russian weapons
Proton JSC manufactures semiconductor devices, LEDs, and electronic components for industrial and specialized equipment. According to Exilenova+, the plant’s products are used in the production of Iskander-M ballistic missiles, S-71 Kover missiles, and the Pantsir-S1 air defense system.
Exilenova+ reported that the plant was struck by Storm Shadow cruise missiles. The weapon type has not been independently confirmed, and the extent of damage to the facility remains unknown.
Russian authorities confirm strike on factory
Oryol Oblast Governor Andrey Klychkov announced a missile threat in the region before reporting that missiles had struck a factory in Oryol’s Sovetsky District, according to Liga.net.
Residents reported explosions, a fire in one part of the city, and columns of smoke rising over Oryol, according to local reports cited by OSINT projects Exilenova+, Supernova, and Astra.

articles.title: Russian Iskander parts plant likely hit by cruise missiles
articles.body:
A missile strike likely hit the Proton plant in the Russian city of Orel, a manufacturer of optoelectronic equipment whose components are used in Russia’s Iskander-M ballistic missiles, Pantsir-S1 air defense systems and Kh-71 cruise missiles, according to the monitoring channel Exilenova+.
Local authorities declared an aviation and missile danger alert in Orel during the attack. Information on the extent of the damage at the plant is still being clarified, and the type of weapon used and the exact time of the strike have not yet been confirmed.
The joint-stock company Proton is part of Russia’s defense industry supply chain and produces optoelectronic equipment and components for military use. Its products include diode modules, switch-inverters and electronic components for onboard weapon systems, which are supplied for the production of the 9M723 missiles of the Iskander-M short-range ballistic missile system, the S-71 Kover air-launched cruise missile and the Pantsir-S1, a truck-mounted system that combines anti-aircraft missiles and rapid-fire cannons to shoot down aircraft, drones and cruise missiles.
The Iskander-M is one of Russia’s main weapons for long-range strikes against Ukraine, firing ballistic missiles with a range of up to 500 km (310 miles). The S-71 Kover belongs to a family of newer Russian air-launched cruise missiles, and Ukrainian military intelligence has previously identified the same R500 turbojet engine in the S-71K Kover and the new Filin ground-launched cruise missile, which Russia began using against Ukraine in late summer 2026.
Orel, the capital of Russia’s Orel region about 160 km (100 miles) from the Ukrainian border, has been the target of repeated long-range strikes. On Oct. 31, 2025, the Ukrainian Navy said it hit the city’s thermal power plant with Neptune cruise missiles, and in May 2025 drones struck the Bolkhov semiconductor plant in the same region, which produces components used by Russia’s defense industry.
Ukraine has increasingly targeted Russian plants that build missiles and their components. In August 2026, Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missiles hit the Progress Rocket and Space Center in Samara, and earlier this month the Ukrainian General Staff confirmed a strike on the Redkino Experimental Plant in Tver region, which produces components for cruise missile fuel.

articles.title: Saudi-led coalition intercepts missiles, drones as Houthis report Saudi airstrikes
articles.body:
RIYADH/SANAA, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- The Saudi-led coalition said Friday that it had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles and two drones launched by Yemen's Houthi group toward Saudi Arabia, while Houthi-run al-Masirah TV reported Saudi warplanes carried out a series of airstrikes on Houthi-held areas in Yemen.
Coalition spokesman Turki Al-Maliki said in the afternoon on X that Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis toward Khamis Mushait in the southwest.
Earlier in the day, the coalition said it intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis toward the Saudi capital, Riyadh, as well as two Houthi drones toward the southern region.
Houthi-run al-Masirah TV on Friday reported continued Saudi airstrikes on Houthi-controlled areas, saying three people were killed and nine others injured near the Houthi-held Yemeni capital, Sanaa.
The broadcaster said the casualties occurred when airstrikes "hit a house" in Nihm district, northeast of Sanaa. Citing a local Houthi security official, it said all 12 victims were members of the same family.
Airstrikes were also reported in the northern province of Saada, the western Red Sea province of Hodeidah, and areas in the southwestern province of Taiz, including the port city of Mocha, reported al-Masirah.
The broadcaster also cited a Houthi military source as saying Saudi aircraft struck a lighthouse on Mayyun Island in the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
There was no immediate comment from the Saudi-led coalition and the casualties could not be independently verified.
The exchange of strikes came amid an escalation in the conflict, with Saudi warplanes carrying out strikes deep inside Houthi-held territory and the Houthis launching repeated missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of the country's north, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene the following year in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. ■

articles.title: Trump hints of new strikes on Iran, ministers gather in Istanbul
articles.body:
This live blog has now ended. Make sure to follow us for the latest news on Facebook, X, and Instagram.
Here were the key updates:
US President Donald Trump suggested possible further military action against Iran, claiming that the US has knocked the "hell out" of it
European and Middle Eastern foreign ministers gather in Turkey's Istanbul for security talks on the Strait of Hormuz and various conflicts in the region
Yemen's Taiz faces severe food and water shortages, with the UN warning that aid delivery has halted for about 800,000 residents. Meanwhile, fighting rages between the Iran-backed Houthis and the internationally recognised Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces
Israeli attacks continue on Gaza, occupied West Bank, south Lebanon, and southern Syria despite any claims of a ceasefire
France shooting 'racist, probably Islamophobic' attack
A deadly shooting in a town outside Paris on Friday was "a racist, probably Islamophobic attack," the mayor of Trappes said, as authorities moved to investigate the case as a "terrorist" incident.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, visiting the area where at least two victims were of foreign origin, said the gunman, who killed one person and wounded five others, "clearly" committed "a terrorist crime."
Six killed, 28 injured in attack at Jordan funeral
Six people were killed and 28 wounded in an attack by unidentified assailants during a funeral in Jordan's Karak governorate, the Public Security Directorate said on Friday, after state-owned media had earlier reported that seven people were killed.
Authorities said an investigation was under way and that they would announce its findings as they became available.
US authorises emergency release of up to 400,000 oil barrels
The US Department of Energy said on Friday it had authorised an emergency exchange of up to 400,000 barrels of crude oil from the nation's Strategic Petroleum Reserve to address a supply disruption affecting Phillips 66's Lake Charles refinery in Louisiana.
France's foreign minister said on Friday that any renewed escalation between Iran and the United States would only have losers and raise oil prices.
"A further escalation between Iran and the United States would leave no winners and would likely have very serious consequences for hydrocarbon prices," Jean-Noel Barrot told reporters in Istanbul after a meeting with counterparts from Britain, Germany, Turkey, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia.
UAE closes beach in Sharjah as precaution over oil spill
The United Arab Emirates has temporarily closed Al Hamriyah beach in Sharjah as a precaution against marine pollution from an oil spill involving a tanker, the Sharjah Government Media Bureau said on Friday.
Authorities were taking measures to protect beaches and prevent pollution from reaching the shore and urged fishermen and sea-goers to follow official safety instructions.
The United Arab Emirates has temporarily closed Al Hamriyah beach in Sharjah. [Getty]
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Friday Israel would lock down Hebron in the occupied West Bank, go house to house and demolish homes after the Israeli military said Palestinian attackers killed two soldiers at a military checkpoint near the city.
The Israeli military said it had killed two Palestinians, and another three soldiers had been lightly wounded in the attack.
"We will act to destroy this place, to change it completely," Netanyahu said in a statement after the attack.
Inside Israel's ties with Bosnia's Serb separatists
This statement was hardly surprising. In recent years, Dodik has been outspoken in his support for Israel and its genocidal war on Gaza at a time in which relations between Republika Srpska and Israel are growing.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has invited his Indian counterpart, Narendra Modi, to light a torch alongside Flydubai pilot Smit Machchhar at Israel's so-called 'Independence Day' celebrations next year.
The occasion marks what Palestinians call the Nakba, or "Catastrophe", when Zionist militias carried out mass expulsions of Palestinians to create the state of Israel.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday warned of an imminent large-scale military operation in the occupied West Bank and vowed to displace some residents of Hebron after Palestinian gunmen wounded five Israelis.
Israeli forces "will enter the neighbourhood from which the terrorists came, evacuate the residents, go from house to house, and destroy the terrorist infrastructure", Netanyahu said during a visit to Hebron, according to his office.
"The defence minister and I are considering a very extensive IDF (army) operation in [the West Bank], such as has not been carried out since the Six Day War," he added, referring to the 1967 Arab-Israeli war. "The IDF is ready to execute it and we will set the timing, but it is on the way."
Oil prices traded at five-month highs Friday, with benchmark crude contract Brent North Sea near $115 a barrel, as the Middle East conflict raged on.
Global markets were contending "with concerns around surging oil prices and the sustainability of AI spending", noted AJ Bell head of financial analysis Danni Hewson.
"Oil is at five-month highs amid speculation there may be renewed US-Israeli strikes after next month's US midterm elections.
"Escalating tensions in Ukraine and the prospect of increased energy demand as the northern hemisphere heads into the winter months are only adding to the upwards pressure on oil and gas prices," Hewson added.
UK stocks set for weekly declines as oil prices soar
UK stocks were set for weekly declines on Friday, as oil prices hit over five-month highs this week, weighing heavily on risk appetite, while investors parsed a slew of corporate earnings and economic data through the week.
The blue-chip FTSE 100 index fell 0.5% to 10,670 points by 1020 GMT. The midcap FTSE 250 was up 0.1%, but was set for its sharpest weekly fall in nearly six weeks.
Oil prices hit their highest levels in over five months, with Brent crude trading close to $114 a barrel. This lifted energy shares 2%
US midterms: Where do candidates stand on Gaza and Iran?
The midterm elections in the United States are in full swing, with early voting starting in most states.
The results will set the tone of US foreign and domestic policy for the rest of President Donald Trump's term. Control of both chambers of Congress—the Senate and the House of Representatives—is at stake.
Far-right Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called on Friday for a military campaign in the West Bank "exactly like in Gaza" following a shooting attack that wounded at least five people in the occupied Palestinian territory.
"There is no other option but a comprehensive military campaign in Judea and Samaria to dismantle the Palestinian Authority, collect weapons and eliminate terrorists. Exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon," said Smotrich, who also holds a position within the defence ministry. "In the next government this will be one of the first measures that we must demand and apply."
UNICEF calls on Israel's military to stop killing children
UNICEF called on Israel's military to take immediate steps to stop the killing of children in Gaza, more than a year into a ceasefire.
On Thursday the group said that the total number of children killed has surpassed 350 since Israel and Hamas reached the agreement last October.
“This level of violence against children is unacceptable,” Edouard Beigbeder, UNICEF’s regional director for the Middle East and North Africa, said in a statement. He called on Israeli authorities to take immediate and decisive action to protect children.
Children make up roughly half of Gaza's population. [Getty]
Strikes by Israel's army killed at least one person in southern Gaza Friday morning, according to Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis.
More than 1,500 Palestinians there have been killed by Israel since an alleged ceasefire began in October 2025, according to the Gaza's health ministry.
All 14 Indians in yacht incident off Yemen coast safe
All 14 Indian nationals on a yacht involved in an incident off Yemen's coast are reported safe, the Indian embassy in Yemen said on Friday.
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Thursday they were rescuing a boat carrying 14 Indians that was attacked off Jabal Zuqar island near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, and blamed Saudi Arabia for the attack.
Saudi authorities did not respond to a Reuters request for comment on Thursday.
"Reports suggest that all 14 Indian nationals are safe and located around Hodeidah in Yemen. We will continue to work for ensuring their well being," the Indian embassy in Yemen said in a post on X, without elaborating.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the closure of the occupied West Bank days before Israeli elections after two Palestinian men wounded six Israeli soldiers on Friday before they were killed in a prolonged shootout.
Netanyahu, facing a tight race for a new term in Tuesday's election, claimed that Israeli troops prevented what could have been a "major attack", with the assailants allegedly carrying a large quantity of ammunition in their vehicle.
UAE reports oil spill from tanker as ships attacked
The United Arab Emirates reported an oil spill from a tanker off its coast on Friday, as numerous vessels in Gulf waters come under attack during the US-Israeli war on Iran.
The authorities "detected a tanker oil spill affecting Umm Al Quwain's beaches," the Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said in a statement, referring to an emirate north of Dubai.
It said "teams immediately began containment, cordoning, clean-up and remediation... to limit environmental impacts", adding that the emirate's beaches had been closed.
Many residents in the north of the country have reported oil smells on social media in recent days, including residents in northern districts of Dubai.
Frequent attacks on ships have been reported in recent weeks near the Strait of Hormuz, at the heart of the conflict between Iran and the United States.
The British maritime security agency UKMTO reported on October 9 that a vessel had been hit by a projectile off the UAE coast, causing a fire that was later brought under control.
According to the maritime security company Vanguard, the vessel in question was the oil tanker GEM NO.2, sailing under the Panamanian flag.
Saudi Arabia postpones UN data forum, statistical event
Saudi Arabia's General Authority for Statistics has postponed the United Nations World Data Forum and the Second Saudi Statistical Forum, previously scheduled for 9 to 12 November 2026, in Riyadh, to 2027, it said in a statement on Friday.
The move follows Saudi Arabia's decision on Monday to delay its flagship investment conference to 2027, after deadly attacks in recent weeks linked to the widening conflict set off by the US and Israel's attack on Iran disrupted business activity. The Future Investment Initiative had been due to take place from 26 to 29 October.
The authority said it postponed the UN data forum and the Saudi statistical forum to ensure broad international participation by speakers, experts and partners, and the delivery of an event that meets the expectations of the global data and statistics community.
Several other major events in Saudi Arabia, including the Six Kings Slam tennis tournament and the World Rally Championship's Saudi Arabia round, have also been cancelled or postponed amid escalating attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis.
Far-right Ben-Gvir calls for ending Palestinian Authority
Israel's far-right national security minister called Friday for the dismantling of the Palestinian Authority after an attack by suspected Palestinian assailants in the West Bank left five Israelis injured days ahead of elections.
"We have to act before it's too late. The Palestinian Authority must be dismantled and demilitarised, and its terror infrastructure wiped out completely," Itamar Ben Gvir said in a statement. There was no immediate indication of any Palestinian Authority involvement in the incident.
How an Israeli spyware is threatening global security
Al Jazeera is the latest target of Israeli spyware weaponising digital ads for surveillance, but the attack is just the tip of the iceberg, warns Silverstein.
Israeli troops on Friday shot dead two suspected Palestinians in the occupied West Bank after a shooting at a military checkpoint in Hebron that left at least six Israeli soldiers wounded, officials said.
The incident comes as tensions soar in the occupied West Bank, including over attacks by extremist Israeli settlers against Palestinian olive harvesters, and days ahead of Israeli elections.
US regulator is probing suspicious Iran oil trading
The US Commodity Futures Trading Commission is probing suspicious oil trading activity around the US war in Iran and scrutinizing prediction market trading around elections, the agency's enforcement director said on Thursday at a conference in New York.
CFTC Enforcement Director David Miller made the remarks in response to a Bloomberg News story last week that said a CFTC political appointee had told market surveillance staff to retract a referral to the agency's enforcement team identifying suspicious trading around President Donald Trump's March decision to back away from strikes on Iran's power plants.
When asked about the story during a panel at the conference, Miller said the agency had "from the beginning" been probing the trading and that the investigation remained open.
The report fueled concerns raised by investor advocates and lawmakers over a decline in enforcement activity at the agency, which is dealing with an exodus of staff as it tries to oversee the growing prediction markets industry. Prediction markets allow people to bet on the outcome of various events, from US elections to sports games.

articles.title: This is the fancy new F-16 Ukraine could get. It’s not what its pilots need most.
articles.body:
- Ukraine's air force has discussed the F-16 Block 70/72 with US manufacturer Lockheed Martin, which then gave President Zelenskyy a model of one
- The Block 70/72 is smarter and tougher than Ukraine's ex-European F-16 Block 15 Mid Life Updates, but that doesn't mean the newer model is a major priority
- The Ukrainian air force needs munitions more than it needs new airframes
When Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met a Lockheed Martin team led by Orlando Sanchez Jr., head of its aeronautics division, in Kyiv on 19 October, the talk was of Patriot interceptors and of repairing the Ukrainian air force's small but growing fleet of ex-European F-16 fighters inside the country. Lockheed designed the F-16 and still builds it.
But the Lockheed officials may have had other things on their minds. They gave Zelenskyy a scale model of a new and improved F-16 variant in Ukrainian livery, according to a photo posted by the MilitaryNewsUA account.
In late September, Ukraine's air force commander, Lt. Gen. Anatolii Kryvonozhko, and Lockheed discussed a possible move to newer F-16s. Now we have a clearer idea what those F-16s might look like—and what they might be capable of. The model Lockheed officials gave to Zelenskyy appears to be based on the Block 70/72 version of the classic supersonic fighter that Lockheed manufactures at its factory in Greenville, South Carolina.
It's a world-class jet. But a pricey batch of factory-fresh Block 70/72s isn't actually at the top of the Ukrainian air force's wish list. Not as long as the air force's existing warplanes lack munitions.
The Block 70/72 boasts a better radar, more fuel capacity, and a tougher airframe compared to older F-16 models, which have been flying since the late 1970s. The F-16 is still one of the most numerous fighter types in US Air Force service. Surplus 1980s-vintage F-16s from Denmark and the Netherlands make up the bulk of the Ukrainian air force's front-line fleet. Norway's six are still being refurbished, and Belgium's are coming.
Whether Ukraine ever gets new F-16s is anyone's guess. Kyiv would need to pay around $100 million per copy, or find an ally to finance the purchase. Either could be a heavy lift. And to be sure, Ukraine has options as it rebuilds its battered air force. Sweden is donating 16 older Saab Gripens, the first due early next year, and Kyiv plans to buy 20 newer ones. Kyiv has negotiated to buy 16 Dassault Rafales from France, which may not arrive until 2028. Belgium has promised as many as 53 older F-16s, the last of them perhaps not until 2029.
Welcome jets
But new Block 70/72 F-16s would be welcome. The Block 70/72 builds on what already makes the F-16 great: its agility, flexibility, reliability, excellent electronic warfare systems, and compatibility with a wide array of munitions.
Trending Now
Where the Block 15 Mid Life Update F-16s Ukraine currently flies have the older analog AN/APG-66(V2) radar, the Block 70/72 has a digital APG-83 active electronically scanned array radar. It can also carry overwing conformal fuel tanks for extra range.
Perhaps most exciting for the Ukrainian air force, a newly made Block 70/72 is good for 12,000 hours of flight: enough for about 30 years at 400 flying hours a year. An aging Block 15 has a structural life of about 8,000 hours, and Ukraine's jets fly hard. Zelenskyy has said about half of them spend long stretches abroad for repairs, many at Sabena Aerospace Engineering in Belgium, a process that can take months.
Newer F-16s require less maintenance. They can fly and fight more often. In that sense, 50 Block 70/72s are worth more than 50 Block 15s.
But the availability of airframes isn't the biggest problem in the 107th Aviation Wing, the Ukrainian air force's sole F-16 unit. The wing is desperately low on air-to-air missiles. Its pilots often resort to gunning down Russian drones and cruise missiles with the F-16's built-in 20-mm cannon—a risky tactic given how close a fighter must get to its target to make use of its gun.
While a few billion dollars' worth of fresh F-16s could keep the 107th Aviation Wing in fighting shape for decades to come, fresh airframes aren't actually the most urgent priority. Given a choice between getting new F-16s or getting substantial supplies of missiles for its old F-16s, the wing would surely opt for the latter.
Belgium’s 10 F-16s bring Ukraine’s promised fleet to about 100 jets. Fewer than 40 are flying, as Russia’s jet drones run them ragged
Read Also
- One year of Ukrainian arms exports, and industry has questions: how much army gained, where Berlin office is, who joins joint ventures
- Ukraine’s answer to Russia’s jet Shaheds: a jet drone named Bars, built to strike Russia and now turned around to hunt them
- Belgium’s 10 F-16s bring Ukraine’s promised fleet to about 100 jets. Fewer than 40 are flying, as Russia’s jet drones run them ragged

articles.title: Denmark sends ammo to Ukraine for F-16 guns to down drones
articles.body:
- Denmark delivered more than 50,000 rounds of 20 mm ammunition to Ukraine on an expedited basis for the cannons on its F-16 fighters.
- Ukrainian pilots are already using the rounds to shoot down Russia’s jet-powered Shahed-type attack drones, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said.
Denmark has rushed more than 50,000 rounds of 20 mm ammunition to Ukraine for the cannons on its F-16 fighter jets, and Ukrainian pilots are already firing them at Russia’s jet-powered Shahed-type attack drones, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said on Oct. 23, 2026.
The ministry announced the delivery on X, saying Denmark sent the rounds on an expedited basis in response to a Ukrainian request. It described aviation, and the F-16 in particular, as one of the most effective tools against jet-powered Shaheds, and said destroying them requires sufficient stocks of ammunition.
“We are grateful to Denmark for its quick and effective response to our request for additional ammunition. This speed matters directly for strengthening Ukraine’s air defence and protecting people from Russian air attacks,” said Minister of Defence Evgeniy Khmara.
Every F-16 carries an internal M61A1 Vulcan, a six-barrel rotary cannon that fires about 6,000 rounds per minute. Using the gun against drones lets pilots save their far more expensive guided missiles for cruise missiles and other high-priority targets, and 20 mm rounds are held in much larger quantities around the world than Patriot interceptors or Western air-to-air missiles.
The guns burn through ammunition quickly, with Bloomberg reporting that destroying a single jet-powered drone can take about 150 rounds and that, at the current intensity of Russian attacks, Ukraine could need around 10,000 rounds a day. At that rate, the Danish shipment would cover roughly 330 engagements.
Russia began using jet-powered versions of its Geran drones, the Russian-built derivatives of the Iranian Shahed-136, in significant numbers in early 2026. The newer jet models can carry up to 90 kg (198 pounds) of explosives, fly up to 1,000 km (620 miles) and reach speeds of up to 600 km/h (373 mph), making them much harder to catch than the earlier propeller-driven drones. Ukrainian Air Force spokesman Yurii Ihnat has said Ukraine shoots down about 60% of the jet-powered drones, compared with roughly 90% to 95% for other types.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said combat aviation, primarily the F-16, accounts for 55% to 60% of all intercepts of jet-powered Shaheds, and that Ukraine has expanded contracts to keep its F-16 squadrons supplied with 20 mm rounds. Germany has delivered its first batch of F-16 ammunition for countering the drones, and Belgium and Spain have also sent urgent shipments.
Denmark has been one of Ukraine’s main F-16 partners, pledging 19 of the jets and hosting early training for Ukrainian pilots. Ukraine is also testing several domestically built interceptor drones designed to catch jet-powered Shaheds, while its F-16 pilots continue to use their cannons against the drones with the new Danish rounds.

articles.title: Russia may stage sabotage in Eastern Europe, but wants Kyiv blamed, Ukraine’s Intelligence warns
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) warned that Russia may stage sabotage in Central and Eastern Europe, including the Baltic states, and blame Ukraine for the attacks, in a Telegram post on 23 October.
The warning comes three days after The Wall Street Journal reported that US intelligence traces Europe’s sabotage wave to Putin’s personal order. If Russia stages new attacks and pins them on Ukraine, as HUR warns, European anger could turn on Kyiv rather than the Kremlin. This goes further than HUR’s statement on 2 October, which named potential Russian targets in Europe but did not mention a plan to blame Ukraine for attacks.
HUR says Moscow wants to discredit Ukraine’s army
Russia is stepping up its hybrid strategy to destabilize the European Union, according to HUR. The agency identified two aims: reducing foreign support for Ukraine by discrediting its Defense Forces, and intimidating European governments and societies.
The accusations would be spread through Russian propaganda channels and international platforms accessible to the Kremlin.
Potential targets include infrastructure and Russian Orthodox Church sites
HUR listed several potential targets for Russian provocations:
- critical infrastructure and areas bordering Russia;
- the Kaliningrad exclave;
- areas of EU countries with Russian-speaking populations;
- Kremlin-controlled sites, including properties belonging to the Russian Orthodox Church network;
- historical sites associated with Russia.
The list reflects HUR’s assessment of potential targets, not confirmation that attacks at these locations are planned.
Earlier warnings and reported sabotage
On 2 October, HUR said Russian intelligence services had been ordered to increase activity in EU and NATO countries. It named military facilities, critical infrastructure, communications systems, and Starlink ground stations as potential targets and said it had alerted partners.
Warnings of Russian false flags on NATO’s eastern flank predate HUR’s. In August, Bloomberg reported, citing an unnamed European intelligence official, that Russia might expand hybrid attacks against Poland and the Baltic states, including false-flag attacks. A European government official separately told the agency that the CIA had warned countries in the region of a possible Russian attack. Lithuania’s military intelligence had warned earlier in August that Moscow might reassemble captured Ukrainian drones for false-flag strikes on critical infrastructure in the Baltic region.
Meanwhile, The Wall Street Journal reported on 20 October that US intelligence agencies believe the attempted drone attack on Leipzig-Halle Airport in Germany in early August was among the opening shots of a sabotage campaign ordered by Russian President Vladimir Putin. The Journal cited European officials briefed on the intelligence findings.
According to the newspaper, at least three drones carrying military-grade Semtex explosives were involved. One struck an Antonov cargo plane used to transport military aid to Ukraine but failed to explode. Another collided with a different aircraft, while a third detonated near the airport perimeter. German newspaper Welt am Sonntag has since named two suspects, citing German investigation files. Earlier German media reports described the sequence differently.
The Journal also reported sabotage attacks on Starlink stations in Poland, Lithuania, and Bulgaria in recent weeks. In August, Slovak authorities said they had foiled a planned arson attack on a Ukrainian drone factory, the Journal reported.
Russia denies involvement in sabotage in Europe. Responding to Berlin’s accusations over the Leipzig incident in early September, Putin asked where the evidence was.

articles.title: A modem from a Russian drone led reporters to its Chinese maker—which invoiced 500 for Russia’s drone plant
articles.body:
Undercover reporters ordered 500 drone mesh modems from a Chinese firm, which billed them to Russia’s Alabuga drone plant, investigation by The Insider found. The outlet estimates the firm makes about half the high-power mesh modems that let Russia steer its drones deep into Ukraine. The firm’s director also named US company AMD as the source of a key chip, and AMD says it has not sold to the firm.
Geran drones and Banderol drone-missiles have become Russia’s main weapons against Ukraine’s energy grid. Russia began this winter’s strike campaign against that grid in late September, ISW assessed. Ukrainians’ survival this winter depends largely on how fast the West halts mesh modem sales to Russia, the outlet argued.
What a mesh modem does
A mesh modem links drones into one radio network. Each unit relays data for the others, so if one drone is shot down, traffic reroutes through the rest. Information keeps flowing even if nearly 80% of the drones are downed, Ukrainian defense adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov said in November 2025.
Range is the other half of the threat. One XK F-359 holds a line-of-sight link over 100–300 km, The Insider says. In theory, a couple of relay drones could keep a whole attack on Kyiv connected. Operators can then send new commands in flight and steer around air defenses. Russia’s Gerbera drones, first built as cheap decoys, increasingly carry these modems.
A modem from an upgraded Gerbera
To trace the part, The Insider’s correspondent in Ukraine examined an unmarked mesh modem from an upgraded Gerbera with a vertical tail fin, a version that appeared this summer. The outlet identified it as Xingkai’s XK F-359, the part Ukrainian intelligence and earlier reporting, Euromaidan Press included, had logged as the XK-F358. The Insider calls that label a misidentification.
Next, The Insider and the Nordsint investigative project contacted Xingkai on WeChat, posing as a Russian military supplier based in Alabuga. A company employee who introduced himself as “Jack Jiang” confirmed the firm is the model’s sole maker. The Insider identified him as Jiang Qin, Xingkai’s director and owner.
500 modems, three banks
The reporters then ordered 500 units for delivery to Alabuga, home to the plant that makes most of Russia’s long-range drones. Jiang invoiced 19.5 million yuan, which The Insider put at about $2.87 million. He offered two ways to pay: dollars to Xingkai’s DBS Bank account in Hong Kong, or yuan to his personal Ping An Bank account.
America has sided with Russia against Ukraine. Europe should stop pretending and build a coalition against Russia, China, and even the US
In the chat, the reporters said outright that the end user was a military production facility. Jiang raised no objection, The Insider reported.
Later, after the reporters asked to update the address, Xingkai sent a revised invoice with “Alabuga” spelled in Latin letters. This time, it routed payment to a China Merchants Bank account in the name of a former Xingkai manager. She left a management post at the company in 2025, according to Tesari corporate records cited by The Insider. None of the three banks answered The Insider’s requests for comment.
Jiang also claimed the modem’s programmable chip is made by AMD. Asked for an AMD license, he refused, saying Xingkai buys the chips through a middleman. AMD told The Insider that Xingkai “is not an AMD customer or authorized partner,” and said it had sold the company nothing. AMD added that it bars exports of its products to Russia that violate US export controls and sanctions.

articles.title: Total of 165 combat clashes occur on battlefield – Ukraine's General Staff
articles.body:

Details: On the North Slobozhanshchyna front, the Russians conducted two attacks near the settlements of Ulanove and Korchakivka.
On the South Slobozhanshchyna front, Ukraine's defence forces repelled 14 Russian attacks near the settlements of Kovalivka, Anyshchyne, Izbytske, Radkivka and Vilkhuvatka.
On the Kupiansk front, one Russian attack occurred near the village of Petropavlivka.
On the Lyman front, Ukraine's defence forces repelled five Russian attacks near the settlements of Katerynivka, Kolodiazi and Lyman.
On the Sloviansk front, the Russians conducted one attack near the town of Mykolaivka.
On the Kostiantynivka front, 11 Russian attacks occurred near the settlements of Druzhkivka, Novoselivka, Kostiantynivka, Dovha Balka and Pavlivka.
On the Pokrovsk front, Ukraine's defence forces stopped 15 Russian assaults near the settlements of Serhiivka, Molodetske and Novopavlivka and towards Kucheriv Yar, Svitle, Sofiivka, Vilne, Novyi Donbas and Myrne.
On the Huliaipole front, Ukrainian forces repelled 12 Russian attacks near the settlements of Charivne, Ternuvate, Verkhnia Tersa, Kosivtseve, Vozdvyzhivka, Kopani, Novoselivka and Bilohiria.
On the Orikhiv front, Ukrainian defenders repelled one Russian attack near the village of Lukianivske.
On the Oleksandrivka, Kramatorsk and Prydniprovske fronts, the Russians did not conduct active offensive actions.
