articles.title: Are Israel's drones signalling a new escalation with Hezbollah?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Are Israel's drones over Beirut signalling a coming escalation with Hezbollah?
Reports of increased Israeli drone activity over Beirut and its southern suburbs have raised questions about whether Israel is preparing for a new escalation against Hezbollah.
But while the flights have become more conspicuous in recent days, analysts told The New Arab that their presence alone does not establish that a wider offensive is imminent.
A report by local Lebanese news outlet Lebanon Files said Israeli reconnaissance flights had "returned" to Beirut and Mount Lebanon’s airspace. However, there is no publicly available evidence establishing that the flights had stopped before recently becoming more noticeable.
Israeli drones have continued to be reported over Beirut and its southern suburbs in recent months, including in reports published in September and footage circulated this week.
The question, therefore, is not simply whether the drones are present, but whether there has been a meaningful change in the frequency, duration or scope of their operations.
Surveillance and pressure on Hezbollah
Elijah J. Magnier, a veteran war correspondent and political analyst, told The New Arab that the activity should be taken seriously, while cautioning against treating visible drone flights as evidence of an imminent attack.
"Local reporting today documented a drone flying at low altitude over the southern suburbs. That establishes a visible presence; it does not, by itself, establish a sustained increase in surveillance or an imminent offensive," he said in comments to The New Arab on 21 October.
Magnier said Israeli drone flights could serve several purposes at once, including gathering intelligence, updating potential targets, monitoring movements and exerting psychological pressure on residents. A conspicuous presence over the capital can also serve as a reminder of Israel’s ability to strike south of Beirut.
If Israel were preparing another operation, surveillance could help it locate commanders, monitor weapons movements and identify suspected military infrastructure. But Magnier stressed that these remained possible objectives rather than evidence of a decision to launch an attack.
"Nor does identifying a target establish that a political decision to strike has been taken," he said. Without comparative flight data or intelligence about operational orders, he added, it was difficult to distinguish routine surveillance from preparations for a particular attack.
Nasser Khdour, an analyst at the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), also said Israeli drone activity over Beirut was not new.
"Israel has continued gathering intelligence and identifying possible targets in preparation for another round of fighting," he told The New Arab.
Khdour suggested the more conspicuous drone presence was likely intended to increase pressure on Hezbollah and the Lebanese government during negotiations between Lebanon and Israel, with the Iran-backed militant group’s disarmament remaining a central point of disagreement.
The latest round of US-mediated military talks between Lebanese and Israeli delegations began in Tampa, Florida, on 20 October. The talks came amid continued Israeli attacks and demolitions in southern Lebanon, as well as renewed threats by Israeli officials against Hezbollah.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has warned Hezbollah against joining Iran in an attack on Israel, threatening a "powerful response" against Beirut’s southern suburbs, which would include a forced evacuation of the whole area. He has also threatened to expand the invasion towards Nabatieh and the Litani River in the south.
Hezbollah has refused to disarm as long as Israeli forces remain in Lebanon.
Could tensions with Iran draw Hezbollah into a wider war?
The risk of escalation also extends beyond Lebanon. With Israel’s general election scheduled for 27 October, renewed threats involving Iran have added another layer of uncertainty to the regional picture.
Magnier said electoral considerations were relevant to the analysis, but cautioned against presenting speculation about a war being launched for political reasons as an established plan. He said there was no publicly established evidence that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu intended to initiate a war to disrupt an election he expected to lose.
A renewed confrontation between Israel and Iran could, however, create a separate decision point for Hezbollah. Magnier said the group’s involvement would become a more serious possibility in such a scenario, but would remain a choice rather than an automatic consequence.
He also cautioned against assuming that Hezbollah’s weakened deterrence meant it had no remaining military capabilities. The group could seek to preserve its personnel and organisational structure while continuing to impose costs on Israel over time, rather than responding to every attack with a major escalation.
That calculation could change, he added, if civilian casualties mounted, senior leaders were targeted or Israel expanded its ground operations.
The conflict between Hezbollah and Israel began in October 2023 and was dramatically escalated by Israel into a full-scale war in September 2024. Fighting resumed on 2 March this year, alongside the US-Israeli war on Iran. Much of Hezbollah’s senior command structure has been eliminated over the past three years, and thousands of its fighters are believed to have been killed.
The drone flights therefore need to be viewed alongside the wider military and political context, rather than in isolation. Israel’s continued strikes, its threats against Beirut’s southern suburbs and the unresolved dispute over Hezbollah’s weapons all contribute to an already volatile situation.
For Magnier, the distinction remains between sustained pressure and a decision to launch a broader campaign. The visible presence of drones demonstrates Israel’s ability to monitor and threaten Hezbollah and its stronghold in Beirut's southern suburbs, but it does not reveal what Israeli leaders intend to do next.
"The drone flights show exposure and pressure. They do not yet tell us whether the next step will be surveillance, a targeted strike or a wider campaign," he said.

articles.title: Inside Russia’s School-to-War Pipeline, Where Students Help Build Drones and Ammunition
articles.body:
- Category
- Investigations
Inside Russia’s School-to-War Pipeline, Where Students Help Build Drones and Ammunition
Students at no fewer than 40 civilian educational institutions across Russia are helping produce military drones and munition components, according to an investigation by Vot Tak published on October 22.
The outlet noted that 33 universities, 5 colleges and 2 technical schools were involved. Participants include not only future engineers but also lawyers, political scientists, teachers and agronomists.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
One of them, 19-year-old Nikita Kazakevich, studies agricultural machinery repair at a technical college in Nazarovo, Krasnoyarsk region. Outside class, he assembles FPV attack drones that are shipped to the front.
“Then these drones are sent to our army, to Donetsk and Luhansk,” Kazakevich told Vot Tak.
Vot Tak noted that the college has assembled the drones since January 2025 from nine-inch carbon frames delivered to the school. Students install electronics and motors, program the aircraft and test-fly them in the gym. Kazakevich explained that he can build one in about half an hour.
Shipments leave every month, he added, with nine drones sent in September. Students are not paid, but teachers reward participation with good grades and sometimes release them from lessons.
The drone assembly program at the technical college in Nazarovo began when Alexei Yolkin, head of a local veterans' organization, was asked by troops for quadcopters. Alexander Aul, a former director of a local insulation plant, buys the frame kits. According to Kazakevich, local Cossacks also help deliver the finished drones. Vot Tak requested interviews with 18 students involved in such work, and only two agreed.
The practice extends well beyond extracurricular workshops. In March 2023, a bakery in Tambov began producing Bekas suicide drones , and students of a local transport college joined within weeks, according to local media.
Vot Tak wrote that production left the bakery in early 2024, and the business closed in July 2026 amid falling demand. The technology was transferred to India, and the EU sanctioned the producer the same month.
Other students are employed rather than volunteering. Under Rostec's “Wings of Rostec” program, launched in 2020, participants work at partner enterprises from their first year and receive a salary plus stipends. Rostec deputy director general Nikolai Volobuev stated that drones are a priority through 2036.
In August 2026, the Moscow Aviation Institute and Rostec completed their first intake for a drone-design degree, with 17 of 60 state-funded places going to program participants. The Kalashnikov plant in Izhevsk joined the list of partners in 2026.
The People's Front movement acts as an intermediary, Vot Tak found, working with at least 11 civilian institutions. It supplies 3D printers and plastic so students can print tail sections, striker parts and electronic drop mechanisms for VOG-17 grenade rounds. By March 2026, Volga State University of Technology had sent 2,500 sets of VOG-17 parts to the front, the university stated.
Some students go further than assembly. Sergei Berstnev, 25, designed the "Russian Mavic" strike drone while studying at Vladimir State University. Vot Tak established that operators of the 28th motorized rifle regiment used one to destroy a building in the Kherson region. Berstnev, who is listed in the Myrotvorets database, told the outlet that Russian security services monitor his team and warned him against publicity.
Student design bureaus follow a similar pattern. At Pacific National University in Khabarovsk, the PolitechProm bureau builds suicide drones, and its members include students of the university's law institute and its institute of social and political technologies. Vot Tak found comparable bureaus in Korolyov, Tomsk and Ulan-Ude.
Universities often leave frontline use off their websites. In Ulan-Ude, graduates made propellers for the Burya-10 drone system. Buryatia deputy premier Ivan Alkheev confirmed in January 2025 that 21 such complexes had been handed over to the combat zone, with three more being transferred. The university's website still contains no mention of this.
The use of students in weapons production has a precedent at the Alabuga complex in Tatarstan, Russia's largest drone-production site.
Ukraine first struck Alabuga in April 2024, when a drone hit a dormitory at its “Alabuga Polytech” college. Students there, including minors, have been drawn into assembling Geran drones. Russian authorities have also used an international youth festival in Yekaterinburg to promote the college to foreign visitors, promising rapid employment.
Discuss this article:

articles.title: Witkoff Meets Putin: the Upshot?
articles.body:
Following the meeting between Vladimir Putin and US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg, talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US are set to resume. However, Witkoff describing Putin as a “humanitarian” during the meeting has drawn criticism even from US Republicans. The press looks at who stands to benefit from Trump’s attempts at mediation.
Embarrassing and incompetent
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Der Standard (Austria) takes issue with the American special envoy’s fawning praise of Putin:
“No one has ever called him that before. That’s a first. How will Vladimir Putin react to Donald Trump’s envoy, Steve Witkoff, calling him a ‘humanitarian’? Witkoff is a property developer and Trump’s golfing buddy, and together with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, he keeps meeting up with Russian envoys and Putin himself in a bid to end the war in Ukraine. Two wheeler-dealers with no clue about foreign policy who have achieved absolutely nothing so far.”
Kremlin relying on attrition
The US’s haste risks rewarding Russia for its patient strategy, La Stampa (Italy) warns:
“Putin can already derive political advantages from the negotiations, without having to halt the war. Winter will put this strategy to the test. Moscow will seek to weaken Ukraine while the Ukrainians try to protect their cities and hold the front line. In the meantime, acts of sabotage, cyber-attacks and disinformation aim to undermine European unity and the consensus on aid to Ukraine. Putin is banking on wearing down Ukrainian resistance and the West’s willingness to support Ukraine.”
US Reportedly Plans to ‘Offer’ Ukraine EU Membership for Dropping NATO Bid
Russia’s victory by no means certain
Ukraine is not about to throw in the towel, says Aamulehti (Finland):
“Even if the United States were to side fully with Russia, the war in Ukraine would not end. The massacre in Bucha has shown what happens to Ukrainians at the hands of the Russians, which is why Ukraine will not give up the fight. How long would the war last, and how would it end? Recent history answers that question. France waged war in Indochina for eight years. The US fought the Vietnam War in that region for 20 years, ten of which with its own troops. The Soviet Union waged war in Afghanistan for ten years, and the US for twenty. Each of these wars ended in defeat for the major power waging the war.”
Diabolical old men
Writing on Facebook, author Carina Cockrell-Ferre (Russia) discusses the possibility of a Russian attack on Europe:
“The greatest danger facing Europe is that Putin could form a full alliance with Trump, who then assures him that he will not honour the terms of Article 5 of the Nato Treaty. ... This could indeed lead to a Russian attack on Europe. This is the common ground over which these two diabolical old men have joined forces. ... While Europe may be able to block a bad deal for Ukraine, it is powerless to push through a good one. All it can do is delay a Russian attack on Europe by supporting Ukraine and its armed forces.”
Kremlin giving no sign of being ready to negotiate
Future meetings are also unlikely to yield any tangible results, The Spectator observes (Germany):
“There has been nothing to suggest yet that the Russian president is genuinely ready to make a deal or concede on his war aims. ... Facing the prospect of brutal midterm results for the Republicans in two weeks’ time, Trump is desperate for a win with Russia. Putin can sense this and appears to be using this to play for time ahead of a winter in which he hopes to make substantial progress on subjugating Ukraine. Not for the first time, it is Zelensky who is being forced to jump through hoops and show willing in the hope that doing so will save his country from a stitch-up by an enemy and supposed ally.”
Encouraged to escalate
The US’s policies of recent weeks are having repercussions across the world, the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (Germany) points out:
“Putin and his inner circle are convinced that in the war against Ukraine and their struggle against the West as a whole, they will firstly have the greater staying power, and secondly be able to play the Americans and Europeans off against one another. Everything the American leadership has done in recent weeks confirms this belief. Consequently, the prospect of a ceasefire, not to mention peace in Ukraine, has become even more remote. Instead, the Kremlin is likely to feel emboldened to escalate the conflict even further. ‘Restoring justice of Russians’ takes place above all on the battlefield, Putin’s foreign minister has said.”
Moscow can take its time
Unlike Trump, Putin is not in a hurry, notes Corriere della Sera (Italy):
“For five years now, Vladimir Putin seems to have been applying the old Russian proverb ‘The slower you go, the further you’ll get’ to a war that he originally thought would last no more than two weeks. … So Putin is biding his time, waiting to see how events unfold and what happens with the elections in the US and Europe – and taking whatever he can get without making any concessions. He has the chance to achieve in Washington what he is unable to achieve on the front line; but he also knows that this window of opportunity could be closed again by a single social media post in the middle of the night. ... What the Russian president needs to work out now is whether the path available to Trump will be long enough.”
Trump wanted Putin to win all along
The US President’s supposedly new stance on the war in Ukraine is not really new at all, argues Dagens Nyheter (Sweden):
“Some interpret this as the US changing sides with regard to Ukraine, and it’s easy to understand why Zelensky feels betrayed. Yet this development is nothing new. The difference is that Trump is no longer making a secret of what he has wanted all along: for Russia and his friend Vladimir Putin to win the war. ... Trump’s eagerness to help Putin now is particularly good news for the Kremlin. Russia is in a bad way, both on the front line and at home, where all its oil depots are burning. So it’s good that it has an ally in the White House.”
What is going on in his mind?
Experts will continue to puzzle over the US president’s policy on Ukraine, says Ilta-Sanomat (Finland):
“A clear intention can certainly be discerned behind Trump’s confused remarks on Ukraine and Russia. He wants to take credit for bringing about peace. But does anyone still believe he could actually achieve such a thing? After all this, can anyone still trust Trump’s word when it comes, for example, to security guarantees for Ukraine, which are a key safeguard for peace? ... When the war in Ukraine eventually ends and Trump is no longer president, a lot will be written about current events. Perhaps the most important question then will be: what on earth was going through Trump’s mind? It won’t make for pleasant reading.”

articles.title: France and UK Simulated a Nuclear Strike
articles.body:
French and British fighter jets simulated a nuclear strike over the Mediterranean Sea in the first joint exercise involving France’s airborne nuclear capabilities, Paris announced, as the two allies deepen military cooperation amid tensions with Russia, Reuters reported.
The exercise followed an agreement reached by France and the United Kingdom in July 2025 to strengthen cooperation on their nuclear arsenals in response to growing threats to Europe and uncertainty over their shared ally, the United States.
French Minister of the Armed Forces Catherine Vautrin said the two countries could coordinate their nuclear forces while maintaining their independence.
“Our nuclear cooperation with the UK continues to deepen: on Tuesday evening, British Typhoon fighter jets participated for the first time in a French nuclear exercise alongside Rafale aircraft,” Vautrin added.
According to a statement from the French Ministry of the Armed Forces, French jets took off from Saint-Dizier airbase in northeastern France, accompanied by British Typhoon fighters, and simulated a nuclear strike during the exercise, codenamed “Rummy.”
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said the joint mission demonstrated the allies’ commitment to European security.
“In an increasingly dangerous world, our adversaries must be left in no doubt: the UK and France are united in their commitment to European security and to maintaining the deterrence that has helped preserve peace for generations,” Streeting said.
French President Emmanuel Macron announced in March that France would increase its nuclear arsenal. He also launched an initiative enabling European partners to take part in joint exercises and potentially host French nuclear-capable military assets on their territory for short periods.
France spends approximately 5.6 billion euros annually maintaining its stockpile of around 290 nuclear warheads, which can be deployed from submarines and aircraft. According to Reuters, France has the world’s fourth-largest nuclear arsenal.
The United Kingdom possesses 225 nuclear warheads, while Russia and the United States each have more than 5,000.

articles.title: World News in Brief: Iran nuclear inspections, deadly church attack in Jordan, El Fasher – one year on
articles.body:
World News in Brief: Iran nuclear inspections, deadly church attack in Jordan, El Fasher – one year on
The head of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Rafael Grossi, called on Friday for a swift return of inspectors to Iran, warning of growing fragility in the global nuclear non-proliferation regime.
The technical groundwork has been done and “the bases on which a diplomatic agreement could be concluded exist,” he told the UN General Assembly.
He urged the parties to “redouble efforts”, adding that inspectors’ return “requires a return to the negotiating table”.
Iran has sharply restricted access since the June 2025 strikes on its nuclear sites during a 12-day war with Israel.
Non-compliance concerns
The IAEA estimated in March that just over 200 kilogrammes of uranium enriched to 60 per cent remained at Isfahan, with more at Natanz.
In September, the agency’s board of governors referred Iran’s non-compliance to the Security Council, which Tehran contests.
“The global non-proliferation regime…depends on dialogue,” Mr. Grossi said, pointing to successful efforts in Syria and war-torn Ukraine, where IAEA has brokered eight localised ceasefires to repair power lines at the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant and deployed 287 missions since Russia launched a full-scale invasion in 2022.
UN chief condemns deadly church attack in Jordan
The UN chief António Guterres on Friday strongly condemned a deadly attack on a church in Hmoud, Jordan.
The terrorist attack on a funeral service at a church in Hmoud in Jordan left seven people dead and many more injured, UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said.
“The Secretary-General expresses his deep condolences to the families of the victims and wishes a speedy recovery to all those injured,” he added.
“An attack not only on a place of worship but during a funeral procession, is especially heinous.”
The Secretary-General also called for all those responsible to be found and to be held accountable, Mr. Dujarric said.
“Attacks against civilians and places of worship are unacceptable,” he said. “Places of worship must be places of peace and must be safe for all.”
Read his full statement here.
Sudan’s El Fasher survivors, one year since city fell
One year since paramilitary forces rampaged through Sudan’s El Fasher, the legacy of fear and trauma continues to haunt thousands of survivors.
That’s the message from gender equality agency UN Women, which reported that nine in 10 Sudanese aid organizations it surveyed had found women or girls in distress who had received no mental health, psychosocial or legal support since fleeing the Darfuri city.
The war in Sudan erupted in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), former allies who had jointly seized power in a 2021 coup.
On Friday, UN Women regional director Anna Mutavati told reporters in Geneva that some people have started to return, “but the fear of violence is constant”.
‘Scars have not faded’
“The scars of the violence in El Fasher have not faded,” she said. “Women and girls continue to live with the trauma of sexual violence, the disappearance of their daughters, their sisters, their mothers, their husbands, and their sons, the killing of family members, and the loss of their homes, property, and livelihoods.”
Reports of deadly strikes on civilians, rape and violence continue, said Ms. Mutavati, emphasising that drone attacks are increasing across Blue Nile, Khartoum, West Kordofan, Gedaref and Kassala.
“Most of those killed or injured are women and children,” she said. “Many had already fled violence, including sexual violence.”

articles.title: Radev Blasts the European Parliament for “Dictating” to Bulgaria
articles.body:
Prime Minister Rumen Radev has sent an open letter to political groups in the European Parliament (EP), accusing Bulgarian MEPs of using the institution for a domestic election campaign after a resolution criticized Sofia’s response to drone attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea, the government press service said.
Addressed to the EP political groups through Parliament President Roberta Metsola, the letter challenges the last-minute addition of what Radev calls baseless and manipulative allegations against the Bulgarian government to a resolution expressing solidarity with Bulgaria’s investigation into the attacks and its efforts to rescue endangered crews.
The resolution, adopted with 432 votes in favor, 52 against and 88 abstentions, expresses concern over what MEPs describe as Sofia’s hesitant diplomatic response to Russia and calls on Bulgaria to confirm its participation in a NATO initiative to counter drones by October 30. The document is not legally binding.
Radev said the addition of Point 6, formally proposed by the Greens, undermines the resolution’s earlier recognition of Bulgaria’s rapid response and rescue operations. The provision alleges a weak diplomatic reaction toward Russia and a lack of concrete action.
The prime minister said it was regrettable that Bulgarian MEPs had submitted the resolution, naming Andrey Novakov, Andrey Kovatchev, Eva Maydell, Emil Radev, Iliya Lazarov, Radan Kanev and Ilhan Kyuchyuk among those involved.
"It is absurd for Members of the European Parliament to call upon us to join NATO’s anti-drone initiative, given that the Bulgarian Minister of Defence has already announced the decision for Bulgaria to join it," Radev said in the letter. He added that the initiative had been announced in February 2025, but governments associated with the MEPs now pressing for Bulgaria’s participation had done nothing to facilitate it.
The prime minister also rejected what he described as a patronizing attempt by MEPs to dictate Bulgaria’s sovereign decisions. He said an investigation into the attacks was underway and that Bulgaria was working with its NATO and EU allies to identify those responsible.
"We have always viewed the European Parliament as a respected institution, the purpose of which is to strengthen the pro-European consensus within our societies, rather than to create fertile ground for manipulation and division," Radev said.
He listed measures taken by his government, beginning with appeals to NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa for joint action to stop attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea.
On October 13, 2026, when two commercial vessels were attacked again near Bulgarian territorial waters, Radev summoned the Russian ambassador in Sofia and described the attacks as unacceptable, saying their logic pointed toward Russia.
Bulgaria joined the multinational European Sky Shield initiative in 2022, during a caretaker government appointed by Radev when he was president. At the European Council meeting on October 15-16, Radev held a trilateral meeting with Rutte and Romanian President Nicușor Dan and proposed a moratorium on attacks against commercial shipping in the Black Sea.
The government has introduced extensive security measures around Bulgaria’s territorial waters, including preventive steps to protect maritime areas and strengthen surveillance in the air and at sea. Additional aircraft have been deployed for aerial patrols, with Bulgarian Air Force crews flying F-16, MiG-29, Su-25 and L-39 aircraft on surveillance, patrol and reconnaissance missions over Bulgarian waters. Three unmanned aerial vehicle surveillance systems have also been deployed in the Black Sea.
Following an extraordinary North Atlantic Council meeting on October 20, 2026, NATO allies expressed solidarity with Bulgaria and Romania and readiness to assist them. Allied forces have since increased surveillance and reconnaissance in the Black Sea, including through additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems and drones. A Boeing P-8A Poseidon reconnaissance aircraft arrived in Bulgaria within hours of the decision and began patrolling the western Black Sea.
A joint mine-countermeasures mission involving Bulgaria, Turkey and Romania is also underway to survey Black Sea shipping lanes and address the threat posed by drifting mines. It is the first initiative of its kind involving the three NATO littoral states.
Despite adverse weather, one of the vessels hit by drones was towed to the port of Burgas for a detailed investigation. An international team of experts invited by the Bulgarian government has arrived with advanced equipment to determine the type of drones used.
Radev said accusations concerning attacks on commercial vessels within Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone must be based on conclusive evidence rather than assumptions.
The EP resolution also calls for stronger EU support for Bulgaria and Romania, including faster implementation of the Black Sea Maritime Security Centre initiative, the reallocation of unspent funds under the Security Assistance for Europe (SAFE) instrument, stronger protection of underwater telecommunications, power and data cables, and adequate funding for Black Sea defense needs in the EU’s future long-term budget.
MEPs condemned Russia’s escalation of its war against Ukraine in the Black Sea, holding Moscow responsible for deadly attacks on civilian commercial vessels off the Bulgarian and Romanian coasts and repeated incursions into Romanian airspace. The resolution calls on the EU to consider a naval operation in the Black Sea and urges NATO to examine a defensive initiative modeled on the Black Sea Guardian concept, emphasizing cooperation among Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey.
Of Bulgaria’s 17 MEPs, eight voted in favor of the resolution: Andrey Kovatchev, Iliya Lazarov, Eva Maydell, Andrey Novakov and Emil Radev from GERB and the European People’s Party; Ilhan Kyuchyuk from DPS and Hristo Petrov, known as Itso Hazarta, from PP; and conservative Taner Kabilov.
Stanislav Stoyanov and Rada Laykova, representing Vazrazhdane and the Europe of Sovereign Nations group, voted against. Elena Yoncheva, Kristian Vigenin and Tsvetelina Penkova abstained. Radan Kanev, Nikola Minchev, Ivaylo Valchev and Petar Volgin did not take part in the vote.
The dispute unfolded as Radev also addressed domestic political issues after a meeting of the Executive Council of his Progressive Bulgaria party. He reiterated the party’s decision to support Iliana Yotova and Kiril Valchev in the presidential election.
"The world is currently in flames, and this is no time for amateurs at the helm of the state. Bulgaria must be in safe hands," Radev said in a statement following the meeting, adding that the party would back Yotova and Valchev for the sake of peace and security.
He also called on voters to end the period of the so-called “assembly,” referring to the informal coalition between PP-DB and GERB-SDS that had the support of DPS, and prevent parties he described as representing the status quo from obstructing political change.
Radev said recent operations by the Interior Ministry against the mayors of Kardzhali, Belitsa and Sungurlare, all affiliated with DPS, were based on reports and evidence of corruption. DPS leader Delyan Peevski and GERB leader Boyko Borissov had accused the government of using the police and security services to intimidate political opponents.
"I truly expect the Ministry of the Interior and the security services to continue their work in this direction, while avoiding any actions that could be exploited for political purposes - especially during this election campaign," Radev said.
He dismissed allegations that the operations amounted to a “new Revival Process,” arguing that the actions targeted suspected corruption rather than people from a particular ethnic group. He cited the Burgas district prosecutor’s remarks that evidence supported a 72-hour detention.
Radev also said the investigation in Sungurlare had produced witness testimony pointing to people and circumstances beyond the municipality. He declined to identify those involved, saying it was for law enforcement authorities to determine whether any currently active politicians were implicated.
Asked about Borissov’s disclosure that the two had spoken, Radev said he had invited all former prime ministers to a ceremony marking the arrival of Tsar Samuel’s relics. He said the conversation with Borissov lasted only a minute or two and was limited to extending the invitation.

articles.title: Ukraine frees 270 from Russian captivity in “historic” prisoner swap, including 5 Olenivka survivors and American teacher Stephen Hubbard
articles.body:
Ukraine has brought home 270 people from Russian captivity, including 261 military personnel and nine civilians, in the third stage of a prisoner exchange process that began on 19 August, Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War said on 23 October.
Amid Russia’s full-scale invasion, prisoner exchanges remain one of the few channels of communication between Kyiv and Moscow. But with thousands of Ukrainian military personnel and civilians still held in Russian captivity, each swap brings home only a fraction of those awaiting release, while negotiations remain tied to the difficult process of securing the return of captives on both sides.
Most of those released today had been held since 2022, including many defenders of Mariupol. Five survivors of the July 2022 Russian attack on the Olenivka prison barracks are also among those returning home.
The exchange also included American Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old English teacher from Izium, Kharkiv Oblast, who was illegally captured in 2022, then sentenced and tortured by Russia, according to the Coordination Headquarters.
Exchange includes soldiers held for up to eight years
The exchange included members of Ukraine’s Armed Forces, National Guard, State Border Guard Service, and other security and defense units, as well as a State Emergency Service rescuer. Thirty-eight of the released military personnel are officers.
According to Ukraine’s Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, the exchange was “historic” because it brought home the largest number of Ukrainian military personnel sentenced by Russia: 86 who had been sentenced and one who had faced criminal prosecution.
Two of those released had been held since 2018 and 2020, spending eight and six years in captivity, respectively.
“The priorities remain unchanged: we bring home those who have been in captivity the longest, the seriously ill, and the seriously wounded,” Lubinets said, adding that efforts to return civilians and people held since 2014 also remain a priority.
Nine seriously ill prisoners among those released
Nine of the returning service members are seriously ill, and some are in critical condition, the Coordination Headquarters said. The youngest person released is 24, while the oldest is 63.
Many of those released had faced criminal prosecution in Russia and been sentenced on what Ukraine describes as fabricated charges, including life imprisonment.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said most of those returning had been captured in 2022, and many had defended Mariupol.
The released also include service members who fought in the Donetsk, Luhansk, Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, Kherson, Kyiv, Mykolaiv, and Chernihiv directions, as well as defenders of the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant.
“We remember every man and woman and continue searching for everyone,” Zelenskyy said.
Russia has kept the Red Cross away from Ukrainian POWs since 2024. Now about 1,500 captives it never confirmed as prisoners face prosecution
US and UAE thanked for assistance
Ukraine thanked the United States and the United Arab Emirates for helping secure the releases.
All those released will undergo medical examinations, receive treatment and financial support, and take part in rehabilitation and reintegration programs after prolonged captivity.
Ukraine’s military intelligence chief and head of the Coordination Headquarters, Oleh Ivashchenko, said the return followed months of negotiations. He stressed that efforts to establish the fate of missing Ukrainians and bring everyone home would continue.
The 23 October exchange follows the previous stage on 19 August, when Ukraine brought home 103 servicemembers from Russian captivity.

articles.title: Beijing’s priority is peaceful coexistence between Iran and neighbors
articles.body:
Beijing’s priority is peaceful coexistence between Iran and neighbors
Majid Sharifi, an international affairs analyst, told the Iran newspaper that China’s approach toward Iran is not based on identity ties or ideological alignment. As a result, Beijing does not necessarily view stronger relations with Tehran as entering into confrontation with the United States.
 
China defines its ties with Iran within the broader network of its regional relationships and seeks to maintain balance among them. Therefore, the expansion of Tehran-Beijing relations cannot be explained solely by the intentions of the two sides or by existing opportunities for bilateral cooperation. From this perspective, one of the key prerequisites for deeper economic cooperation and stronger political relations is Iran’s achievement of peaceful coexistence and stable ties with neighboring countries. Such a situation could reduce the complexity of China’s strategic calculations and create more favorable conditions for expanding cooperation.
Kayhan: US not seeking negotiations
Kayhan addressed Trump’s unsuccessful effort to force Iran into submission through negotiations. The newspaper wrote that the confrontation between Iran and the United States spans four dimensions: military, economic resilience, diplomacy, and cognitive-psychological warfare. According to the article, the last of these has become the backbone of Washington’s strategy. It argued that the Trump administration, having failed to achieve its goals in reality, has relied heavily on psychological and influence operations. Recent US military movements, while appearing to signal war preparations, were portrayed as part of a broader strategy aimed at creating the illusion of diplomacy and inducing miscalculations among officials and the public. Referring to the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding and Washington’s repeated violations of its commitments, the paper argued that these experiences demonstrate that the United States is not genuinely interested in real negotiations or meaningful concessions.
Ettelaat: Short but intense
Ettelaat explored the possibility of another military confrontation in the Persian Gulf region. The newspaper argued that the previous round of conflict involving Iran, the United States, and Israel increased energy prices, accelerated global inflation, weakened Middle Eastern security, and placed significant pressure on Pentagon air defense stockpiles. Citing reports from The New York Times, it said that the United States and Israel have prepared plans to resume military operations against Iran after the US midterm elections in early November. According to the article, planning is underway for a short but highly intense operation. Some officials reportedly believe that another large-scale wave of attacks could push Iran’s economy toward crisis and force Tehran to make political concessions. Iranian officials, however, have stated that they are aware of such plans and are developing new targets and tactics in response. Tehran has also warned that any future conflict would not be brief and could extend to infrastructure in the region, including submarine internet cables and major Saudi oil facilities such as Aramco.
Hamshahri: Iran knows how to play the game
Hamshahri argued that the Islamic Republic, through its firm adherence to its principles, has sent a clear message to the White House that it does not trust the United States. According to the article, Trump and Netanyahu openly speak of weakening or destroying Iran, while soaring energy prices have become the main source of pressure on Trump. Rising oil prices have increased diplomatic activity by mediators seeking engagement with Tehran. The paper suggested that Munir’s recent visit was intended to help stabilize oil markets and provide political relief for Trump ahead of elections. Nevertheless, it argued that the united stance of Iran’s political leaders and senior military officials demonstrated that Tehran fully understands regional power politics. As a result, Munir reportedly left without achieving his objectives.
Sazandegi: America’s strategy through psychological warfare
Sazandegi examined remarks attributed to Trump regarding the possibility of Iranian attacks on cities such as Los Angeles and San Diego. The newspaper argued that, if the statements were accurately reported, they could serve several purposes. First, they may be designed to amplify perceptions of an Iranian threat among the American public and justify confrontational policies or potential military action. Second, they could help rally international allies, increase pressure on Iran, and strengthen support for containment policies. Third, the rhetoric may carry domestic electoral benefits, ranging from reducing voter dissatisfaction to boosting Republican candidates. The article also suggested that such statements could indirectly strengthen the political position of Netanyahu and his allies in Israel. According to Sazandegi, the success of this strategy depends on the credibility of the claims, developments on the ground, and public reaction. It concluded that Iran’s most effective response would be fact-based communication, active diplomacy, and efforts to prevent the country from being portrayed internationally as a threat.

articles.title: MEP Dan Barna: Bulgaria must clearly name Russia’s aggression in the Black Sea
articles.body:
Author
Irina Nedeva
Interview
MEP Dan Barna: Bulgaria must clearly name Russia’s aggression in the Black Sea
The EU will accelerate the creation of a European Martime Security Center
Friday 23 October 2026 14:58
Friday, 23 October 2026, 14:58
MEP Dan Barna in Radio Studio 2 at the European Parliament in Strasbourg
PHOTO Irina Nedeva
Font size
The Black Sea is no longer merely a trade corridor. It has become a test of European security. In a resolution adopted on Thursday, the European Parliament expresses solidarity with Bulgaria and Romania over the escalation of Russian attacks on commercial shipping, while also voicing serious concern about “the unclear and ambiguous response of the Bulgarian authorities to the escalating Russian threat in the Black Sea”.
How does the Romanian government view the response of the Bulgarian government led by Rumen Radev to Russian threats in the region? And how can Europe protect shipping in the Black Sea without waiting for the next attack? Is a common European response possible when national governments are sending different signals to Moscow?
In Strasbourg, BNR's Irina Nedeva spoke to Romanian MEP Dan Barna, a former deputy prime minister of Romania and one of the driving forces behind the resolution on behalf of the Renew Europe group. Their conversation addressed the need for a European Maritime Security Centre, the protection of commercial vessels, and the role of Bulgaria and Romania in defending NATO’s eastern flank.
But there is also a broader question facing the EU: can Europe finance its defence, maintain support for poorer regions and avoid new political crises within the Union at the same time?
You are calling for a European maritime security centre in the Black Sea. What exactly should this centre do, who will fund it, and when could it become operational? Is there not a risk of creating yet another institution while ships continue to come under attack?
“This resolution is also a very swift response by the European Parliament. I am pleased that, on the very day it was debated in the European Parliament, NATO also brought the Black Sea into focus. The resolution has two main objectives. The first is to recognise the need to designate the Black Sea as a priority area on the eastern flank. The second, as you rightly pointed out, concerns the establishment and funding of a European Maritime Security Centre.
The purpose of this structure, this centre, is to enhance the capacity to respond rapidly to attacks and security threats in the Black Sea. War is no longer just a war of tanks and aircraft. It is a drone war, and in this kind of warfare, time is of the essence. That is precisely why this centre must strengthen NATO’s and the eastern flank’s ability to respond appropriately and in a timely manner. What we are talking about is building technical infrastructure capable of addressing the realities of Russian aggression.”
Romania and Bulgaria are directly exposed to these risks, but the Black Sea is also an external border of both the EU and NATO. What concrete action do you expect from European partners: military surveillance, air defence, escorts for commercial vessels or some other form of presence?
“Everything you have mentioned is important. I mean the ability to identify risks and drones in a given area as quickly as possible. It is also important to have the capacity to scramble aircraft to destroy these drones. In this context, I would like to commend the Romanian and Spanish pilots who have managed to shoot down several drones in recent days. In the near future, we may also have to address the need to protect commercial vessels and provide them with escorts if Russian drones continue to operate aggressively in the region.”
Irina Nedeva and MEP Dan Barna in Radio Studio 2 at the European Parliament in Strasbourg
PHOTO Rositsa Petkova, BNR
Romania has clearly identified the aggressor. For the first time, Prime Minister Rumen Radev has mentioned Russia as being logically linked to the attacks, while adding that there is no evidence confirming their origin. From Romania’s perspective, how do you view the Bulgarian government’s response?
“We must be absolutely clear, and this resolution emphasises the point: Russia is the aggressor and is carrying out attacks against NATO’s eastern flank, including against Romania and Bulgaria. The text of the resolution, which we agreed on only yesterday, also refers to the perception that Bulgaria’s position is unclear and insufficiently categorical. I am optimistic that the Bulgarian government, too, will demonstrate solidarity and determination by acknowledging that these attacks originate from Russia and that a coordinated response is needed.This is one of the main problems associated with these attacks.
Commercial shipping is crucial not only for the countries of the Black Sea region. Food and essential goods are transported by sea to Africa, Asia and many other countries that depend, for example, on Ukrainian grain. The key question is how to protect this commercial traffic. If the Black Sea were to become a situation resembling that in the Strait of Hormuz, brought about by the war with Iran, this would put enormous pressure on the gas and hydrocarbon markets. Agricultural products could also be seriously affected.”
You advocate both stronger European defence and continued support for cohesion policy and agricultural subsidies. When resources are limited, who should make the compromise? Can countries such as Romania and Bulgaria expect more funding for security without losing support for their regions?
“Europe is under intense pressure from anti-European, sovereigntist and extremist movements. Weakening cohesion policy is precisely the argument used by sovereigntist and pro-Russian forces. They are trying to convince European citizens that Europe no longer works. That is why cohesion policy acts as a bond holding European values and European solidarity together. For this very reason, I believe it is important, for Romania, Bulgaria and Europe as a whole, that cohesion policy remains in place and continues to be strong.”
Romania is emerging from nearly six months of political deadlock with a minority government. Is this a temporary arrangement, or are there grounds to expect stability?
“The outlook is relatively optimistic in terms of stability, though not necessarily in terms of the quality of governance. Romania is currently facing a similar situation within its government, and I am sure Bulgaria has been through many such situations as well. We are talking about parliaments divided into three roughly equal blocs, none of which is willing to work openly with the other two. Yesterday, parliament approved a new government. So we now have a new cabinet. That is good news for the country’s stability.”
You have criticised the lack of tangible progress on enlargement. Is the EU ready to admit Moldova and other candidate countries before reforming its own decision-making processes? And how would you prevent a scenario in which new members bring unresolved rule-of-law problems into the Union?
“I must express my deep respect for Marta Kos, the European Commissioner for Enlargement, because she has managed to turn enlargement policy into a consistent and effective one. Two weeks ago in Strasbourg, she announced the new enlargement strategy, under which the four most successful and best-prepared countries were given roadmaps. This is a significant step forward. I am referring to Montenegro, Moldova, Albania and Ukraine. They are receiving roadmaps that set out a clear path forward, with specific conditions and reforms to be completed. These have been presented to their governments. This represents considerable progress because, at the very least, there is now a clear prospect.
I fully agree that Europe needs reforms, including to its voting system and the way its decision-making mechanisms operate. These reforms must prevent a repeat of what happened with Hungary and Viktor Orbán, when Russia managed to block one link in the chain and bring the entire mechanism to a standstill. To avoid this negative experience and this vicious practice, it is clear that Europe must move towards qualified majority voting instead of the current requirement for unanimity.
As regards enlargement, one approach under the new strategy is to retain unanimity only for the first and final stages of the process, while applying qualified majority voting to the intermediate stages. We are working in this direction, too. I am also a member of the European Parliament–Moldova Parliamentary Association Committee. We are working to help the country carry out the necessary reforms.”
Bulgaria is already in the eurozone. When will we stop having to convert our currencies as two neighbouring countries?
“For us Romanians, and for me personally, this is a painful issue. I would like to congratulate Bulgarian citizens, politicians and society on managing to adopt the euro, despite changing seven governments in roughly two years. The fact that all these governments managed to maintain the course and meet the convergence criteria, enabling Bulgaria to join the eurozone at the beginning of this year, is a source of pride.
I know that Romania and Bulgaria have a healthy sense of neighbourly competition on various issues. I know many people on both sides who take pride in their country’s achievements, in the areas where Romania excels and those where Bulgaria performs well. But when it comes to the euro, you have done better than we have. You have my admiration.”
Irina Nedeva’s full interview with MEP Dan Barna was aired on the 12+3 programme on BNR's Horizon channel.
This publication was created by: Rositsa Petkova

articles.title: Iran slams IAEA for silence towards attacks on its sites
articles.body:
The statement criticized the IAEA for applying double standards and discriminatory approaches, emphasizing that the Statute is a binding legal document and must not be used as a political instrument to serve the interests of certain powerful states.
Iran also condemned the unacceptable silence of the Agency’s governing bodies regarding the military attacks by the US and the Zionist regime on its peaceful nuclear facilities in 2025 and 2026. Furthermore, it highlighted the IAEA's failure to address the lack of comprehensive safeguards on the Zionist regime’s nuclear activities.
The Islamic Republic also called for the full, balanced, and non-discriminatory implementation of the IAEA Statute for all member states, particularly regarding technical cooperation and access to peaceful nuclear energy.
The full text of statement by the Iranian permanent mission in Vienna is as follows:
Permanent Mission of the Islamic Republic of Iran  
  
to the United Nations and other International Organizations in Vienna 
 
PRESS RELEASE  
   
On the Anniversary of the Approval of the IAEA Statute   
   
23 October 2026  
   
Seventy years after the adoption of the Statute of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) 
 
on 23 October 1956, a fundamental assessment is required as to the level and extent of the 
 
adherence to the principles and objectives of the Agency’s founding document. 
This anniversary must therefore be more than an occasion for commemoration; it must serve as 
 
a moment of critical reflection, institutional accountability and a renewed commitment to the full, 
 
impartial and non-discriminatory implementation of the Statute. 
The Statute: A Binding Mandate, Not a Political Instrument
The continued relevance of the IAEA Statute lies in the objective it establishes and the principles 
 
it enshrines. It implementation over the past seven decades has produced achievements in 
 
important areas. However, the failure to implement it fully, consistently, effectively and without 
 
discrimination, under all circumstances and with respect to all Member States, has caused the 
 
Agency to drift away from its core objective and priorities, undermine the principles governing its 
 
conduct, compromise its professionalism, and tarnish its authority and credibility. 
The undeniable fact is that the Statute is the Agency’s constitution, not a document to be invoked 
 
selectively or interpreted according to the interests of powerful States or a group of States. 
Beyond Safeguards: Upholding the IAEA’s Full Statutory Mandate
Article II establishes the Agency’s fundamental objective: to accelerate and enlarge the 
 
contribution of atomic energy to peace, health and prosperity throughout the world. Article III.A.1 
 
requires the Agency to encourage and assist research, development and the practical application 
 
of atomic energy for peaceful purposes. Article III.B.3 further requires the Agency to allocate its 
 
resources efficiently to achieve the greatest possible general benefit, with due regard to the special 
 
needs of developing countries. 
While safeguards are part of the IAEA’s mandate, the Agency is not merely a “watchdog” 
 
organization, as some Member States, in contravention of the Statute, seek to portray it. Such a 
 
narrow and politically motivated characterization distorts the Agency’s mandate and shifts its 
 
priorities away from its broader statutory objective that is the promotion of peaceful nuclear 
 
applications and international scientific and technical cooperation. Verification must not eclipse 
 
peaceful nuclear cooperation, development and the legitimate rights of Member States. An Agency 
 
that concentrates on scrutiny while failing to advance its key statutory responsibilities cannot claim to be fulfilling its mandate in a balanced manner.
Sovereign Equality Cannot Coexist with Double Standards
Article IV.C expressly establishes that the Agency is based on the sovereign equality of all its 
 
members and requires them to fulfil their statutory obligations in good faith. Article III.C prohibits 
 
the Agency from making assistance subject to any political, economic, military or other conditions 
 
incompatible with the Statute. Article III.B.1 requires the Agency to conduct its activities in 
 
accordance with the purposes and principles of the United Nations, while Article III.D requires 
 
due observance of the sovereign rights of States. 
These provisions are neither optional nor subordinate to geopolitical calculations. Sovereign 
 
equality requires that every State be treated fairly and without discrimination under the legal 
 
instruments applicable to it, free from double standards, selective interpretation and politically 
 
motivated action. 
A clear example is the continuing disparity between the scrutiny applied to Iran and the absence 
 
of comprehensive safeguards covering all nuclear activities of the Israeli regime, which remains 
 
outside the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. This disparity raises 
 
fundamental questions about the credibility and consistency of the international nuclear non-
 
proliferation norms. A credible, comprehensive and non-discriminatory approach to nuclear 
 
verification throughout the Middle East is a legitimate demand and a longstanding objective of 
 
regional countries that are parties to the NPT. Regional security cannot be built on selective 
 
scrutiny and unequal expectations. 
Peaceful Nuclear Cooperation: A Right, Not a Political Privilege
Peaceful nuclear cooperation must not be subject to political pressure. Article III.C of the Statute 
 
is clear: assistance must not be subjected to conditions incompatible with the Agency’s legal 
 
mandate. Political pressure and geopolitical rivalries must not obstruct legitimate scientific 
 
cooperation or turn access to peaceful nuclear technology into a privilege reserved for selected 
 
countries. The Agency is expected to defend the integrity of its technical cooperation mandate 
 
and ensure that its programs serve the development needs of all Member States fairly and without 
 
discrimination. 
Attacks on Nuclear Facilities and Unacceptable Institutional Silence
Attacks on safeguarded nuclear facilities demand strong and unequivocal condemnation. The 
 
military attacks by the U.S. and the Israeli regime against Iranian nuclear facilities in 2025 and 2026 constituted serious and material breaches of peremptory norm of international law on the 
 
prohibition of aggression.  They presented a grave challenge to nuclear safety, nuclear security, 
 
peaceful uses of nuclear energy, the credibility of the IAEA and its safeguards system.  
The Agency’s General Conference and Board of governors has repeatedly adopted resolutions 
 
expressly stating that armed attacks on, or threats against, nuclear facilities devoted to peaceful 
 
purposes violate the principles of the UN Charter, international law and the Agency’s Statute. 
 
Nevertheless, the Agency’s governing bodies and Secretariat failed to issue even a simple statement to condemn clear acts of aggression against Iran’s nuclear facilities – unprecedented in the Agency’s history. This failure represents a serious institutional shortcoming and raises troubling questions about the consistent application of the principles the Agency is mandated to uphold. 
The Agency cannot credibly defend the integrity of safeguards while treating attacks against 
 
facilities subject to those safeguards as a secondary concern. The Agency must therefore 
 
unequivocally reaffirm that attacks against peaceful nuclear installations are unlawful and 
 
unacceptable and must not be tolerated under any pretext.
Safeguarding the IAEA’s Independence, Integrity and Confidentiality Principle
Independence, confidentiality and professional integrity must be protected. Article VII.F of the 
 
Statute prohibits the Director General and Agency staff from seeking or receiving instructions 
 
from external sources. It also requires the protection of confidential information acquired in the 
 
course of their official duties and obliges Member States to respect the international character of 
 
their responsibilities and refrain from seeking to influence them improperly. 
These are concrete institutional safeguards, not ceremonial principles. Reports, assessments and 
 
decisions must be based on verifiable evidence, sound technical analysis and applicable legal 
 
obligations—not political demands, unsupported allegations or selective approaches. Any breach 
 
of confidentiality or attempt to instrumentalise safeguards information undermines cooperation, 
 
erodes trust and may compromise the safety and security of nuclear activities. The Agency must 
 
address credible concerns, protect sensitive information and ensure accountability. 
Restoring the IAEA’s Credibility: From Selective Implementation to Full Compliance
Cooperation must be matched by institutional responsibility. Iran recognises the importance of 
 
credible safeguards and professional verification and remains committed to engagement within 
 
the framework of its applicable legal obligations and its inherent and sovereign rights and interests. 
However, cooperation requires good faith, mutual respect, professional integrity and the 
 
consistent implementation of agreed legal commitments.  
On this anniversary, Iran calls upon Agency, particularly the Board of Governors and the Director 
 
General to end double standards, resist politicisation, protect confidential information, condemn 
 
attacks against peaceful nuclear facilities, and restore the full and balanced implementation of the 
 
Agency’s statutory mandate. Iran also calls for an effective and non-discriminatory technical 
 
cooperation policy that enables all Member States, particularly developing countries, to benefit 
 
from nuclear science and technology. 
The Agency’s credibility cannot rest solely on its authority to inspect. It depends equally on its 
 
adherence to the law, its impartiality, its independence and its willingness to uphold the legitimate 
 
rights of all its members. 
The Statute must be implemented as a whole, equally and in good faith—not selectively, not 
 
conditionally and not according to political convenience. The Agency owes this obligation to every 
 
Member State. On the seventieth anniversary of the Statute’s adoption, the Agency is expected to 
 
honour letter, spirit, object and purpose of the Statute through concrete action, not merely words, 
 
and to uphold its principles without political selectivity, discrimination or exception. 
MNA
Seventy years after the adoption of its Statute, the IAEA’s credibility rests on upholding its Statute 
 
in full, serving all Member States equally, and demonstrating that international law and statutory 
 
principles cannot be sacrificed to political convenience.

articles.title: European, Middle East ministers urge US-Iran diplomacy, not new attacks
articles.body:
European, Middle East ministers urge US-Iran diplomacy, not new attacks
An escalation would ‘create nothing but losers’, French foreign minister says as US official warns of possible strike.
Foreign ministers from eight countries are cautioning the United States against further attacks on Iran after meeting in Turkiye to discuss the Strait of Hormuz and other regional developments.
Ministers from the United Kingdom, France and Germany, known as the E3, convened with counterparts from the R4 group of Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt on Friday, along with Italy.
Speaking after the meeting in Istanbul, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said that none of the countries participating in the meeting approved of another military intervention or attack on Iran.
Such a move would only exacerbate tensions and further expand the conflict, he said, adding that diplomacy and dialogue were the only way to end the war.
A further escalation between Iran and the US “would create nothing but losers and would undoubtedly have very serious consequences for hydrocarbon prices”, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot told reporters.
“And so the first thing this group of eight countries … will do is call on both sides to exercise the utmost restraint, because we cannot afford another escalation in the region,” he added.
Italy’s Antonio Tajani said the aim was to work for “de-escalation to guarantee freedom of navigation”.
“I do not believe the problem can be solved from a purely military standpoint,” he said, noting that “we must promote dialogue” in order to reopen Hormuz.
The warnings came as the US ambassador to Turkiye, Tom Barrack, said Washington could “absolutely” strike Iran this weekend.
Speaking to X podcast host Mario Nawfal, Barrack said that although US President Donald Trump is “open and available and accessible to a deal … he’s also been very clear about what he wants”.
Barrack claimed that any potential US military action against Iran would not be aimed at regime change, saying Trump is “interested in rebalancing so that there’s no hostages, no threats, and the world can calm down”.
‘First of its kind’
The eight ministers discussed Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, escalating fighting in Yemen and prospects for ending the Russia-Ukraine war.
Reporting from Istanbul, Al Jazeera’s Sinem Koseoglu said the eight-nation summit was a “first-of-its-kind” attempt to discuss the parameters of regional conflicts and possible solutions.
Although participating countries “all have different national interests, especially when it comes to the crisis in the Gulf”, the Turkish foreign minister “underlined that what is happening in the Gulf … is affecting the other parts of the world”, Koseoglu added.
Foreign ministers of the R4 group issued a joint statement after a separate group meeting on Friday, saying that Israeli occupation “constitutes the fundamental source of instability in the region and beyond”.
The group urged Israel to “bring an end to further destruction and humanitarian tragedy in Palestine”.
The ministers also “condemned in the strongest terms the unacceptable escalation by the Houthi militia”, expressing full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and the internationally recognised Yemeni government. They also called on the Houthis to cease all military actions and return to the political process.
The ministers underlined the urgent need for dialogue and diplomacy concerning the US-Israel war on Iran. They rejected any measures that restrict lawful navigation and called for the full resumption of secure passage through the Strait of Hormuz.
Turkiye’s regional efforts
The meeting at an Istanbul hotel came as Turkiye seeks to bolster its role in the region, including through the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, the trilateral pact launched with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia in August.
Turkiye has said that the pact is not aimed at any specific country and remains open to others joining, including Egypt.
Referring to the diplomatic platform, Fidan said it has “several advantages, particularly because it is informal and flexible and focuses specifically on the issues we face”.
“We are not aware of any other platform that brings together countries with such different geographical and political backgrounds,” he said, noting that Ankara “is well placed to play a constructive role in this process”.
Cairo has yet to decide whether to join the agreement. President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi recently said that Egypt would “carry out any measure to protect” Saudi Arabia.
The Iran-backed Houthis are fighting Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces, who are backed by Saudi Arabia, and have launched a series of deadly attacks on the kingdom.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Battlefield Lessons Reshape How Bundeswehr Trains Its Combat Medics
articles.body:
Germany’s armed forces are overhauling the way they train their combat medics, evacuate casualties and protect field hospitals, after closely studying Ukraine’s experience in treating soldiers wounded in a war now dominated by drones.
The changes follow a September visit by Surgeon General Ralf Hoffmann, commander of the Bundeswehr’s Central Medical Service, and a team of specialists to Kyiv and to Dnipro, a city in southeastern Ukraine roughly 60 to 75 miles (100 to 120 kilometers) from the active frontlines.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to a report published Monday, Oct. 19 on the Bundeswehr’s official website, Ukrainian figures reportedly shared with the delegation show that drones now cause roughly 90% of combat injuries among Ukrainian soldiers.
The Ukrainian doctors also told the delegation that about 100,000 military personnel have undergone amputations since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Wounds above the body armor
Ukrainian medics described a front line where close-quarters fighting has become increasingly rare. Surveillance and strike drones cover a zone stretching about 25 kilometers (15 miles) behind the line of contact, making any movement in that area extremely dangerous.
The type of wounds has shifted accordingly.
According to the Bundeswehr’s report, drones that drop grenades or detonate on impact tend to strike soldiers from above and in front, with the blast often hitting areas left exposed by body armor.
Oleshky Evacuation: Russia Announces Kherson Frontline ‘Silence Regime’
Ukrainian doctors reported a high number of severe wounds to the face, neck, arms and hands, saying that eye injuries now make up a large share of upper-body trauma. Protective eyewear, they noted, is rarely worn in Ukrainian military units.
The German delegation concluded that personal protective equipment needs to be reassessed with these new patterns in mind.
Medical facilities moved underground
Due to the constant threat of strikes, Ukraine’s Defense Forces have moved some frontline medical facilities underground.
These include Role 1 facilities, where wounded soldiers are first stabilized, and Role 2 facilities, where surgeons perform emergency operations to save lives before patients are transferred to other medical institutions.
In a war where drones can spot and strike almost anything above ground, a visible aid station has itself become a target.
According to Ukrainian accounts cited in the report, one of the buried medical facilities in the Zaporizhzhia region was hit by 10 glide bombs without a single member of its staff being injured.
The German medical service is now examining how to build and run such treatment facilities, hidden and protected under a persistent drone threat.
Following the trip, Hoffmann announced closer cooperation with the Special Engineer Regiment 164, a specialized unit under the Bundeswehr’s Logistics Command based in Husum, whose heavy equipment could be used to dig in field hospitals quickly and test new procedures.
The threat is no longer theoretical for Germany.
On Wednesday, Oct. 21 Germany’s armed forces raised the Russian sabotage threat to “significant,” the second-highest level on its internal scale, after an explosives-laden drone was found near Wunstorf air base in Lower Saxony mid-September.
Increased hybrid warfare tactics from Moscow prompted Berlin to strengthen its protective measures.
Up to 12 hours between injury and surgery
Because of the dangers a ground evacuation under drone surveillance poses, it can take up to 12 hours before a wounded Ukrainian soldier reaches a medical facility.
According to the report, Ukrainian doctors told the German delegation that these delays are a major reason for the high number of amputations.
A tourniquet applied on the battlefield can quickly stop bleeding and save a soldier’s life, but if surgery does not follow quickly, the limb often cannot be saved.
The long wait has also made the first hours of care far more important, with soldiers and frontline medics now responsible for keeping severely wounded comrades alive for much longer than military medical doctrine traditionally assumed.
To limit long-term damage, Ukraine has moved specialists, including eye surgeons and ear, nose and throat doctors, unusually close to the frontline. Early treatment of facial and eye injuries, which are now common in drone attacks, significantly improves soldiers’ chances of recovery.
Because of this, the Bundeswehr is now testing both ground and aerial drones for medical use.
A first drone sub-unit is being trialed by Medical Regiment 3 in Dornstadt, and Hoffmann said medics will need to learn to operate a range of unmanned systems, potentially including drones that deliver blood supplies.
Ukraine is applying the same approach. On Oct. 16, the government approved a pilot project to deliver medicine, medical devices, blood samples and donor organs between hospitals through drones, aiming to make deliveries significantly faster, particularly to remote areas.
The Health Ministry’s Heart Institute in Kyiv will serve as the first site of the pilot and it already operates three specialized drones capable of flying up to 700 kilometers (435 miles) and landing at hospital sites.
Reshaping German training
The Bundeswehr said it has already substantially reworked its first-aid and medic courses based on lessons from Ukraine.
New programs, including Combat Life Saver, Combat Paramedic and Combat Physician courses, are designed to prepare frontline troops to keep severely wounded comrades alive for longer before professional medical teams can take over.
The courses are being rolled out this year, with the aim of eventually training the entire force.
The German medical service said it has worked closely with Ukraine’s Defense Forces for years and plans to deepen the cooperation, covering surgical care, medical logistics, training, drone use and digitization.

articles.title: Zelensky Says Starlink Caps Persist as Kyiv Eyes November Talks With Russia, US
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Starlink and Starshield restrictions remain in place, disrupting drone operations, while delays in agreed US interceptor missile deliveries continue to further strain Ukraine’s defense ahead of winter.
Zelensky made the remarks in a speech at the Hudson Institute on Friday, Oct. 23, excerpts of which he shared in a statement on Telegram. Around the same time, US President Donald Trump claimed he had no idea who ordered Starlink limitations on Ukraine and that he heard “it’s fixed.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“[SpaceX CEO] Elon Musk is a very good person. He is not going to do anything wrong regarding Ukraine,” Trump claimed. “He is a fair person.”
The dispute over Ukraine’s satellite access has dragged on since Oct. 13-14, when Starlink’s operating parameters in Ukraine were first altered. Since then, the White House and Musk have each denied responsibility, while pointing to the other.
Musk claimed Starshield is controlled by the US military, including Trump himself, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio insisted SpaceX, as a private company, makes Starlink’s operating decisions.
Despite constraints, Zelensky said Ukraine’s frontline is holding. The operations have so far been fairly successful, though the restrictions have made the fighting harder.
“This is a real problem, because the Russians attack us almost every day,” he continued.
Air Defenses at Russian Drone Factory Linked to Forced Labor Rival Putin’s Residence
Zelensky’s hopes for a trilateral meeting
During his speech, Zelensky also said that he and his team had spoken with senior US envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, about the outcome of their recent meetings in Oslo and St. Petersburg earlier this week.
Steps on how to advance diplomacy next month were on the agenda as well.
“We are ready to meet any day, even tomorrow. But everything depends on the Russians,” Zelensky said, noting that a trilateral meeting had also been on the agenda in October, but fell through after Moscow “came up with yet another reason not to meet.”
So far, the Kremlin has rebuffed every proposal for a direct meeting with Ukrainian authorities, particularly with Zelensky himself.
Zelensky argued that progress remains unlikely without Washington’s direct involvement and pressure on the Kremlin, while urging the US to keep the issue a priority at all levels.
Ukraine’s goal, he said, remains to move beyond technical-level negotiations to a meeting of leaders, since the most important issues can only be settled through direct discussions.
The Kremlin, for its part, rejected an energy ceasefire with Kyiv, arguing that Moscow wants a broader peace agreement instead.
Kremlin’s spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday, Oct. 21, that a full settlement of the war would be impossible without the participation of Ukrainian officials, signaling a shift from Moscow’s earlier position.
Russian President Vladimir Putin reportedly proposed a trilateral summit with his US and Chinese counterparts on Monday, Oct. 19 to discuss a settlement in Ukraine, excluding Kyiv from the meeting.
