articles.title: Media reports: Fire breaks out near military airfield in Voronezh after missile alert
articles.body:
Media reports: Fire breaks out near military airfield in Voronezh after missile alert
This was reported by the ASTRA Telegram channel, according to Ukrinform.
Alexander Gusev, governor of the Voronezh region, stated that “dry grass caught fire as a result of falling debris from downed targets.”
“Air defense forces on duty detected and destroyed several aerial targets in the sky over Voronezh. According to preliminary data, there were no casualties. Debris from the downed targets caused a fire in dry grass in the suburbs; the fire has already been extinguished,” he wrote on social media.
Earlier, Gusev had reported a missile threat in the region.
According to publicly available data, the 47th Guards Bomber Aviation Regiment is stationed at the “Baltimore” airfield.
The airfield has been regularly used by the Russian Air Force to launch airstrikes against Ukrainian territory since February 24, 2022.
A fire near the “Baltimore” airfield in Voronezh was previously reported on September 2. Prior to that, the airfield had been attacked on May 27.
As reported by Ukrinform, just last week, the Ukrainian Navy, using the “Neptune” coastal missile system, struck six Su-34M bombers at the “Borisoglebsk” military airfield in the Voronezh region of the Russian Federation.
The first photo is for illustrative purposes only

articles.title: Interview: Stratonex wants to bring Ukraine’s innovation loop to Britain
articles.body:
- British company Stratonex Defence Technologies is developing the VARAN unmanned ground vehicle, which has completed initial mobility and remote-operation testing but is not yet operationally ready.
- Co-founder Ben Everitt told The Defence Blog that Ukrainian feedback pushed Stratonex to prioritize affordable unmanned logistics over autonomy.
British defense technology company Stratonex Defence Technologies is developing a range of unmanned ground vehicles, tactical drones, counter-drone systems and military mobility platforms, with a focus on reducing the exposure of personnel to battlefield threats.
The company’s VARAN unmanned ground vehicle is among its central projects. The platform has undergone initial mobility and remote-control testing, but further engineering and integration work is required before it can be considered ready for operational deployment.
In an interview with The Defence Blog, Stratonex co-founder Ben Everitt discussed the development of VARAN, the company’s relationship with technology partners, its approach to manufacturing and the challenges of moving military hardware from prototypes into serial production.
Everitt also outlined the company’s plans for 2027, including closer cooperation with British manufacturers, universities and military operators. He described lessons drawn from Ukrainian battlefield innovation and explained why Stratonex is placing increasing emphasis on connecting ground vehicles, aerial drones, sensors and other technologies into integrated mission systems.
The following interview is presented in full, with the interviewee’s answers reproduced without editorial changes.
Q: Stratonex Defence Technologies is entering a market where established defense contractors and smaller technology companies are competing to develop autonomous military systems. What specific technological or industrial gaps are you seeking to address, and how does your business model differ from that of traditional defense manufacturers?
A: I think you have to start with what’s actually happening on the battlefield, because it’s changing incredibly quickly.
The traditional idea of a frontline is becoming increasingly meaningless. What you’ve really got is a contested kill zone, potentially 20 kilometres or more either side of the line, where drones, sensors and precision weapons mean that if you can be seen, you can potentially be targeted.
So that’s the problem we’re building Stratonex around. How do you operate in that environment without unnecessarily putting people in it?
That’s where the product set starts to make sense. We’ve got unmanned systems that can move equipment, sensors and other capabilities into that space. Then we’ve got fast, stealthy, relatively inexpensive mobility platforms for those occasions when people do need to go into it and need to get back out again quickly.
The phrase we’ve started using is: keep the humans in the kill chain, but out of the kill zone. I really like it because it sums up what we’re trying to do.
The other thing that’s really struck me is the speed at which all of this is changing. I was recently out in eastern Ukraine, near the frontline, in a car with the manager of a UGV factory. His phone goes and it’s a battalion commander on the frontline who is using his vehicles. He’s basically saying, “This works, this doesn’t, and this is what I want the next batch to do.”
I remember thinking: this is extraordinary. You’re watching the innovation loop happening in real time. The customer is on the battlefield and the factory manager is taking the next requirement directly from him.
Obviously we’re operating in a very different environment in Britain, but that sense of pace and urgency is something we really want to capture at Stratonex. We’re not trying to recreate a traditional defence prime. We want to be agile, work with really good technology partners and get really, really cool technology integrated and into the hands of operators quickly.
Q: Stratonex has presented a portfolio spanning unmanned ground vehicles, tactical aerial systems and counter-UAS technologies. How much of this portfolio is being developed internally, and what role do technology partnerships, licensing arrangements and third-party integration play in bringing these products to market?
A: It’s deliberately a mixture. I don’t think there’s any great virtue in saying that every nut, bolt, sensor and line of code has to have been invented inside the same building.
There are technologies and IP that sit within Stratonex, and then there are areas where we work with partners, licence technology or integrate specialist systems developed by other people.
And that’s exciting, because there is some really, really cool technology being developed by smaller companies in Britain and elsewhere. The problem is often not the technology. It’s getting it integrated, tested, manufactured and ultimately bought.
That’s where I think Stratonex can add a lot of value. We can start with the operational problem and ask: what’s the best combination of platform, sensor, communications, autonomy and payload to solve it?
We’re quite deliberately technology-agnostic about that. If somebody has already invented a brilliant sensor, I don’t want to spend three years and a fortune inventing another one just so we can put our badge on it. I’d rather work with them, integrate it and get the capability out there.
Q: VARAN is presented as a modular unmanned ground vehicle capable of operating in GNSS-denied environments using passive 3D sensing and onboard autonomous navigation. How mature is this technology today, what capabilities have been demonstrated during physical testing, and what engineering challenges remain before the platform can be considered operationally ready?
A: VARAN is a real vehicle. We’ve built it, driven it, tested it and spent quite a lot of time getting it muddy, which is the fun bit.
But we’re also careful not to pretend that having a really good prototype is the same thing as having a fully operationally proven military system. There is still engineering, integration and testing to do.
We’ve demonstrated the fundamental mobility of the platform, remote operation and elements of the sensing and navigation architecture. The next phase is about making all of that increasingly robust across different terrain, payloads, communications environments and operational conditions.
What’s been particularly interesting is the feedback we’ve had from Ukraine. We started out, naturally enough, being really enthusiastic about the autonomy. It’s technically fascinating and there are some really cool things you can do with it.
But the Ukrainians keep bringing us back to something much simpler: the really important thing is that it’s unmanned.
If you can remotely drive ammunition, water, batteries or other equipment those last few kilometres instead of putting people in a vehicle and sending them into the kill zone, you’ve already achieved something incredibly valuable.
So we’re still developing the autonomy, absolutely. But we’re not developing autonomy because autonomy happens to be fashionable. We’re developing the capabilities operators actually want.
Q: Published information describes VARAN as a multi-mission platform capable of carrying reconnaissance, electronic warfare and counter-UAS payloads. How does the vehicle’s modular architecture accommodate different power, communications and payload requirements, and which mission configurations have progressed beyond the design stage?
A: This is one of my favourite things about VARAN because you can get terribly technical about modularity, power, data and payload integration, and I have a tendency to do exactly that.
We took VARAN away for a weekend of testing and filming with a group of former Special Forces guys who our Chairman, Major General John Holmes, knows.
I’m there waving my arms around getting incredibly enthusiastic about all the clever things we can do with it. We can forward-deploy surveillance drones on it. We can remotely recharge them. We can put different sensors and payloads on it. We can use it as part of a much wider unmanned system. All really, really cool stuff.
And the former SAS guys basically looked at it and said: “Yeah, but we can chuck all our kit on that and it’ll carry it for us.”
And they’re absolutely right.
Sometimes the simplest use case is the best one. Logistics is the backbone of successful warfighting. If VARAN can carry the heavy stuff while the operator concentrates on doing his job, that’s incredibly useful.
It also goes back to what the Ukrainians have been telling us. Sometimes we get very excited about the word “autonomy” when the thing the soldier really values is the word “unmanned”.
That’s why modularity matters. VARAN isn’t supposed to be one exquisite vehicle designed around one exquisite mission. The base platform gives you mobility, power and communications and then we can configure it around what the operator actually needs, whether that’s logistics, surveillance, EW, counter-UAS or something we haven’t thought of yet.
Q: VisionWave announced a conditional $20 million purchase order for 200 STRATUM VARAN vehicles in September 2026. What role does Stratonex play in the development, integration and potential production of these vehicles, and what milestones must be achieved before the programme moves into manufacturing and customer deliveries?
A: VisionWave is an important partner of ours and we have a distribution agreement with them, but they are a completely separate company, so I don’t really want to speak for them or get into the detail of their commercial announcements.
What I can talk about is what we’re doing with VARAN.
Our focus is on continuing to develop the platform, testing it, integrating different capabilities and getting it ready for manufacture at scale. And that’s a really exciting challenge in itself.
As I said earlier, the defence technology world is actually pretty good at producing prototypes. The difficult bit is getting from prototype to procurement and then into repeatable, affordable production.
That’s what we’re concentrating on. Making VARAN faster, tougher and more useful, testing it properly, listening to operators and making sure that when demand comes we can actually build the thing at meaningful volume.
Ultimately, I’d much rather be judged on the vehicles we build and deliver than the numbers in a press release.
Q: Moving from prototypes and technology demonstrations to serial production remains a major challenge for emerging defense companies. How is Stratonex addressing manufacturing scalability, supply-chain resilience, unit costs and long-term maintenance, and what production capacity do you realistically expect to achieve?
A: Price really matters to us, particularly with VARAN.
Its three big advantages are its price point, speed and durability. It’s more cost-effective than the heavier platforms in this space, it’s fast and agile, and it’s designed to take punishment.
And you have to be realistic about why the price point matters. These things are going into war zones. At some point some of them are going to get blown up.
One Ukrainian battalion commander put it brilliantly when we were talking about equipment: “If you can make it out of wood, make it out of wood.”
That’s obviously an exaggeration, but there’s a really important philosophy behind it. Don’t add cost and complexity unless they actually give the operator something useful.
There’s a tendency in defence to make everything exquisite. But if making something twice as expensive only makes it ten per cent more capable, and you’re operating in an environment where you’re going to lose platforms anyway, that’s not necessarily a good trade.
So we’re designing around manufacturability, modular components, repairability and supply-chain resilience from the start. We don’t want to build a vast Stratonex factory and manufacture every component ourselves. We’d much rather work with established manufacturing partners and scale production as demand develops.
That’s also why durability and field repair matter. Make it tough. Make it repairable. Make it affordable enough that commanders are actually prepared to use it.
Q: Beyond VARAN, your portfolio includes the D-FLY counter-UAS interceptor and TALON tactical unmanned aircraft. What technical or operational capabilities are you prioritising in these programmes, and can you share any previously undisclosed details concerning prototypes, testing results, new configurations or upcoming product introductions?
A: Again, I think it makes more sense if you look at the portfolio through the kill-zone problem rather than looking at each product individually.
You’ve got this 20-kilometre-plus contested space. So how do I see into it? How do I move equipment through it? How do I operate inside it without unnecessarily exposing people? How do I counter the drones that are creating part of the threat?
VARAN answers part of that. TALON answers another part through tactical aerial capability. D-FLY tackles the counter-UAS problem, including the really important question of cost exchange.
And then you’ve got the mobility platforms, which I think are fascinating. E-bikes and e-scooters might look slightly odd sitting next to drones and UGVs until you think about the operational problem. If somebody does have to enter that kill zone, you want them moving quickly and quietly with as little signature as possible.
That’s the common thread.
What gets me really excited now is joining those things together. A UGV shouldn’t just be a UGV and a drone shouldn’t just be a drone. How do the platforms, sensors, communications and effectors start working together as one mission system?
That’s where I think some of the really, really cool stuff is going to happen.
Q: Looking ahead to 2027, which developments do you expect to define Stratonex’s next phase of growth? Are there any new programmes, industrial partnerships, customer agreements or technological milestones that you are prepared to announce or discuss in greater detail with The Defence Blog readers?
A: There’s loads going on and I’m genuinely really excited about 2027.
Obviously there’s the product side. VARAN will continue developing, we’ve got other products coming through, and we’re increasingly interested in what happens when you connect all these different capabilities together rather than thinking about a UGV, a drone or a sensor in isolation.
But the bigger idea we’re working on is what I’d describe as on-shoring the innovation loop.
That comes directly from what I’ve seen in Ukraine. I keep going back to that phone call in the car between the battalion commander and the factory manager. Operator feedback, engineering, testing and production are happening incredibly close together. That’s one of the reasons they are innovating at such extraordinary speed.
We’re obviously not going to recreate the circumstances that have driven that in Ukraine, but we absolutely can learn from it.
So how do we build our own version of that loop here in Britain? How do we bring operators, engineers, SMEs, manufacturers and academia much closer together, so that an operational problem can become an engineering problem, become a prototype, get tested, generate feedback and go around the loop again quickly?
That’s why we’re looking at academic partnerships as well as product-development partnerships. Universities bring extraordinary engineering expertise, research capability, testing facilities and, importantly, really bright people. Industry brings products, manufacturing and commercial pace. Then you need the operator constantly feeding reality back into the process.
For me, that’s potentially much bigger than any individual product.
Britain doesn’t have an innovation problem. There is some really, really cool technology being developed here. The challenge is connecting it, testing it against real requirements, iterating quickly and then actually manufacturing it.
If we can help build that ecosystem around Stratonex, shorten the distance between the operator saying “I need this” and somebody putting a working solution in their hands, then I think we’ve got something genuinely exciting.
That’s a big part of where I want us to go in 2027: on-shore the innovation loop, build sovereign capability and keep turning really good British technology into things that operators can actually use.
And all of it still comes back to the same mission: keep the humans in the kill chain, but out of the kill zone.

articles.title: Trump Invokes Defense Production Act to Boost Oil Production
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has invoked a Cold War-era law in an effort to boost oil production and lower energy prices.
In a presidential memorandum issued Thursday, Trump determined that petroleum production, refining, and related activities are essential to national defense under the 1950 Defense Production Act. The determination follows Trump’s declaration of a national energy emergency in January 2025.
“Ensuring resilient domestic petroleum production, refining, and logistics capacity is central to United States defense readiness,” the memo reads. “Without immediate Federal action, United States defense capabilities will remain vulnerable to disruption.”
The memo comes as the price of gas and diesel has soared across the country amid supply disruptions caused by the U.S. and Israel’s war against Iran. Brent crude futures rose 1.2% to $114.47 a barrel early Friday, extending gains after Thursday hit a five-month high. U.S. diesel pump prices averaged $6.32 a gallon, slightly higher than Thursday but below the September record, according to AAA. The high energy prices, and related inflation, have become a defining issue for voters in the coming midterm elections.
Here’s what to know.
What does the memo mean for energy production?
The memo means that energy production shortfalls are seen as a national defense risk.
The memo invokes Section 303 of the Defense Production Act, a law that allows the federal government to intervene in private industry for national defense. Section 303 allows the President to make purchases, purchase commitments, provide financial support and equipment, and expand production through other measures.
The memorandum also removes certain Section 303 requirements through an emergency waiver, including ordinary congressional notification and authorization constraints.
While the memo does not specify which projects could be funded, Vice President J.D. Vance said last week that the Administration would use the Defense Production Act to expand capacity at a Delek U.S. Holdings-owned refinery in Texas.
Without taking action, the memo said, U.S. industry would be unable to provide sufficient energy services in a “timely manner due to constrained financing, long lead times, permitting and infrastructure bottlenecks, and supply chain limitations.”
Has the Defense Production Act been invoked before?
Enacted during the Korean War, the Defense Production Act was first used to expand domestic industries in critical materials, such as aluminum and titanium, for national defense.
Section 303 of the act was also used during the pandemic to fund domestic production of medicines and vaccines. Former President Joe Biden also invoked the statute to support clean energy manufacturing and supply chains, including minerals used in electric vehicle batteries and the production of of energy-efficient heat pumps and insulation.
In April, more than a month after Iran began disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation for U.S.-Israeli Feb. 28 strikes, Trump invoked the act to declare petroleum, natural gas, coal, electricity grid, and other energy infrastructure essential to national defense. Citing April’s natural gas determination, the Department of Energy on Monday committed up to $42 million to advance the proposed Constitution Pipeline linking Pennsylvania and New York. The department also announced up to $50 million last week for transmission upgrades in Virginia and West Virginia, citing April’s grid determination.
Last year, Trump signed legislation providing $1 billion for Defense Production Act activities, including energy projects deemed critical to national security.
Trump’s use of Section 303 of the act for fossil fuel projects has drawn criticisms from environmentalists, with the Center for Biological Diversity calling the April memoranda, which waived congressional notification, “unlawful.” Nevertheless, the statute expressly includes energy production and construction in its definition of national defense.
How else has Trump tried to lower energy prices?
The Trump Administration has pursued a number of other measures aimed at lowering energy prices since the Iran War began. Earlier this month, Trump signed an executive order temporarily expanding access to tax-exempt dyed diesel, which is typically reserved for off-road farm and construction vehicles. The Group of 7 countries, including the U.S., also agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil reserves to the world over four months.
In August, the Administration extended the Jones Act waiver for another 90 days, allowing foreign-flagged ships to transport oil and certain other commodities between U.S. ports.
Trump also announced an agreement with Putin earlier this month to import diesel from Russia, alongside temporary sanctions relief. The deal has faced significant backlash from lawmakers.
For many of these measures, industry analysts and stakeholders have said the reduction in energy prices is likely to be limited and possibly short-lived. Analysts estimated that the Jones Act waiver was expected to reduce gasoline prices by only pennies per gallon. Capital Economics economist Hamad Hussain said the reserve release could lower diesel prices temporarily, but would not resolve the underlying supply crunch. And analysts warned that the dyed diesel measure would have a limited effect on most consumers since the tax-exempt fuel isn’t widely available at ordinary commercial pumps. A Council on Foreign Relations analysis also suggested that damaged Russian refining capacity may make a near-term effect of the Russia deal on diesel markets unlikely, although Trump said the agreement would supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to U.S. and global markets immediately.
Meanwhile, oil exports from the Middle East topped prewar levels last week, marking a rebound in regional oil shipments despite continuing security risks. Ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz, however, still face attacks from Iran, while the Bab el-Mandeb Strait near Yemen has been threatened by the Houthi rebels. Analysts previously told TIME in June that the risk of further attacks and damage to facilities could delay a full-scale recovery.
Thursday’s memorandum could support investment in fuel capacity, but it’s uncertain how quick or measurable an effect it will have on energy prices. Gas prices still depend heavily on globally traded crude, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, although they can be influenced by domestic refining and distribution conditions. The U.S. was the largest crude producer globally last year, averaging 13.6 million barrels of crude a day.
Analysts warned, after the April memorandum, that federal support would not necessarily translate into immediate price relief.
“Until the pipes are in the ground and the fuel is flowing or transported, it may not be able to be called a true structural shift,” Cyrus Brooks, director of marketing at energy research firm RBAC, wrote in April.
Still, Brooks said of the April action that federal recognition of energy as important to national security could support important infrastructure investment, potentially relieving a bottleneck in domestic fuel production, refining or transportation.
“Energy security seems to be the brightest neon sign flashing,” he wrote. “Not because it’s everything, but because nothing works without it.”

articles.title: 40,000 tons of Russian diesel are bound for New York—due four days after Americans vote
articles.body:
A Malta-flagged tanker carrying Russian diesel is heading for New York after the fuel deal between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, Reuters reported in an exclusive on 23 October, citing LSEG shipping data. Two weeks earlier, the US Treasury temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel.
The tanker is due in the US on 7 November, four days after Americans vote in the midterms. So the first US-bound cargo cannot reach American pumps before the election. Energy analysts also doubt the deal will lower diesel prices meaningfully. US fuel prices rose mainly because the war with Iran disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Trump, however, has blamed Ukraine’s strikes on Russian refineries.
Loaded on the day Moscow promised
The medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes took on 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low sulfur diesel at the Baltic port of Primorsk on 22 October, shipping data showed. In March, Ukraine’s General Staff said its drones hit the Transneft oil terminal at that same port.
A day before the loading, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak announced that the first tanker would sail for the US on 22 October. He pledged more shipments and said Russia would meet US needs within its capabilities.
Russia resumes diesel exports to Türkiye, Brazil, after Trump lifts sanctions on fuel supplies, boosting Moscow’s war revenue – Reuters
From a pledge to a partial lift
On 9 October, Trump wrote that Russia would immediately supply over 300,000 tons of diesel “to the American and Global Marketplace.” Another 500,000 tons would follow in November, then 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.”
Moscow had banned diesel exports on 8 July, after Ukrainian drone strikes shut down refineries and caused fuel shortages inside Russia. The Russian government stated on 10 October that it had partially lifted the ban, clearing 500,000 tons for the world market at this stage. Russian diesel shipments to Türkiye and Brazil have since resumed, boosting Moscow’s war revenue.
Trump has made other moves to cut diesel prices before the vote, Reuters reported. He waived parts of a new sanctions law against Russia. He also threatened Europe with a US diesel export ban unless countries released more fuel from their emergency reserves.

- Russian plant supplying components for Iskander missiles reportedly struck by Ukrainian Storm Shadow missiles

articles.title: Zelensky says Ukraine’s speed restrictions remain on Starlink and its military version, Starshield, despite Trump’s assurances
articles.body:
Zelensky says Ukraine’s speed restrictions remain on Starlink and its military version, Starshield, despite Trump’s assurances
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said speed restrictions on Starlink satellite communications terminals and their military version, Starshield, remain in place in Ukraine. He spoke in a video address to the Hudson Institute in Washington, Interfax-Ukraine reported.
“The speed limits on Starlink and Starshield are still there. The speed has not been restored. And the delivery of interceptors to protect us against Russian ballistic missiles is still delayed. We’re waiting for interceptors that were already agreed on. But they are still not coming. Hope that everything is on the way. And this is a real problem for us, because the Russians attack us almost every day. Russia attacks us massively. So that’s where things stand today,” Zelensky said.
He added that this was happening as Ukraine continues its “quite successful operations on the front,” and said the Starlink and Starshield restrictions had complicated the situation.
“But our front line is still holding, and we are doing our best to keep our logistics working, and we continue defending ourselves,” he said.
On October 14, Ukrainian military personnel reported encountering restrictions on Starlink satellite communications terminals — specifically, their military version, Starshield. The connection cut out when drones exceeded 160 kilometers per hour (about 100 miles per hour). This came amid a sharp deterioration in relations between Zelensky and U.S. President Donald Trump.
Two days later, Trump said he had not ordered Starshield service in Ukraine to be restricted and did not know who could have done so. However, The Telegraph, citing four sources, reported that Musk had approached Trump with a proposal to restrict Starlink speeds in Ukraine. The Wall Street Journal later reported that Musk had ordered Starshield service in Ukraine to be restricted.
The Wall Street Journal also reported that Trump called Musk and asked him to lift the restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine. Trump later said Musk had lifted the restrictions.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].

articles.title: Germany wants to buy thousands of missiles from European and Ukrainian manufacturers, Bloomberg reports
articles.body:
Germany wants to buy thousands of missiles from European and Ukrainian manufacturers, Bloomberg reports
Germany is negotiating the purchase of thousands of European-made high-precision long-range missiles to replenish its arsenal amid delays in the delivery of US Tomahawk missiles.
Source: European Pravda, citing Bloomberg
Details: Manufacturers that could win German contracts include Dutch company Destinus SA with its Ruta cruise missiles and German-British defence startup Hypersonica, which is developing the ultra-fast HS1 missile.
Negotiations are also underway for a contract worth over €1 billion with US defence startup Covenant to supply thousands of its ground-launched Anthem cruise missiles.
Furthermore, sources indicate that the German Ministry of Defence is holding talks with Ukraine regarding the co-production and procurement of Ukrainian Bars cruise missiles.
Their manufacturer has not yet been disclosed. The idea behind acquiring thousands of new, inexpensive missiles is to saturate enemy air defences, thereby ensuring that strikes reach their targets.
The German armed forces currently only use the air-launched Taurus cruise missile, which has a relatively short range of about 500 km.
Germany's plan to purchase the powerful BGM-109 Tomahawk missile and the Typhon ground-launch system from US manufacturer Raytheon could be delayed for up to five years.
Background:
- The German government expects that creating a new arsenal of long-range weapons designed to deter Russia will require nearly €12 billion.
- The day before, Denmark announced a billion-dollar deal for the purchase of high-precision long-range missiles for the first time in history, amid intentions to strengthen its security.

articles.title: Iran has plans to hit Gulf undersea cables if war resumes
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran has detailed plans to hit Gulf undersea cables if war resumes, officials say
Tehran has drawn up detailed plans to target undersea communications cables in the Gulf if the United States and Israel attack Iran again, two senior Iranian security officials told Reuters.
Their comments followed warnings by Iranian officials that undersea cables in the region could become targets in any renewed conflict if diplomacy with Washington collapses.
The two Iranian security officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, gave few details and did not say how or where exactly Tehran would carry out such attacks. But one of them said Iran would aim to prevent repairs after any attacks to prolong disruptions to communications, including internet connections.
"If Iran is attacked, there will be no more red lines ... from undersea cables to military bases, including covert ones," one of the officials said.
The official warned Washington not to "play with fire", and said Iran had full access to the undersea cables and could easily destroy them.
Yadollah Javani, the deputy head of political affairs for Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC), said on Wednesday that Iran could target seven major internet cables beneath the Strait of Hormuz if Iranian infrastructure came under attack.
Undersea cables carry around 99% of global internet traffic, according to the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency. But the global impact of such attacks by Iran could be limited as less than 1% of international bandwidth passes through the Strait of Hormuz, said Alan Mauldin, research director at telecommunications research firm TeleGeography.
The strait separates Iran and Oman, linking the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea.
The US Department of State and Iran's Foreign Ministry did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment on the Iranian security officials' remarks. There was no immediate comment from Gulf states.
'Stronger response'
The plans for possible attacks on undersea cables reflect a conviction in Iran's leadership that a renewed US military campaign would have to be met with a stronger response than before.
Top security official Mohsen Rezaei warned this month that US-linked digital infrastructure across the Gulf, including data centres and AI facilities, could be targeted in a renewed conflict.
Washington's Gulf allies have invested heavily in such infrastructure and they "should hold Washington, not Tehran, responsible for any damage to undersea cables," the second Iranian security official said.
Alex Vatanka, director of the Iran program at the Middle East Institute in Washington, said such threats were intended to deter renewed conflict and put pressure on Washington by making Gulf governments and US companies fear for their investments in the region.
"Tehran wants Gulf states and corporate executives to press (US President Donald) Trump over the risks his policies pose to their investment plans," said Vatanka.
Multiple cable cuts could slow internet services and disrupt financial transactions, e-commerce and cloud computing, analysts said. The impact would depend on how operators rerouted traffic and the capacity available on alternative connections, Mauldin said.
Restoring connections during wartime could be difficult, experts said, and higher insurance costs and delays in obtaining permits to enter territorial waters could further complicate repairs.
The Red Sea could offer a more significant target than the Strait of Hormuz, particularly if Iran had support from its Houthi allies in Yemen, though Tehran has made no public statement indicating it plans to target cables there.
The Red Sea carries data between Europe, East Africa and Asia, with capacity routed through it accounting for about 3% of global international demand and around 10% of traffic travelling between regions, Mauldin said.
Gulf governments have been investing heavily in technology to diversify beyond oil and become global artificial intelligence hubs, deepening ties with US technology firms.
Iranian strikes directly hit two Amazon Web Services facilities in the UAE in March and damaged infrastructure near one of its facilities in Bahrain. The IRGC named US tech companies including Microsoft, Google, Apple and Nvidia as legitimate targets at the height of the war in March.
Land-based connections can provide alternative routes for internet traffic, and Gulf states and US technology companies are investing in additional infrastructure to improve resilience.
Microsoft plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Only thing we really need from USA is shipment of interceptor missiles
articles.body:
Ukraine's biggest challenge for the winter, amid intensifying attacks from Russia, is its air defense capabilities, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
"Air and missile defense remains a real challenge, especially the availability of interceptors for the Patriot systems. We are facing a shortage in this area. We are negotiating with various countries – in Asia, the Middle East, and with our European partners. And, of course, we are counting on an aid package from the United States. This primarily involves energy support and interceptor missiles – which are the most important – as well as funding," Zelenskyy said during an online meeting at the Hudson Institute on Friday.
According to him, effective communication has been established with the United States and the EU. "The necessary decisions are being made every week in Brussels. The Europeans support us; they understand who we are and what challenges we face. I think we'll be ready. The only thing we really need from the United States is a shipment of interceptor missiles. We urgently need interceptors for the Patriot systems, and we hope that the U.S. administration will help us. We expect the Pentagon to ensure the delivery and to provide other necessary support," the President of Ukraine said.
He also noted that Ukraine has agreements with partners regarding gas supplies. "In addition, we have our own natural gas reserves – in this regard, we've prepared quite well," Zelenskyy said.

Australia said on Friday it had sanctioned two North Korean individuals and companies over the use of “fraudulent” IT workers and cybercrime to earn cash for the isolated nuclear-armed state.
The two men are alleged to be key operators in Pyongyang’s cybercriminal activities overseas, estimated by analysts to bring in billions for the country’s weapons programme.

articles.title: Drone Strike Capsizes Tanker Just Off NATO Coast—Romania Calls It Another Russian Escalation
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Drone Strike Capsizes Tanker Just Off NATO Coast—Romania Calls It Another Russian Escalation
A civilian tanker was severely damaged and capsized in the Black Sea after being struck by drones roughly 13 nautical miles, or 24 kilometers, off the Romanian coast near Constanța, leaving one crew member dead and three others missing, according to Romanian outlet Digi24 on October 23.
The Comoros-flagged tanker KHORYV, IMO 8138712, was carrying a crew of 13—10 Ukrainian citizens and three Azerbaijani nationals—when a fire broke out aboard the vessel following the strike, according to Romanian outlet Digi24, citing the Romanian Coast Guard and maritime authorities.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The distress call reached the Constanța Maritime Coordination Center at around 10 am, prompting an immediate search-and-rescue operation involving Romanian Coast Guard vessels and crews from the country’s maritime life-saving agency.
Another civilian ship in the area initially took 10 crew members aboard before transferring them to Romanian rescuers. Authorities later said nine sailors had been rescued alive, one had died, and three remained missing.
The tanker suffered extensive damage and eventually overturned.
Romanian President Nicușor Dan described the incident as another escalation by Russia in the Black Sea region.
The threat to civilian shipping has recently been discussed both by Romania’s Supreme Council of National Defence and during a special NATO consultation requested by Romania and Bulgaria, Dan said.
Romania is now seeking additional defensive capabilities as attacks and other security incidents increasingly threaten commercial shipping close to NATO territorial waters.
Previously, Romanian F-16 fighter jets shot down two Russian jet-powered attack drones over the Black Sea after the aircraft entered Romania’s airspace.

articles.title: Can Serbia’s student protesters stop Aleksandar Vučić from becoming prime minister? The country’s longtime leader has called an early election to extend his hold on power.
articles.body:
Can Serbia’s student protesters stop Aleksandar Vučić from becoming prime minister? The country’s longtime leader has called an early election to extend his hold on power.
Just over a month ago, Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić addressed the nation on television. He lamented the difficult circumstances but said that, despite everything, the country had “managed to preserve stability.” To ensure that Serbia could continue “to develop and maintain its internal unity in the face of external threats,” Vučić announced that he would dissolve parliament and call early elections for October 25, 2026. He resigned shortly afterward. Vučić needs the election to stay in power: His presidential term would have expired soon. But he may not succeed. His main rival is the “Student List — Students Win” movement, which formally emerged a month ago but became known around the world during mass protests across Serbia in 2024. We explain why Vučić called the election now, what the main parties are campaigning on, and who is most likely to win.
Why Serbia’s election matters
Aleksandar Vučić joined the Serbian Radical Party as a young man and became known as an ardent Serbian nationalist. He became prime minister in 2014 and was elected president three years later. With the backing of the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), Vučić built a regime that political scientists abroad describe as authoritarian.
As early as 2019, the U.S. nonprofit Freedom House downgraded Serbia’s status from free to partly free. That same year, the European Parliament said Vučić and the SNS were blocking parliamentary debate on bills they opposed, accusing their critics of betraying the country, and suppressing independent media.
Five years later, Freedom House said the ruling party was undermining political rights and civil liberties and putting pressure on independent media and civil society organizations. In 2024, V-Dem, an independent Swedish research institute that studies democracy worldwide, called Serbia an “electoral autocracy.” This year, the German think tank Bertelsmann Stiftung classified it as a moderate autocracy, citing the concentration of power in Vučić’s hands.
Other indicators also show the problems facing Serbian democracy. Between 2014 and 2026, the country fell from 54th to 104th place in the annual press freedom index compiled by the international organization Reporters Without Borders.
Transparency International ranked Serbia 78th in its Corruption Perceptions Index in 2014 and 116th in 2025. A survey conducted last year by Transparency Serbia found that 22% of respondents considered corruption the country’s biggest problem — the highest share in a quarter century.
All this makes the coming election especially consequential. It will determine whether Serbia continues on the authoritarian course it has followed over the past decade and a half under Vučić and the SNS, or gets a chance to democratize if the Student List, the main opposition group, wins.
How the electoral system works
Serbia is a parliamentary republic. Parliament, officially known as the National Assembly, elects the government and holds it accountable.
The constitution limits the president’s powers: He commands the armed forces, signs laws, and nominates a prime minister for parliament’s approval. He can also dissolve the Assembly — for example, if it fails to approve a government within 90 days. But the president cannot dismiss the government or hold other positions while in office. Vučić disregarded the latter rule: From his first election as president until May 2023, he also led the ruling party.
The Assembly has a single chamber with 250 members. Under the constitution, elections are held every four years, but early elections have effectively become the norm since 2000. Only the 2012 and 2020 elections took place on schedule.
Voters cast ballots for party lists; there are no single-member districts. Parties must clear a 3% threshold to enter parliament, but this requirement does not apply to ethnic minority parties. The current Assembly includes parties representing Hungarians, Bosniaks, Croats, Albanians, and even Russians. If the ruling party or coalition needs a few more votes to secure a parliamentary majority, ethnic minority lawmakers can wield disproportionate influence.
Serbia has seen sustained anti-government protests over the past three years
The previous parliamentary election, held on December 17, 2023, was marred by serious irregularities, including the so-called Bulgarian train ballot-swapping scheme, busing in voters from Republika Srpska, and vote-buying. These practices helped the SNS win nearly 47% of the vote and a parliamentary majority, while the opposition Serbia Against Violence coalition had to settle for 23.7% and 65 seats.
The vote-rigging triggered mass protests, but they had petered out by the end of December 2023. New grievances soon emerged. In July 2024, thousands took to the streets against a project to extract lithium at the Jadar mine in western Serbia. Events in Novi Sad, Serbia’s second-largest city, prompted a far larger response.
On November 1, 2024, a canopy at the city’s railway station collapsed, killing 16 people, including children. The irony was that renovations at the station had been completed just four months before the disaster. Two Chinese state-owned companies had carried out the work under a contract awarded by the Serbian authorities without competitive bidding.
Officials initially denied any responsibility. Pro-government media and Goran Vesić, the construction, transport, and infrastructure minister, repeatedly said that the station canopy had not been part of the renovation. The Transport Ministry refused journalists’ requests for financial documents relating to the work.
All this raised suspicions of corruption and sparked large protests in Novi Sad and other cities. Many students joined and became the protests’ main driving force. The largest demonstration, on March 15, 2025, drew up to 325,000 people — an enormous number in a country with a population of just over 6.5 million. In addition to calling for the release of documents relating to the station’s renovation and for increased spending on higher education, protesters demanded the government’s resignation and early elections.
The government could hardly ignore the protests. Vesić resigned in November 2024 and was behind bars a few weeks later. He and 12 other officials faced charges, but these were later dropped for lack of evidence. Prime Minister Miloš Vučević resigned in January 2025.
Vučić, meanwhile, suggested that unnamed foreign powers were instigating the protests. Pro-government media accused protesters of betraying their country and committing crimes and called for their arrest and lengthy prison sentences.
Police treated demonstrators harshly. Participants in a mass demonstration in Belgrade in March 2025 said a sound cannon had been used against them. During protests in Valjevo in August, police beat 25 demonstrators with batons. In Belgrade, police arrested, beat, and humiliated 15 protesters and threatened women with sexual violence.
Why did Vučić call the election now?
Protesters have been demanding new elections for the past two years, but Vučić did not dissolve parliament to accommodate them. He has his own reasons. His second presidential term was due to expire in May 2027, and Serbia’s constitution bars him from running again. But Vučić does not want to relinquish power.
He is well positioned to hold on to it. He has the backing of the SNS, which has come to dominate Serbian politics over the past decade and a half. The party enjoys substantial political advantages through its access to state institutions and directly or indirectly controls all the country’s major television channels. These advantages helped it secure a decisive victory in the 2023 election. On October 25, it hopes to repeat that success and preserve the current regime.
Under these circumstances, Vučić’s calculation is clear: He wants to move from the presidency to the prime minister’s office. That post would give him considerable powers. Under the constitution, the prime minister determines domestic and foreign policy, can introduce bills in parliament, oversees the state administration, appoints and dismisses ministers, and can even initiate the dissolution of parliament.
The election date is no accident. First, Vučić has sought to deny the students time to build a stronger political organization. Their movement is not even a party, and it has yet to establish an extensive network of local branches to mobilize voters. Second, the election was scheduled for the earliest date legally possible after parliament’s dissolution: 46 days later. That gives the students as little time as possible to campaign, while Vučić and the SNS have been promoting themselves for months.
Serbia will elect a new president in December, and Vučić will try to install a loyalist. One possibility is Ana Brnabić, the Assembly’s speaker and now acting president. She has already proved her loyalty to Vučić: During her years as prime minister, she effectively ceded all real authority to the president. Another candidate is Miloš Vučević, the SNS leader and a close Vučić ally, who ranks second on the party’s electoral list.
The main contenders and their platforms
A total of 18 parties and coalitions, including those representing ethnic minorities, will contest the October 25 election. But the main battle will be between the Aleksandar Vučić — United Serbia coalition and the opposition Student List.
The pro-government camp
The dominant party on the government side is the Serbian Progressive Party, founded in 2008 after a split in the Radical Party. The SNS espouses nationalist, conservative, and populist views, while its economic positions lean toward neoliberalism. With around 800,000 members in 2020 — 13% of Serbia’s population — it is Europe’s largest party by membership. It is running as part of the Aleksandar Vučić — United Serbia coalition, but its partners carry little weight.
The SNS platform rests on several key tenets. These include defending Serbia’s territorial integrity — meaning refusing to recognize Kosovo’s independence — and supporting Serbs living abroad; steady economic development and efforts to combat corruption; social justice; and joining the EU while cooperating with Russia, the United States, and China. There is one problem with the platform published on the party’s official website, however: It dates from 2011 and has not been updated since.
In the current campaign, the ruling party and Vučić are focusing primarily on recent economic successes. Serbia’s GDP has indeed grown steadily in recent years. According to the World Bank, it rose by 3.9% in 2024 and 2% in 2025, while the International Monetary Fund forecasts growth of 3.3% this year. Serbia has also been actively attracting foreign investment, which reached 5.2 billion euros in 2024 and nearly 3.5 billion in 2025. This September, Vučić proudly said Serbia accounted for 62% of all foreign direct investment in the Western Balkans.
To sustain growth, the authorities are banking on large projects that can double as publicity opportunities. Work has recently picked up, for example, on the Belgrade metro, a project first launched in the 1990s. Chinese companies are now involved, and Vučić said with great fanfare that two enormous tunnel-boring machines were due to arrive in the capital in October — just in time for the election. For now, however, the spectacle of their arrival has had to be postponed: Technical problems have left the machines stuck in the Romanian port of Constanța.
But nothing is stopping the ruling party from constantly talking about Expo 2027, the world’s fair that Belgrade will host. Vučić frequently visits the construction site and says the “historic” exhibition is moving the capital and the country as a whole “forward.” The exhibition was also one of the official reasons given for calling the early election: Vučić said the vote needed to be timed so that afterward the country could focus on preparing for Expo.
The authorities also emphasize the need for stability. Serbia went through a turbulent period in the 1990s, and the authorities now use fears of a return to that era to argue that people should vote for the SNS. In their view, the main threat to stability comes, naturally, from the protesting students, who they say receive foreign funding and want to organize a “color revolution” in Serbia.
SNS lawmaker Biljana Pantić said the choice in this election was clear: On one side are the SNS and Vučić, who put “care for citizens, stability, and Serbia’s continued development” first; on the other are those “who have no concrete platform or results and have reduced their politics to hatred, violence, and attacks on everything Aleksandar Vučić does or says.”
The opposition
The students, who form the backbone of the protests, hold a wide range of views, and their ranks include both nationalists and liberals. Nevertheless, they have managed to stay united by avoiding contentious issues such as European integration, relations with Russia, and Kosovo’s independence.
On September 9, 2026, the day parliament was dissolved, they announced the formation of their own political movement, Student List — Students Win. In just a few days, the students collected the required number of voter signatures to run in the election and submitted their candidate list to the Electoral Commission, which unanimously approved their inclusion on the ballot on September 15.
The list contains 250 parliamentary candidates. None are students; instead, they include scholars, university professors, experts, and athletes. At the top is cardiologist Ilija Srdanović, a professor at the University of Novi Sad, although the students stress that they are not looking for “a new leader around whom another personality cult could form.”
The movement’s election platform is called the ”Student Plan” and consists of 11 points grouped into three sections. The first, “Serbia or the Mafia,” calls for stronger efforts to fight corruption, barring from public office officials who have broken the law and have ties to the mafia, and guaranteeing media freedom.
The second section, titled “Knowledge Is Power,” calls for adapting the education system to modern needs, introducing competitive selection for teaching positions, and subsidizing startups and innovation.
The third section, “Serbia Grows With Us,” addresses social and economic issues. Among other things, it proposes providing housing for young families and essential workers, and improving health care by standardizing medication prices nationwide and modernizing hospitals, particularly in rural areas.
The other parties
Among the other contenders, two coalitions — Stability Factor and European Serbia — have a chance of clearing the 3% threshold, according to a poll conducted by Serbian market research agency Factor Plus and published on September 21.
Stability Factor, led by Ivica Dačić, brings together the Socialist Party and partners such as the Social Democrats and the Greens. The coalition presents itself as an alliance of the patriotic left and intends to work with the SNS and Vučić. It is going through a difficult period, however, facing criticism for cooperating with the regime. On August 31, the Socialist Party expelled its vice president, Branko Ružić, for supporting the protesting students. Two members of its main council and several regional party leaders then left in protest.
European Serbia, meanwhile, consists of pro-European parties and has a detailed plan to dismantle the regime built by the SNS within 100 days and begin building a “European Serbia.” The coalition did not join forces with the students but is willing to cooperate with them after the election.
How the campaign unfolded
Although the official campaign began on September 9, Vučić and the SNS effectively started much earlier. The SNS put its own spin on the student movement’s main slogan, “Students Win!” For several months, enormous billboards reading “Serbia Wins!” could be seen across the country.
Government-controlled TV channels heavily promote Vučić. An analysis by the Friedrich Naumann Foundation found that he appeared on various channels 129 times in August — an average of four times a day. He appeared in his capacity as head of state, meaning he did not pay for the airtime.
Vučić has used other methods as well. In September 2026, the government set aside money for one-time payments of 160 to 300 euros to pensioners. Vučić also promised to raise public-sector salaries by 8% and social workers’ salaries by 12% — but only starting in December, after the election.
The students have no such resources, so they have to rely on social media and direct campaigning. They have set up booths in various Serbian cities where people can talk to candidates and learn about their platform. The students are also going door to door, trying to persuade voters to support the Student List.
Meanwhile, opposition supporters face direct pressure and restrictions from the authorities. Universities are firing professors sympathetic to the protesters, while television gives the opposition half as much airtime as pro-government parties and portrays it negatively. CRTA, an independent Serbian election-monitoring organization, says opposition candidates, observers, and activists face surveillance, insults, intimidation, and even physical attacks.
Who will win?
It is difficult to gauge support ahead of the election: Opinion polls vary widely. According to Factor Plus, 48.7% of voters are prepared to vote for the SNS and its coalition partners, and 37.1% for the Student List. European Serbia, at 3.6%, and the Socialist Party-led coalition, at 4.9%, also cleared the 3% threshold in the poll. But opposition politicians accuse the agency of bias and of working for the SNS, whose support it consistently overstates.
On September 30, Đorđe Vukadinović, editor in chief of the independent political science journal Nova srpska politička misao (New Serbian Political Thought), put support for the students at 44.4% and for the pro-government coalition at 41.7%. He did not explain the basis for those estimates. On October 15, political analyst Mirko Dautović suggested that support for the students had risen above 50% over the preceding month, but he too cited no specific poll.
Serbia faces a fierce electoral contest, but observers say tensions could persist afterward. First, there is no guarantee that Vučić would willingly step back if he lost — he could declare the results invalid. But that would risk a repeat of Slobodan Milošević’s fate: In the fall of 2000, he too refused to acknowledge defeat, only to be forced to give in after 10 days of mass protests.
Second, the students are determined and make no secret of the bleak future awaiting Vučić if they win: He will be put on trial. In September, a student-made video appeared online showing Vučić in various settings, followed by a figure mopping a prison floor. The video achieved its aim — it infuriated the Serbian authorities.
Even setting Vučić’s fate aside, a student victory would leave the movement facing the question of what to do next. Once their common opponent is gone, their disagreements over Kosovo, European integration, and relations with Russia and China — which they have set aside for now — will surface. Maintaining a consensus will be very difficult. And winning an election alone will not be enough to eradicate corruption. As the example of 2000 shows, democrats coming to power does not necessarily mean a victory for democracy.
What the election means for Russians living in Serbia
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Serbia declined to impose sanctions on Russia while also taking in tens of thousands of Russians. By December 2024, the Serbian authorities had issued 67,000 temporary residence permits.
Estimates put the number of Russians in Serbia at 55,000 to 62,000 at the end of 2025, with more than 80% living in Belgrade. Most are young: People ages 24 to 39 account for 55%. And 66% of the Russians who have relocated to Serbia have a university education.
Temporary residence does not, of course, give Russians the right to vote, but Serbian politics is of little interest to them. A survey by the Belgrade Centre for Security Policy found that 72.8% of Russians who had moved to Serbia did not want to take part in political or civic activities. They were far more concerned about their personal safety and economic well-being.
The government’s approach to Russians who have relocated appears unlikely to change if the pro-government coalition wins. The Serbian authorities, for example, have repeatedly said they have no plans to revise the existing visa-free travel agreement with Russia.
If the Student List wins, its policy toward Russian emigrants is impossible to predict at this point: The students have carefully avoided commenting on Russia or on Russians who have moved to Serbia.

articles.title: Trump turns to Cold War-era law to tackle fuel crisis
articles.body:
Trump turns to Cold War-era law to tackle fuel crisis
US President Donald Trump has invoked a Cold War-era national security law to boost domestic oil production and refining, as rising fuel prices threaten the Republicans’ chances in November’s midterm elections.
Speaking on Thursday at a Republican campaign rally in Iowa – an agricultural state where farmers have been hit hard by the oil crisis – Trump announced that his administration would use the Defense Production Act (DPA) to provide up to $150 million to expand American refining capacity and produce diesel and gasoline “at record levels.”
He also predicted that the Iran and Ukraine conflicts would end soon, sending gasoline and oil prices “tumbling down.”
Enacted in 1950, the DPA allows Washington to financially support industries deemed essential to national defense. In a presidential memorandum, Trump designated domestic petroleum production, refineries, pipelines, and storage facilities as critical to national security, arguing that private companies could not expand capacity quickly enough without federal intervention.
Energy Secretary Chris Wright promised the funds would be deployed in cooperation with private companies, while the Department of Energy separately projected the initiative would increase refining output by millions of gallons of gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, and other products per day.
Vice President J.D. Vance had earlier announced plans to invoke the law to expand a Delek-operated refinery in Tyler, Texas, although such projects typically take months, if not years, to complete.
Trump’s announcement comes as his approval rating has plunged to a record low of 31% – compared with 47% when he began his second term – ahead of the midterm elections on November 3, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll published Monday. The survey also found that 68% of Americans disapproved of his handling of the economy.
Fuel prices in America sharply rose after the US and Israel launched their war against Iran in late February, disrupting global energy supplies. According to the US Energy Information Administration, average gasoline prices have climbed from $2.94 per gallon immediately before the conflict to $4.28 in the week ending October 19, while diesel has jumped from $3.81 to $6.28 over the same period.
The Trump administration has sought to tackle the fuel crisis through several emergency measures, including releasing 172 million barrels from strategic oil reserves, relaxing gasoline-blending requirements, temporarily easing diesel regulations, and announcing additional subsidies for struggling farmers.
In early October, Trump also announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to release more than 300,000 tons of Russian diesel onto global markets, with additional supplies expected later. He has also repeatedly pressed Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he blamed for rising fuel prices.
The president’s pressure sparked pushback from Zelensky, who called Trump’s diesel deal with Moscow “a weak decision” and “not fair and not honest” while refusing to comply with the refineries ultimatum. In response, Trump suggested that Ukraine should “get a new president” instead of Zelensky, whose term expired more than two years ago, while calling continued Ukrainian strikes a “disgrace.”

articles.title: Putin’s key remarks on peace talks and Europe’s ‘schizophrenia’ (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Putin’s key remarks on peace talks and Europe’s ‘schizophrenia’ (VIDEO)
Russia remains ready to negotiate a lasting settlement in Ukraine but will achieve its objectives regardless, Russian President Vladimir Putin told journalist Pavel Zarubin on Thursday. He also outright rejected “schizophrenic” claims in Western media that Moscow could be seeking a war with Europe.
Putin’s comments followed nearly three hours of talks with US envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on Wednesday. Witkoff brought new peace talk proposals following his own discussions with Vladimir Zelensky, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s Chief of Staff Bjoern Siebert, and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store in Oslo.
The new diplomatic engagement comes after Putin’s October 9 agreement with US President Donald Trump on Russian diesel supplies, whereby Washington eased fuel export restrictions while engaging with Moscow on broader economic cooperation.
Lasting peace, rather than a temporary pause
Putin confirmed Russia’s readiness to resume trilateral contacts with the US and Ukraine, focusing on security arrangements for both countries after a final settlement. The goal is to achieve definitive peace agreements, rather than “a suspension of hostilities for some short period,” he stressed.
The Russian leader also stated that he agrees with Witkoff’s argument that such discussions would also need to address Europe’s wider security architecture.
Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov previously suggested the talks could resume around mid-November, potentially in Abu Dhabi.
Putin said an agreement was possible, but insisted that “all the goals of the special military operation will be achieved” one way or another.
Europe’s ‘political schizophrenia’
European claims that Russia poses a military threat and preparations for confrontation amount to “political schizophrenia,” Putin said, arguing that European populations do not want war with Russia and explicitly rejected suggestions that Moscow is preparing to attack them.
“We do not want, we are not preparing for any war with Europe,” he said.
Putin described inflicting a strategic defeat on Russia as unrealistic, expressing hope that its opponents would recognize that peaceful relations better serve their own populations.
‘Historic Russia’ and the territorial question
Asked about Zelensky’s recent comments to Fox News that he would be willing to give up 25% of his territories in order to freeze the conflict on the current battle lines, Putin rejected the premise.
“It is not their territory, it is the territory of historic Russia,” he said, citing residents’ votes for independence and subsequently for reunification with the Russian Federation.
He acknowledged that the issue remained disputed, but argued that describing these developments as Ukraine losing territory was inappropriate.
Fighting ‘to the last Ukrainian’
Putin called it “incomprehensible” that Kiev expects that “the entire world should pay them, fight for them, supply them with weapons, ammunition, equipment,” and stressed that Russia has no desire to fight Ukraine.
“If Ukraine’s current leadership wants to wage war, let them fight. But why do they think everyone should pay for it and supply them with weapons?” Putin questioned.
He noted that much of this desire for war can be attributed to foreign countries that want to fight against Russia in order to weaken it and have promised support to Kiev.
However, Putin stressed that these foreign entities are prepared to fight until “the last Ukrainian” and questioned whether Ukraine’s leadership similarly treats its citizens as expendable cannon fodder.
Putin accused Ukrainian authorities of rounding up men “like stray dogs” and forcibly sending them to the front, undermining motivation. He also argued that nationalist groups that carry out this so-called “busification” do not always bear the frontline burden themselves.
He recalled that, according to official figures, there have been half a million deserters in Ukraine and over 300,000 criminal cases opened, adding that the actual numbers could be significantly higher.
Shared history and missed opportunities
Putin said Moscow had sought a negotiated resolution with Kiev since 2014, including through the Minsk agreements intended to settle the Donbass conflict. He blamed Ukrainian authorities for repeatedly rejecting opportunities to reach an agreement before Russia’s military operation began in 2022.
He described Ukrainians as a people closely related to Russians, pointing to genetic research that has shown they are “one people.” However, he acknowledged that some wished to identify differently and said Russia accepted that reality.
“We are ready even now to negotiate and seek solutions to this difficult, complicated situation,” Putin said. “Everything can be agreed upon.”

articles.title: Romania Blames Russia for Drone Strike That Sank Black Sea Ship
articles.body:
One crew member was found dead and three were missing after the Khoryv sank near Romanian President Nicușor Dan blamed Russia for a drone attack that sank the Comoros-flagged cargo ship Khoryv in the Black Sea on Friday, Oct. 23. One crew member was killed, three were missing and nine were rescued, Romanian authorities said.
“It is part of Russia’s escalation process in its war in Ukraine,” Dan told reporters, according to Reuters. He said the ship had been hit by a drone.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The vessel sent a distress signal about 13 nautical miles (24 kilometers) off Constanța, just beyond Romania’s territorial waters, according to Romania’s naval authority. The crew included 10 Ukrainians and three Azerbaijanis.
Rescue teams continued searching for the three missing crew members, but rough seas and poor visibility prevented the use of a helicopter, the Associated Press reported.
The ship caught fire and capsized before sinking, according to Romanian officials. It had departed Turkey on Oct. 21 and was headed for the Romanian port of Sulina.
Latest in a series of Black Sea ship attacks
The sinking comes amid a series of attacks on commercial shipping near the Black Sea coasts of Romania and Bulgaria. At least seven cargo ships have been hit in the area this month, Reuters reported, with about 30 sailors reported dead or missing.
The attacks have raised security concerns for NATO members Romania and Bulgaria, as well as for commercial vessels using routes that connect the Danube River to the Black Sea. Ukraine relies on Danube ports and nearby Romanian waters to ship grain and other goods, particularly as Russia continues to attack Ukrainian ports.
All 4 Moscow Airports Halt Flights as Sheremetyevo Issues Air Raid Alert
Earlier this month, the Turkish-owned grain carrier Royad Mammadov caught fire and sank near Romania’s coast, killing two crew members. As Kyiv Post reported, Ukrainian officials blamed Russian drones, while Romanian authorities initially confirmed the fire but did not establish its cause or attribute it to Russia.
NATO to reinforce Black Sea surveillance
Dan urged Russia to accept US and European ceasefire proposals and end its war against Ukraine.
NATO said on Oct. 20 that it would send additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems and drones to the Black Sea. The alliance did not specify the equipment or numbers involved.
Romanian fighter jets shot down two drones over the country’s territorial waters on Oct. 17. Defense Minister Radu Miruța said the following day that they were likely Russian drones of the latest generation.
Ukraine, Romania and Bulgaria have called for greater NATO support to protect commercial shipping in the Black Sea.
