articles.title: Russian losses in the war with Ukraine.
articles.body:
This publication is divided into two parts:
Bi-weekly Summary. A text summary, updated every two weeks, in which we report on what we have learned about recent losses and the frontline events that led to the deaths of Russian soldiers.
Interactive Infographics. The second part provides visualisations of the losses since the start of the war, showing, for example, where the dead served or which regions they came from. We update the data for these graphics, while the accompanying text is refreshed but remains largely the same.
A detailed description of our method for estimating total deaths using Probate Registry data can be found at this link.
Last update to the named list: October 23, 2026.
Last update to the Probate Registry estimate: May 9, 2026; estimate as of late December 2025
Full named list and a map of verified losses is available here: 200.zona.media.
This week, we are only releasing updated numbers for Russian losses in the war against Ukraine.
The map below shows the distribution of casualties across Russia’s regions. These are absolute figures and have not been adjusted for population or number of military units.
You can filter the map to show total losses, losses by branch of service, or the home regions of mobilised soldiers who were killed.
In most cases, official reports or visual cues like uniforms and insignia allow us to determine a soldier’s branch of service, or how he came to be in the army (mobilised, volunteer, prisoner, etc.).
The chart below compares these different groups of servicemen.
From early summer and into the mid-fall season of 2022, volunteers bore the brunt of the losses, which is strikingly different from the situation in the initial stage of the war: in winter and early spring, the Airborne Forces suffered the greatest damage, followed by the Motorised Rifle troops.
By the end of 2022 and the beginning of the next year, losses among prisoners recruited into the Wagner PMC increased markedly. They were formed into “assault groups” to overwhelm Ukrainian positions near Bakhmut.
By March 2023, prisoners became the largest category of war losses. After the capture of Bakhmut, there have been no cases of mass use of prisoners so far.
By September 2024, volunteers once again emerged as the largest category among the KIA. This shift reflects a cumulative effect: prison recruitment had significantly waned, no new mobilisation had been announced, yet the stream of volunteers continued unabated.
By October 23, 2026, the death of 7,920 officers of the Russian army and other security agencies had been confirmed.
The proportion of officer deaths among overall casualties has steadily declined since the conflict began. In the early stages, when professional contract soldiers formed the main invasion force, officers accounted for up to 10% of fatalities. By November 2024, this figure had dropped to between 2–3%—a shift that reflects both evolving combat tactics and the intensive recruitment of volunteer infantry, who suffer casualty rates many times higher than their commanding officers.
Officers killed in Ukraine
To date, the deaths of 15 Russian generals have been officially confirmed: five Lieutenant Generals, seven Major Generals, two who had retired from active service, and one Ukrainian SBU general who had fled to Russia.
Lieutenant General Oleg Tsokov, deputy commander of the Southern Military District, was killed in July 2023—the first officer of that rank to die in the war. In December 2024, Lieutenant General Igor Kirillov, head of the Nuclear, Biological, and Chemical (NBC) Protection Troops, was killed by a bomb in Moscow. Lieutenant General Yaroslav Moskalik, a senior officer in the General Staff’s Main Operational Directorate, was killed by a car bomb in a Moscow suburb in April 2025. In December 2025, Lieutenant General Fanil Sarvarov, head of the Operational Training Directorate of the Russian General Staff, was killed in Moscow by a car bomb. On March 31, 2026, Lieutenant General Alexander Otroschenko, commander of the mixed aviation corps of the Northern Fleet, was killed in the crash of an An-26 transport aircraft in Crimea.
Two deputy army commanders, Major General Andrei Sukhovetsky (41st Army) and Major General Vladimir Frolov (8th Army), were killed in the first weeks of the war. In June 2022, Major General Roman Kutuzov was killed in an attack on a troop formation.
Major General Sergei Goryachev, chief of staff of the 35th Combined Arms Army, was killed in June 2023 while commanding forces against the Ukrainian counter-offensive in the Zaporizhzhia region. In November 2023, Major General Vladimir Zavadsky, deputy commander of the 14th Army Corps, was killed near the village of Krynky.
In November 2024, Major General Pavel Klimenko, commander of the 5th Separate Motorised Rifle Brigade (formerly the “Oplot” Brigade of the so-called Donetsk People’s Republic), was fatally wounded by an FPV drone.
In July 2025, a strike on the headquarters of the 155th Naval Infantry Brigade killed at least six officers, including the Deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Russian Navy, Mikhail Gudkov.
The two retired generals on the list are Kanamat Botashev, a pilot who had been dismissed for crashing a fighter jet and was fighting for Wagner PMC when his Su-25 was shot down in May 2022, and Andrei Golovatsky, a former Interior Ministry general serving an 8.5-year prison sentence (but maintained his rank) who was killed in June 2024.
On March 17, 2026, SBU Major General Volodymyr Lyapkin was killed in the Kherson region. Until February 2014, Lyapkin headed a department in the Ukrainian special services, but after the victory of the Maidan revolution, he fled to Russia. After the war began, he served in the occupation administration of Kherson and then transferred to the “Bars-33” unit.
The date of death is known in 266,700 cases. While this data does not capture the full daily reality of the war, it does suggest which periods saw the most intense fighting.
Please note that data for the most recent months is most incomplete and will change significantly in the future.
The age of the deceased is mentioned in 268,100 reports. For the first six months of the war, when the fighting was done by the regular army, the 21-23 age group accounted for the most deaths.
Volunteers and mobilised men are significantly older: people voluntarily go to war over 30, and the mobilised are generally over 25.

articles.title: Finland gives Ukraine 10 diesel locomotives that keep trains running when Russian strikes cut the power
articles.body:
Finland will donate diesel locomotives to Ukraine’s state railway, the Office of Ukraine’s President reported. Helsinki also pledged new winter aid, and the two countries signed deals on drones, housing, and satellite communications during Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo’s visit to Kyiv. One of them is a first step toward a satellite link Ukraine would control itself.
With Russia replacing its missiles as fast as it fires them, Ukraine heads into winter needing equipment that works without the grid. Russian strikes have damaged or destroyed almost 600 locomotives of Ukraine’s state railway since the full-scale invasion began, more than 300 of them diesels, the infrastructure minister said. The attacks have reached engines even near the Polish border, on the railway that carries Ukraine’s evacuations, grain, and cargo.
Diesels that keep moving when the grid goes down
Finland will hand 10 locomotives and their spare parts to Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine’s state railway, free of charge. Infrastructure Minister Mykola Kalashnyk announced the deal, signed on 22 October at a Ukrainian-Finnish business forum. The engines need no power from overhead lines, so trains can keep running during blackouts.
The engines are Dv12 diesels that VR, Finland’s state rail company, is taking out of service. A VR shareholders’ meeting moved them into state ownership, and the Finnish state is donating them, Yle reported. VR puts their value, spare parts included, at about €2.1 million. Finland’s government said the gift will not affect VR’s ability to run trains at home.
Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi and Orpo signed the donation certificate, one of seven documents signed that day. Two others plan Ukrainian-Finnish drone production in Finland, one for military and dual-use systems and one for heavy drones. Another covers a precast concrete plant for industrial housing construction.
The day’s agreements are worth around €300 million in total, Zelenskyy said. Projects worth €200 million are already under way within the two countries’ Drone Deal, he added. Under an earlier plan, most drones made in Finland would go to Ukraine.
Finland backs €28.5 million power plant project as Ukraine braces for Russia’s next winter energy assault
Winter money now, a 36th military package by year’s end
Orpo announced a new €10 million package. Of it, €5 million goes to the Ukraine Energy Support Fund and €2 million to humanitarian aid for winter. The last €3 million goes to the Ukraine Recovery Program, for energy and water supply. Finland will also deliver mobile heating containers by December.
Finland has given Ukraine five defense packages this year, worth more than €500 million combined, Militarnyi reported. A 36th package is being prepared together with Ukraine’s military. “We plan to make a decision by the end of this year,” Orpo said. In September, Finland approved a package worth about €290 million.
A satellite link Ukraine would own
Ukraine’s Defense Ministry signed a letter of intent with Finnish satellite firm ICEYE and telecom company Nokia, Militarnyi reported, citing ICEYE. The parties will explore building a secure satellite communications system under Ukraine’s control. The aim is to reduce Ukraine’s dependence on foreign commercial operators.
In this model, the state customer owns the satellites, ground stations, and user terminals, RBC-Ukraine reported. The network could serve defense, border protection, emergency services, and disaster recovery. The letter sets out no timeline or funding.
“Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security,” Zelenskyy said in the companies’ statement. ICEYE CEO Rafal Modrzewski said Ukraine needs “secure, sovereign and high-performance satellite communications systems that it controls.”
The deal comes after a speed cap on Starlink disrupted Ukrainian drone missions this month. The EU, meanwhile, is pushing three European firms to merge into one SpaceX rival. ICEYE has supplied Ukraine with radar satellite imagery for years.
Days before the signing, tracking firm LeoLabs said a Russian government-owned satellite, Cosmos 2612, had spent weeks shadowing an ICEYE radar satellite, coming within 500 meters. The ICEYE satellite is widely believed to provide imagery to Ukraine.
Neither fix is quick. Ukraine’s big locomotive order arrives from 2027, and the first satellites of the ICEYE-Nokia system are expected to launch only in 2028.

articles.title: Russia vows ‘inevitable’ retaliation over Austrian diplomat expulsions
articles.body:
Russia vows ‘inevitable’ retaliation over Austrian diplomat expulsions
Russia will retaliate against Austria for expelling four of its diplomats over alleged misconduct, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Dmitry Lyubinsky has said.
The warning follows Vienna’s decision to declare four Russian diplomats personae non gratae over alleged violations of diplomatic rules, without publicly presenting evidence of wrongdoing.
“A response will follow inevitably,” Lyubinsky told TASS on Friday. He did not specify what retaliatory measures Moscow could take.
Austria announced the expulsions earlier on Friday, citing findings by its security services. Three of the diplomats were stationed at the Russian Embassy in Vienna, while the fourth worked at Moscow’s delegation to the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), dealing with military security and arms control.
The Austrian Foreign Ministry accused the four of engaging in “activities incompatible with their diplomatic status” and ordered them to leave the country. It did not identify the diplomats or provide details of the alleged violations.
The Russian Embassy rejected the accusations as “outrageous” and unfounded. Responding to Friday’s decision, the mission accused Vienna of blindly following Western anti-Russian policies and described the expulsions as another unfriendly move against Moscow.
Austrian media have sought to link the expulsions to alleged Russian espionage, although Vienna has provided no public evidence to substantiate the claims. According to the magazine Profil, the country’s Defense Ministry circulated a warning to military personnel and reservists in August about supposed Russian intelligence operatives, complete with the names and photographs of 21 individuals.
The warning reportedly prompted a wave of reports about suspicious contacts, though their nature and credibility remain unclear. Profil also claimed that disagreements between Austria’s Defense and Foreign Ministries had delayed the expulsions. None of the allegations have been publicly substantiated, and no evidence directly implicating the four Russian diplomats in espionage has been presented.
Austria has expelled 18 Russian diplomats since 2020. Despite its longstanding military neutrality, Vienna has joined EU sanctions against Moscow and provided political and financial assistance to Ukraine.
Moscow has previously responded to Austrian expulsions with reciprocal measures. In September 2025, Russia declared an Austrian diplomat persona non grata after Vienna expelled a Russian envoy over alleged espionage involving an employee of the Austrian energy company OMV. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said at the time that Moscow would respond to such moves in kind.
The diplomatic standoff escalated again in May, when Austria expelled three Russian Embassy employees over allegations that antennas installed on diplomatic buildings in Vienna were being used to intercept satellite communications. The Russian Embassy dismissed the accusations as “outrageous,” “unjustified” and politically motivated, warning of a harsh response.

articles.title: 491 days in the grey zone and losing both feet: exclusive details of the first-ever aerial evacuation aboard a Heavy Shot drone
articles.body:
491 days in the grey zone and losing both feet: exclusive details of the first-ever aerial evacuation aboard a Heavy Shot drone
In October, Ukraine's defence forces carried out the first-ever medical evacuation of a wounded soldier using a heavy unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV). The soldier, a member of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade who goes by the alias Magura, was airlifted from the grey zone aboard a Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 drone. No evacuation vehicle had been able to get to the area for over a year.
The roads are heavily mined, and FPV drones prowl the skies, destroying anything that moves within tens of kilometres. The brigade spent over six months preparing the daring rescue operation, which brought together heavy and light quadcopters, ground robots, electronic warfare units and even artillery.
"I realised there was a person down there: I wanted to get him to safety as quickly and safely as possible," a drone pilot recalls.
Ukrainska Pravda has interviewed the soldiers behind the operation, the drone's developers and the wounded serviceman. Find out how troops from the 2nd Mechanised Battalion of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade, named after Kostiantyn Ostrozkyi, teamed up with neighbouring units to pull off the evacuation and make history.
The operation was made possible by the coordinated efforts of the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade, the 14th and 30th Separate Mechanised Brigades, and the 10th Army Corps.
491 days
Sadly, this story began quite some time ago. On 2 June 2025, Kostiantyn "Magura" Vlasenko, an infantryman with the 2nd Mechanised Battalion of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade, set off from the rear with a fellow soldier for their positions on the Kupiansk front, which were on the left bank of the Oskil River. In the grey zone, Magura initially took shelter in one spot. But when it flooded, he had to move into an abandoned building.
His brother-in-arms was killed while making his way to a fallback position. Then, on 14 February 2026, a Russian drone dropped a munition that wounded Magura in both legs. Faced with a fight for survival and having lost one of his feet, he amputated the other foot himself, leaving him unable to get out of his position on his own.
There was no way to drag him out overland: the Oskil River, dense minefields and relentless Russian drone patrols made the approaches impassable. The battalion tried to use a ground robotic system to evacuate him, but Russian forces spotted and destroyed it while it was still on its way. Infantry groups also failed to reach him. Russian drones filled the skies, and Russian infantry had infiltrated the area around his position, effectively sealing it off.
All this is further evidence that the "golden hour" – the crucial first 60 minutes after an injury, when prompt medical treatment can mean the difference between life and death – is becoming increasingly difficult to meet on the modern battlefield. Evacuating wounded soldiers is a dangerous mission in its own right, and one that becomes harder with every passing year.
Every four to five days, drones brought Kostiantyn food, cigarettes and sweets. He kept in touch with his brothers-in-arms by walkie-talkie. He held out in his position until his evacuation on 4 October.
It was Alex, the reconnaissance chief overseeing UAV operations for the 2nd Mechanised Battalion, who came up with the idea of evacuating the soldier by air. It took around six months to move from the initial concept to the flight itself. The military had conventional Heavy Shot bomber drones, but these were not up to the task. The soldiers instead turned to the newly developed Heavy Shot Ayudag-6, a heavy-lift drone that can carry up to 130 kg and is equipped with a cargo winch.
"We'd been using Heavy Shot bomber drones for a long time and had an established line of communication with Gurzuf Defence," Alex said. "When I found out they were testing the new Ayudag-6 heavy-lift drone, I went to them immediately with this unconventional task. The drone was still a work in progress, but the developers were immediately fired up by the idea."
Gurzuf Defence designed the drone primarily for frontline logistics, as a heavy-lift modular platform. However, the engineers ensured from the very beginning that it had enough thrust to lift a person. The drone underwent two years of testing, during which the company's chief developer, Oleh Hynda, became the first person to fly aboard the test model.
"We never intended this drone to be just for evacuations – it's a heavy-duty logistics platform," Pavlo Feldblium, co-founder of Gurzuf Defence, told Ukrainska Pravda. "But we always knew it might have to be used for a rescue mission in certain circumstances. To prepare for this operation, we brought in units with experience of evacuating people using ground robotic systems. It was their experts who configured the winch and the mounting systems."
The company spent several months fine-tuning the platform at the unit's request. Experts from the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade's unmanned ground systems company then fitted the aircraft with additional equipment, and the 2nd Battalion's headquarters spent two months planning the operation. Around 15 military personnel were involved in preparing and planning the mission.
Pre-flight preparations took seven days. The military personnel worked out the flight routes, planned cover corridors and identified alternative emergency landing sites in case of a technical failure.
The evacuation drone was operated by Chornyi ("Black"), a squad leader in a mortar battery at the 2nd Mechanised Battalion of the 30th Mechanised Brigade. "I first got to know the Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 a week before the mission, when I took part in special training exercises. Until then, I'd only worked with standard Heavy Shot drones," he says.
The most dangerous part was hoisting the soldier, who had to attach himself to the cable on his own. The day before the flight, the drone delivered off-the-shelf mountaineering equipment and a phone loaded with a video explaining how to put on and secure the harness.
According to the plan, the soldier had to attach himself to the drone's winch with carabiners, sitting in a semi-reclined position. Any mistake when securing himself, or losing consciousness during the flight, could have sent him falling to the ground.
16 kilometres
Russian FPV anti-aircraft drones meant the cargo drone could not fly alone. Slow and bulky, with a payload suspended beneath it, it would be immediately spotted by Russian reconnaissance. The headquarters planned a diversionary manoeuvre to draw attention away from it.
Several formations helped provide cover for the operation. Alongside the 2nd Battalion of the 30th Mechanised Brigade, units from the 14th and 43rd Separate Mechanised Brigades took part, as did personnel and equipment from the 10th Army Corps. The day before the flight, the neighbouring units involved suggested putting it off because there was no fog. But the forecast showed no fog was expected any time soon, so the command decided to go ahead.
"We studied enemy drone activity to find the time when it was at its lowest. We decided to fly at first light, as night gave way to day," explains Alex, the battalion's reconnaissance chief.
The main diversion was carried out by Vampire heavy bomber drones, which flew into neighbouring sectors simultaneously to draw the attention of Russian anti-aircraft drone operators. The Russians shot down one Vampire, but the Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 carrying out the evacuation went unnoticed.
Alex spent 48 hours studying data on Russian assets around the planned mission area. Experts from the 3rd Army Corps also helped prepare the Ayudag's electronic warfare system for the flight.
An Autel quadcopter operated by the battalion provided visual cover for the Ayudag-6, giving the crew a pair of eyes in the sky. However, it struggled to keep pace with the faster evacuation drone. A Ukrainian Lucky Strike drone waited nearby, ready to ram any Russian reconnaissance or strike UAVs that appeared. As the aircraft carrying Magura returned, artillery from the 10th Army Corps delivered concentrated suppressive fire against the identified launch points used by Russian drone operators.
Headquarters had a backup plan in case the drone malfunctioned or was shot down over the left bank of the Oskil River. Reconnaissance teams and ground robot crews were standing by near the designated emergency landing sites, ready to respond.
The Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 relied on Starlink for communications, which kept Russian electronic warfare systems from jamming it. No interference was detected on the control links. The drone's altitude was adjusted to suit the terrain, and it took a different route back to prevent the Russians from identifying its outbound flight path.
The drone was in the air for less than an hour and a half. The operator spoke to the wounded soldier through the drone's onboard camera and microphone.
The drone could not cover the full 16 km on a single charge: carrying a person drained its batteries too quickly. Two ground support teams were deployed along the route in advance to provide the necessary support.
"On command, I flew to a waypoint, where the team changed the batteries. Then I continued to the evacuation point, picked up the wounded soldier and flew him back," says Chornyi, who piloted the evacuation drone.
At the transfer point, the wounded soldier was detached from the winch. The next leg of the evacuation was carried out by a Peacemaker ground robotic system, as using vehicles would have risked exposing the operation to the enemy.
The troops camouflaged the platform and laid mattresses in its cargo compartment. The remotely controlled Peacemaker then covered another 8 km off-road. Once in a safe area, the team transferred Kostiantyn to a vehicle and took him to a frontline stabilisation point for emergency surgery. The Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 returned to base intact after a battery change at a stop along the route.
Kostiantyn told Ukrainska Pravda: "The flight went smoothly. I spent most of the time looking at the terrain below. When I landed, I felt safe and relieved – I'd finally be able to see my family soon. A special thank you to my unit clerk, Livsha, for keeping me well supplied with treats."
Despite the soldier's calm assessment, the actual flight revealed issues that had been difficult to anticipate during training with a dummy load. He had not been given protective goggles, so the powerful airflow beneath the rotors and the headwind caused discomfort. However, this did not detract from the mission's overall success.
Alex also credited Kostiantyn's calmness during boarding with helping make the mission a success. He had to get onto the drone in an open area while its rotors were spinning above him.
"The soldier was exceptionally quick-thinking and determined to survive," he said. "We had already dropped off his equipment and instructions. When the quadcopter approached, he did everything exactly as instructed, as quickly as possible. There was no panic or hesitation – the whole thing took just seconds and went exactly to plan."
The future of aerial evacuation
One successful operation does not make aerial evacuation a regular option, nor can it replace ground-based evacuation. Missions like this require extensive preparation and coordinated support from multiple units. This operation involved reconnaissance, artillery, decoy-drone crews and ground teams. Without them, the aircraft carrying the wounded soldier would have been shot down by the first Russian interceptor drone on its way.
The drone's developers take a similar view. Gurzuf Defence says the risks to a casualty's life during flight are simply too high for aerial medical evacuation to become standard practice.
"We don't see aerial evacuation becoming routine," says Pavlo Feldblium, co-founder of Gurzuf Defence. "When people talk about thousands of such missions or suggest that drones could help meet the 'golden hour', I think of the science fiction of Ray Bradbury or Stanisław Lem. You can't launch an operation like this on the spur of the moment. Every mission is unique and has to be planned around the specific conditions on that section of the front line. It's important to understand that this is always a last resort."
The experience of rescuing Magura, however, has prompted changes to drone development. Gurzuf Defence has decided to equip its mass-produced Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 logistics drones with the technical modifications and mounting kits needed for emergency evacuations, enabling them to be used for rescue missions when necessary.
The company stresses, however, that the evacuation equipment will not necessarily be used on every flight: the drone remains primarily a logistics platform. The developers are also working on entirely new variants of the platform with a substantially higher payload capacity.
The operation has shown that wounded soldiers can be evacuated by air even if they cannot walk and are stranded in remote positions. Other manufacturers are also exploring this capability. SkyFall recently unveiled its StarGate evacuation drone.
This evacuation, carried out by the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade and the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade, has proved the viability of the concept and highlighted the urgent need for an evacuation method that can be used when all other options fail. Magura's rescue has set a precedent for saving lives in situations where conventional evacuation is impossible.
Kostiantyn "Magura" Vlasenko, who held a position on the left bank of the Oskil River for 491 days despite losing both feet, has been nominated for the title of Hero of Ukraine.
After Magura was evacuated to the rear, the commander of the 10th Army Corps visited him in hospital and personally presented him with the Order of Bohdan Khmelnytskyi, 3rd Class. The infantryman had been awarded the order in May, while still holding his position. Soldiers from the 2nd Mechanised Battalion of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade, who planned and carried out the aerial evacuation, have also been nominated for state awards.
Representatives of Gurzuf Defence – the manufacturer of the very Ayudag-6 that flew him out of hell – also visited Magura in hospital.
Yurii Denysiuk
Translated by Artem Yakymyshyn
Edited by Susan McDonald

articles.title: Railcar depot, temporary deployment sites for USV operators hit in Russian strikes
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Russian forces continued overnight strikes with unmanned aerial vehicles against railway infrastructure facilities, as well as Ukrainian ports and vessels used to support the Ukrainian armed forces, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
TASS has summarized the key details about the targets of the strikes.
Defense Ministry statement
Russian forces continued strikes with unmanned aerial vehicles against railway infrastructure facilities, as well as Ukrainian ports and vessels used in the interests of the Ukrainian armed forces, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
Targets hit
According to the ministry, the Poltava railcar depot in Poltava Region was hit. Its grounds are used by the Ukrainian armed forces to store and repair military equipment.
Russian forces also struck two temporary deployment sites for unmanned surface vessel (USV) operators, a boat mooring area and a USV storage site at the port of Vilkovo in Odessa Region, as well as port infrastructure used to store USVs and prepare them for deployment.
In addition, a cargo ship carrying supplies for the Ukrainian armed forces to the port of Odessa was struck at sea.
Russian troops used Geran drones to strike Norwegian-made mobile NASAMS surface-to-air missile systems in Zaporozhye and Dnepropetrovsk Regions, the Russian Defense Ministry reported, releasing footage of the strikes.
Russian forces also used Geran drones to strike a parked Mi-24 helicopter, a military supplies depot and a production building at one of Ukraine’s industrial enterprises.
Situation in Ukraine
A thermal power plant in Ukraine was damaged in explosions, and electricity generation was halted, Ukrainian energy holding company DTEK said on its Telegram channel.
The company did not disclose the name or location of the thermal power plant.

articles.title: Finland Prepares 36th Military Aid Package for Ukraine, Decision Expected by Year-End
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Finland Prepares 36th Military Aid Package for Ukraine, Decision Expected by Year-End
Finland is preparing its 36th military aid package for Ukraine, with a decision on its approval expected before the end of 2026, Militarnyi reported on October 23.
Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo announced the plans during a joint press conference with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv on October 22.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"We are currently preparing the 36th package in close cooperation with the Ukrainian military. We plan to make a decision by the end of this year," Orpo stated.
The Finnish government is coordinating the contents of the upcoming package directly with Ukraine's military to address its operational requirements. Details of the equipment and weapons under consideration have not yet been disclosed.
Orpo noted that Finland had already provided Ukraine with five military aid packages in 2026. He confirmed that Helsinki would continue supplying military equipment and supporting the training of Ukrainian personnel.
The planned delivery is part of Finland's continued military assistance to Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Previous shipments have included artillery ammunition, armored vehicles, and other military equipment.
Among the Finnish weapons already deployed by Ukrainian forces are 120 KRH 85 92 mortars and Crotale air defense systems, designated ItO 90M in Finnish service. The Crotale systems are designed to intercept low-altitude aerial targets, including aircraft, helicopters, and drones.
Finland approved its 35th military assistance package on October 9 in response to an urgent Ukrainian request. That shipment contained a single type of defense equipment from Finnish military stocks, while preparations for a larger follow-up package were already underway.
The upcoming package builds on a sharp increase in the scale of Finnish assistance earlier this autumn.
On September 15, Finland allocated its 34th package, worth approximately $335 million, its second-largest defense allocation to Kyiv since the full-scale invasion began. Part of the equipment was purchased directly from the Finnish defense industry, while the contents and delivery schedule remained confidential for operational security.
That decision raised the total value of Finnish defense aid to roughly $4.15 billion, up from about $3.68 billion after President Alexander Stubb approved the $138.5 million 33rd package on May 29.

articles.title: Signs point to renewed major US military ops against Iran
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Signs point to renewed major US military ops against Iran
The United States appears to be preparing to resume large-scale strikes against Iran, but there is unlikely to be a military solution for either side in the devastating conflict, experts say.
Washington and Tehran's forces have settled into a pattern of strikes on commercial ships, with the United States seeking to enforce a blockade of Iran's ports and the Islamic republic trying to exert control over the key Strait of Hormuz waterway.
Neither country has engaged in major attacks on land-based targets since early September, but that may soon change.
"I'm banking now on the likelihood of strikes shortly after the midterms," said Suzanne Maloney, director of the foreign policy program at the Brookings Institution, referring to November 3 elections in the United States.
She pointed to potential signs including the movement of additional US military assets and troops to the Middle East, warnings issued to Americans in the region, and a high alert status for Israeli forces.
Additionally, President Donald Trump "came out publicly and said that he wouldn't strike before the midterms," and "it wouldn't seem to help him at the polls to do so," Maloney said.
The US-Israeli war against Iran -- launched in late February -- is largely unpopular in the United States, especially because it has sharply driven up fuel prices, and is likely to be a drag on Trump's Republican Party in the key vote.
"Fundamentally, the situation isn't sustainable in its current state," Maloney said, noting that the US blockade is "creating greater pain for the Iranians," while Washington has a large number of naval assets tied up in enforcing it.
"There has to be some kind of a resolution, either through diplomacy or through military action," she said.
Asked about the Iran on Friday, Trump told journalists that "we could end it very quickly," but said the question is "do we want to finish it off, or... do we just want to let it wither?"
Tom Barrack, the US ambassador to Turkey and special envoy for Syria and Iraq, meanwhile said Friday that there could "absolutely" be a strike this weekend, ahead of Tuesday's Israeli elections.
'Impossible to predict'
Jason Campbell, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, said there have "certainly been recent signs that renewed strikes may be in the offing," or that "the US is expecting strikes carried out by Iran" or their Houthi allies in Yemen.
He noted the planned deployment of the USS Theodore Roosevelt to the Middle East -- which could at least temporarily bring the number of carrier strike groups there to three -- as well as the decision to dispatch another Marine Expeditionary Unit to the region.
Campbell also said Israeli warplanes recently carried out a "show of force" mimicking previous strikes on Iran, and noted that US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel.
However, "timing here is impossible to predict," he said of renewed strikes, while noting that "this is admittedly an expansive set of actions to take if the intent is to simply pressure Iran to the negotiating table."
Campbell said Trump's options are more limited than they were earlier in the conflict, with damage to US bases in the region having made any potential ground operation more difficult.
"At this point, there is no safe place to stage the thousands (in some scenarios tens of thousands) of forces that would be required for such an operation," he said.
Maloney meanwhile said that "most of the conventional military sites (in Iran) have already been heavily degraded" by previous strikes, meaning any new campaign will likely "entail more strikes on civilian infrastructure and targets that impact the Iranian population."
But that -- or any type of military action -- is unlikely to bring about a resolution to the conflict.
"From the start... this has been a war that can't be ended with further escalation on either side," Maloney said.
Campbell agreed, saying: "I do not see how renewed strikes on Iran akin to the first fifty days of the war will move the strategic needle for the Iranian regime."
"They have demonstrated a willingness to absorb a significant amount of physical pain and even some alterations to targeting that includes key mixed or even civilian infrastructure will not significantly change this," he added.

articles.title: Streeting declines to discuss Faslane shelters
articles.body:
The Secretary of State for Defence has declined to discuss reported ballistic shelters at Faslane in open session, telling the Defence Committee there is a difference between what others report and what the department is willing to say.
Wes Streeting was giving evidence to the committee on the work of his department.
Michelle Scrogham, the Labour member for Barrow and Furness, raised air and missile defence, noting the committee had heard that covering what is needed would cost a billion pounds per city. She said: “I am interested to hear it reported that Faslane is getting ballistic shelters. Are you looking at rolling that out in other areas?”
Streeting said: “There is a danger of my being dragged into a level of operational security detail that I would not want to share in this format.”
Scrogham replied: “It is public knowledge. It is in the UK Defence Journal.”
Streeting said: “There is a difference between what others report and what we are willing to say. Given the spirit in which we engage with this Committee, first, I would always be happy to try to share with the Committee in a closed format as much as we can of that which we would not want to share in an open session. Given your constituency interest in this, I can reassure you that the security of our nuclear deterrent and the enterprise that underpins it is obviously of the highest importance to us. I would be very happy to make sure that we properly brief you as the Member of Parliament for Barrow.”
Faslane on the Clyde is the base for the Vanguard class ballistic missile submarines that carry the continuous at-sea deterrent, and for the Astute class attack submarines. Coulport, a few miles away, stores and loads the warheads. Barrow-in-Furness, which Scrogham represents, is where the submarines are built by BAE Systems.
Earlier in the same exchange Streeting addressed homeland air defence more generally, saying the government is putting £790 million into integrated air and missile defence to modernise older systems and that a layered approach is needed. He noted that Luke Pollard had described the idea of an iron dome for Britain as an iron sieve.
Ministers confirmed in Parliament this month that a future requirement for hardened aircraft shelters across Royal Air Force bases in the United Kingdom has been identified, and that hardened shelters may form part of future infrastructure considerations at RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus.
The Defence Committee reported this week that Russian submarine and sabotage forces in the High North pose direct risks to the North Atlantic and to Britain, including to the nuclear deterrent, and that failure to deter Russia from underwater threats puts subsea data cables and energy pipelines in British waters at particular risk.

articles.title: Exclusive: Ukraine fears Trump could grant Russia long-sought relief for fertilizer industry
articles.body:
Exclusive: The next Russia deal Trump may be weighing after diesel
U.S. President Donald Trump looks on during an event in the Oval Office of the White House on Oct. 20, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
U.S. President Donald Trump may be considering further sanctions relief for Russia following his recent diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, several Ukrainian and U.S. officials familiar with the matter told the Kyiv Independent.
The potential move would fit an approach in which the Trump administration offers Russia economic benefits in hopes of persuading Moscow to end its war against Ukraine, one U.S. government official and one Senate official said.
Trump's diesel deal with Putin has drawn bipartisan criticism in Washington and strained relations with Kyiv. President Volodymyr Zelensky called the agreement a "weak move," warning that it could pave the way for further sanctions relief.
Now, Ukrainian officials fear the administration could explore a deal involving Russia's fertilizer industry, two people familiar with the matter said.
The U.S. has not directly sanctioned Russia's fertilizer industry or banned imports of Russian fertilizers. But any potential agreement could provide sanctions relief for vessels, companies, banks, and individuals linked to the industry, one senior Ukrainian official said.
Russia has long sought an ease of restrictions affecting its agricultural exports, arguing that banking, insurance, and shipping barriers have limited its access to markets.
Moscow raised the issue repeatedly during negotiations over the Black Sea Grain Initiative (BSGI) back in 2022, but Western governments maintained that Russian food and fertilizer exports were not directly sanctioned.
"The fertilizer story is quite old, and Russians were trying to push it long ago," a Ukrainian intelligence official told the Kyiv Independent.
"Russians always lobbied for fertilizer relief in contacts with Americans and Europeans," the official added. "They actually left BSGI because of no progress on fertilizers."
Russia withdrew from the Black Sea Grain Initiative in July 2023, saying insufficient progress had been made on its demands.
Ukrainian officials now fear Washington could be prepared to offer Moscow concessions on an issue it has pursued for years.
A sanctions-for-peace push
Trump announced the diesel deal on Oct. 9, saying Russia had agreed to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel to the U.S. and international markets.
"Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
The announcement raised questions in Washington about the deal's legality.
"We view the Russian diesel deal as illegal as per the 2022 law that had passed both chambers and was signed into law," one Senate official said.
Congress passed the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act in 2022, banning imports of Russian-origin energy products, including diesel.
Several people familiar with the matter said Democratic officials were contacting U.S. industries involved in facilitating the deal to ensure they understood the potential legal and investigative risks.
The deal could face further scrutiny in Congress. But as questions over its legality mount, Ukrainian officials fear Washington could seek other ways to offer Russia economic concessions, with fertilizers emerging as one possible area.
"Well, they clearly have some kind of plan," one official said.
Some Senate officials also believe the Trump administration overestimates the scale of the economic deals Russia could offer Washington in return.
The potential fertilizer deal remains unclear, and the officials who spoke to the Kyiv Independent named no specific sanctions Washington might lift.
The Kyiv Independent has contacted the White House for comment and will update the story when it receives a response.
read also
Kyiv warns against further concessions
The Ukrainian president has publicly warned that the diesel deal could be the start of a broader rollback of sanctions against Russia.
"There's intuition, there's intelligence, and there are various details," Zelensky said Oct. 16. "In my view, we cannot accept these agreements. Because gas deals will follow. And I am absolutely certain of this. After gas, they will lift sanctions on other things as well."
The warning shows Kyiv's concern that Washington is shifting toward economic incentives for Moscow even as Russia continues its war against Ukraine.
Before the diesel announcement, Russian officials had repeatedly argued that Moscow and Washington should expand their business ties. The Trump administration, meanwhile, had maintained that economic deals should follow an end to Russia's war.
Ukrainian officials argue that offering concessions before securing a ceasefire is unlikely to persuade Putin to stop fighting. Instead, they say, such agreements could provide Russia with additional revenue while leaving Moscow's military objectives unchanged.
The concern is especially acute because, according to Ukrainian officials, Russia offered the U.S. nothing meaningful in return for the diesel deal.
"It's clear that this only encourages Putin," one senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent.
"He feels that he can go with a war against us, and on top of that, our allies are lifting sanctions against him and striking deals with him."
Speaking to Russian media on Oct. 22, Putin once again made his intentions clear.
Asked whether he would agree to a ceasefire allowing Ukraine to retain the territory it controls, he replied: "It's not their territory; it's the territory of historical Russia."

articles.title: Europe will have to accept dependence on us – US tech giant
articles.body:
Europe will have to accept dependence on us – US tech giant
European governments should stop worrying about their growing dependence on American AI, US tech giant Palantir’s top executive for the UK and Europe has said. Instead, they should focus on the advantages the products offer, particularly against Russia, Palantir UK CEO Louis Mosley believes.
The European Commission is frantically trying to reduce reliance on American tech and the US in general.
“Europe is going to have to accept some dependency,” Mosely told Bloomberg News this week.
The Commission estimates that the bloc relies on foreign providers for over 80% of its digital products, services, infrastructure, and intellectual property. However, many are skeptical that replacement is possible. In a Wire’s 2025 survey cited by the European Parliament, only 16% of regional IT leaders said the bloc could achieve digital sovereignty within five years, with almost 60% citing US dominance as a key obstacle.
Nevertheless, this year several European governments have rejected Palantir products or announced plans to phase them out. France’s domestic intelligence agency, the DGSI, which adopted the company’s analytical software in 2015, has plans to drop it over the coming years in favor of a domestically developed alternative from ChapsVision.
“We cannot depend on the goodwill of certain partners who, as we’ve seen in recent days, are capable of cutting off access to models,” Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said when announcing the decision in June.
Berlin has reportedly chosen the same French competitor over Palantir for Germany’s domestic intelligence agency BfV.
Similar moves to ostracize the American firm have been reported in Spain and Denmark, as well as the non-EU nations of Switzerland, Norway, and the UK.
Mosley cited Palantir’s extensive use of the Ukraine conflict as a testing ground for its military solutions, saying “the questions around sovereignty are secondary” for Kiev. The company got involved in Ukraine following the escalation of Kiev’s conflict with Russia in 2022, supplying what it calls “targeting packages.”
One of Palantir’s flagship products is Maven, an AI-powered system that processes vast amounts of intelligence data to help identify targets and generate strike recommendations for troops. It accelerates the so-called “kill chain,” allowing the military to consider substantially more potential targets than human personnel previously could.
Originally developed as a Pentagon project, Maven involved Google until 2018, when employee protests prompted the company to withdraw from the initiative. NATO purchased its own version of the system for use at its European headquarters in March 2025.
“I can provide categorical reassurance that where customers have bought our software, they are in full operational control of that software,” Mosley assured in a separate interview with Reuters concerning NATO’s purchase.
There are no kill switches. There’s no ability for Palantir or the US government to reach in and switch it off.
The US government has a track record of restricting foreign access to flagship AI models. The French prime minister’s remark about a lack of goodwill was a reference to Washington’s blockage of Anthropic’s Mythos 5 tool, which lasted for almost three weeks.

articles.title: Air Force Considering Air-to-Air Role for Bombers amid Fighter Procurement Constraints
articles.body:
The Air Force’s future strategy for fighting wars could include arming bombers with air-to-air strike capabilities, the service said in a new report to Congress.
The report, titled “Long-Term USAF Fighter Force Structure” and submitted to lawmakers Oct. 16, said that “developing air-to-air capabilities on bombers” is being considered as a way to expand the service’s combat capabilities.
In the report, which was briefed to reporters Oct. 20 and obtained by Air & Space Forces Magazine, the Air Force estimates it will need 1,509 combat-coded aircraft by 2035 to meet the demands of the National Defense Strategy at moderate risk, with about 40 percent of its fighter fleet consisting of F-35A Joint Strike Fighters. That’s up from the 1,288 combat-coded fighters the service has today.
The Air Force is working on ways to procure as many Lockheed Martin F-35As, Boeing F-15EX Eagle IIs, and Boeing F-47 sixth-generation fighters as possible, the report said. However, the report acknowledges that hitting its fighter procurement targets may not be achievable due to “fiscal realities and industrial production limitations.”
Other recapitalization options could include acquiring an entirely new fighter, relying more on semi-autonomous drone fighters known as Collaborative Combat Aircraft—and giving air-to-air roles and capabilities to bombers, the report said.
Air Force fighters have long carried out air-to-ground strikes, but bombers have not traditionally performed air-to-air missions.
However, with the Air Force’s fleet constrained by slow procurement of new fighters and the retirement of aging ones, the service has been looking for new ways to accomplish its missions.
Former Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. David Allvin signaled an openness to the B-21 Raider stealth bomber carrying out a greater role in the service’s air dominance plans in an October 2024 discussion with reporters in Washington.
At the time, the Air Force had put its F-47 program—then called Next-Generation Air Dominance—on hold amid concerns about its potential costs. The Air Force was reviewing its approach to air superiority to try to figure out ways to get the job done, potentially without the plane that would become the F-47.
When asked if the air superiority review could lead to a more prominent role for the B-21, Allvin said “We have not taken that off the table.”
A year later, in September 2025, sources told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the Air Force was studying whether a large flying wing-type stealth aircraft—potentially based on a B-21—armed with dozens of air-to-air missiles could be an element of its future air superiority force.
In its latest report, the Air Force wrote that it is “committed to the full modernization and recapitalization of its legacy fighter fleet, while placing an enormous effort into our newest fighter, the F-47.”
CCAs are also rapidly advancing and likely to at least meet, if not beat, the program’s schedule, the report said. But the Air Force said CCAs aren’t yet ready to change how the service plans for its future fighter fleet, though that day will come.
“There is absolutely a world in which the incorporation of CCAs into the force will mitigate the requirement for the number of fighters,” Lt. Gen. David Tabor, deputy chief of staff for plans and programs, told reporters Oct. 20.
The report also said it will be “essential” to modernize its current cadre of older F-15s and F-16s into a fleet of “advanced fourth-generation capability” jets—planes that do not have stealth capabilities but can still operate in highly contested environments, often with the aid of advanced sensors and electronic warfare weapons.
But it would take more than a decade of investments in the Air Force’s current depot infrastructure to modernize enough jets to increase the Air Force’s aircraft availability, the report said, calling that approach “insufficient, as it perpetuates reliance on a fleet averaging 30+ years in age.”
Aside from upgrading existing fighters, the service could also buy new advanced fourth-gen jets like the F-15EX and, potentially, a new version of Lockheed Martin’s F-16 Fighting Falcon, dubbed the F-16G. Tabor said the service has not yet made any decision on buying new F-16s, “and we’re not in a position where that decision has to be made immediately.”
In its report, the Air Force said it has to pursue a two-track strategy of modernizing existing aircraft to meet immediate operational requirements, while recapitalizing its legacy fighters at the same time.

articles.title: US offers Russia Nord Stream restart as part of peace deal
articles.body:
US proposes restart of Nord Stream as part of peace deal with Russia
The United States is proposing that Russian gas supplies to Europe and the operation of the Nord Stream pipeline be resumed as an economic incentive for Moscow as part of a potential peace settlement to end Russia's war against Ukraine.
Source: The Economist
Details: The Economist describes the gas proposal as the latest concession Washington is offering Vladimir Putin. Ukrainian officials, meanwhile, do not yet know all the details of the latest US proposals.
The magazine reports that Russia would be offered commercial deals with US companies, sanctions relief and the normalisation of political relations. Ukraine would be offered an investment package and EU membership in exchange for abandoning its bid to join NATO. The proposals also envisage the creation of a demilitarised zone in Donbas.
The Economist stresses that the US cannot unilaterally decide to restore Russian gas supplies to the European market. It assesses that such a proposal would run counter to EU law.
Ukrainian negotiators fear that US representatives could strike lucrative economic deals with Russia even before the war ends.
The Economist itself questions Moscow's willingness to make peace. It assesses that Russia is likely to drag out the negotiations while securing immediate concessions on sanctions.
The renewed diplomatic push comes after US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff visited St Petersburg on 21 October, The Economist notes.
Background: On 18 October, it was reported that the Trump administration had proposed that Europe resume purchases of Russian gas. According to The New York Times, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff raised the idea during talks with Ukrainian and European officials.

articles.title: Israeli airstrikes, artillery shelling hit southern Lebanon amid intensified drone activity
articles.body:
Israeli warplanes carried out airstrikes and artillery shelling in southern Lebanon on Friday, while drones flew intensively at low altitude over the capital Beirut and the southern city of Tyre, Lebanese state media reported, Anadolu reports.
Lebanon’s state-run National News Agency (NNA) said Israeli fighter jets struck the vicinity of Ali al-Taher hill on the outskirts of Nabatieh al-Fawqa in the Nabatieh district.
The agency reported intermittent Israeli artillery shelling near the town of Zawtar al-Sharqiya in the same district before noon.
In Kfar Shouba, in the Hasbaya district, an Israeli drone dropped a stun grenade in the Khallet Zuhair area on the outskirts of the town.
The agency also said Israeli forces carried out a large explosion overnight in an area between Zawtar al-Sharqiya and Kfar Tebnit in the Nabatieh district.
Israeli forces continued setting fire to wooded areas in the town of Qantara toward the Salouqi area in the Marjayoun district, it added.
Meanwhile, Israeli drones were observed flying at low altitude over Beirut, Tyre and surrounding areas in southern Lebanon.
The attacks came after two days of US-sponsored technical military talks between Lebanon and Israel that began Tuesday in the US state of Florida, with no results announced.
On June 26, Beirut and Tel Aviv reached a US-mediated framework agreement providing for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from occupied Lebanese territory in exchange for the deployment of the Lebanese army and the disarmament of armed groups.
The agreement also introduced a pilot-zone approach to implementation, but its provisions have so far been applied in only three southern Lebanese towns: Froun, Srifa and Zawtar al-Gharbiya, while more than 50 towns remain under Israeli occupation.
Despite the agreement, Israeli attacks on Lebanon have continued, killing at least 4,386 people and injuring 12,407 others since March 2, while displacing more than 1 million people.
Israel continues to occupy areas of southern Lebanon, including territory held for decades and other areas seized during previous conflicts.

articles.title: The new Arab bargain: When Egypt offers to protect Saudi Arabia
articles.body:
When Egyptian officials signalled their readiness to support Saudi Arabia against attacks by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis, the announcement was presented as a familiar display of Arab solidarity. Yet beneath the diplomatic rhetoric lies a much more significant story, one that says less about military cooperation and more about the changing balance of power in the Middle East.
The immediate question appears straightforward: What kind of protection can Egypt realistically offer Saudi Arabia?
The more important question is whether Egypt’s offer reveals that the traditional hierarchy of the Arab world has been quietly reversed.
For decades, Egypt occupied a unique position in Arab politics. It was the state that projected military weight, diplomatic influence, and cultural authority across the region. Saudi Arabia possessed financial power, but Cairo was widely regarded as the Arab world’s strategic center of gravity.
Today, however, the relationship between the two countries is increasingly defined by a different reality. Egypt remains demographically and militarily significant, but its economic fragility has created a level of dependence on Gulf stability that would have been almost unimaginable in previous generations.
The offer to help defend Saudi Arabia therefore deserves to be viewed not as a demonstration of Egyptian strength, but as evidence of a broader geopolitical transformation.
Military realities explain why.
Despite possessing one of the Arab world’s largest armed forces, Egypt is neither politically nor economically positioned to undertake a large-scale military intervention in Yemen.
The trauma of Gamal Abdel Nasser’s disastrous Yemen campaign in the 1960s remains deeply embedded in Egyptian strategic thinking. That conflict consumed enormous military resources, cost thousands of lives, and distracted Cairo from more immediate national priorities.
No Egyptian leadership is likely to repeat that experience.
Moreover, Egypt today faces a crowded security agenda closer to home. Instability in Sudan, uncertainty in Libya, tensions in the Red Sea, challenges in Sinai, and concerns surrounding the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam all compete for Cairo’s attention. Under such circumstances, the prospect of deploying large numbers of Egyptian troops into another protracted Yemeni conflict appears highly improbable.
If Egypt contributes militarily, its role will likely be concentrated in the maritime domain: securing sea lanes, protecting Red Sea navigation routes, enhancing intelligence cooperation, and supporting regional deterrence efforts. These are meaningful contributions, but they fall far short of the image invoked by traditional narratives of Arab military intervention.
This is where the deeper story emerges.
The Houthis are not merely threatening Saudi Arabia. They are threatening Egypt’s economic lifeline.
The disruption of shipping through the Bab al-Mandab Strait has severely affected traffic through the Suez Canal, one of Egypt’s most important sources of foreign currency. Every escalation in the Red Sea directly translates into economic pressure on Cairo.
In practical terms, Egypt’s interest in stabilizing the Gulf and confronting threats to regional navigation is not an act of altruism; it is an act of economic self-preservation.
That should not be surprising.
States do not mobilize because of gratitude. They mobilize because of interests.
Yet Middle Eastern political discourse still tends to frame relations between Arab states through the language of fraternity, loyalty, and historical obligation. Such language often obscures what is actually taking place. Egypt’s support for Saudi Arabia is driven not by sentiment but by a recognition that Egyptian prosperity is increasingly linked to Gulf stability.
The irony is striking.
For much of the twentieth century, wealthy Arab states depended upon Egypt as a source of political legitimacy, military expertise, and strategic backing. Today, Egypt’s own economic stability has become intertwined with Gulf investment, Gulf aid, and Gulf confidence.
This is not a temporary fluctuation. It reflects a structural shift in how power operates within the Arab world.
The rise of Gulf sovereign wealth funds, ambitious development strategies, and expanding regional investment networks has altered the traditional equation. Political influence is no longer derived primarily from military manpower or ideological leadership. It increasingly flows from economic resilience, investment capacity, and the ability to shape regional outcomes through finance.
Under this new reality, Saudi Arabia has become not merely an oil producer or regional actor, but one of the principal anchors of economic stability across significant parts of the Arab world.
Seen from this perspective, another apparent contradiction suddenly becomes easier to understand.
While expressing support for Saudi Arabia, Egypt also maintains diplomatic communication with Iran. To some observers, this appears inconsistent. Why would Cairo coordinate with Riyadh while simultaneously engaging Tehran?
The answer lies in the changing nature of Middle Eastern politics.
The region no longer operates according to the rigid bloc politics that defined much of the past decade. Saudi Arabia itself has restored relations with Iran. The United Arab Emirates maintains extensive economic links with Tehran. Across the region, governments increasingly seek to combine deterrence with dialogue rather than choose between them.
Egypt’s communication with Iran therefore reflects a wider regional trend: reducing the risk of escalation while maintaining strategic alignments. Cairo has little interest in becoming a frontline participant in a broader regional confrontation. Its primary objective is stability, particularly in waterways and trade corridors that directly affect its economic survival.
This calculation exposes a larger truth about the contemporary Middle East.
The old question, “Who protects whom?” may no longer make sense.
Saudi Arabia does not require Egyptian divisions stationed on the Yemeni front to guarantee its security. Equally, Egypt cannot sustain its economic stability without a relatively secure Gulf environment. What has emerged instead is a relationship of mutual dependence, in which military capability and economic power reinforce one another.
The traditional image of Egypt as the Arab world’s protector and Saudi Arabia as its financier belongs increasingly to another era.
A new bargain is taking shape.
Egypt remains too important to be ignored. Saudi Arabia remains too influential to be separated from broader Arab stability. Yet neither country occupies the role it once held. The balance has become more symmetrical, more transactional, and arguably more honest.
That is why Egypt’s offer to defend Saudi Arabia matters.
Not because it signals the beginning of a new war, but because it reveals the emergence of a new Arab order. An order in which economics has become as important as armies, investment as influential as ideology, and mutual dependence more decisive than old narratives of leadership.
The real significance of Cairo’s offer is therefore not military at all.
It is historical.
For the first time in modern Arab politics, the region’s traditional center of political gravity is openly acknowledging that its own security and prosperity are inseparable from the stability of the Gulf. And in that admission lies one of the most consequential geopolitical shifts the Arab world has witnessed since the end of the Cold War.
The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Monitor.

articles.title: Zelensky accuses Trump of ‘totally false’ statements
articles.body:
Zelensky accuses Trump of ‘totally false’ statements
President Donald Trump made “totally false” statements when he blamed rising US diesel prices on Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, Vladimir Zelensky has claimed, accusing the American leader of “deflecting the focus away from Iran.”
Zelensky’s remarks came amid a growing spat with Trump, who has repeatedly accused Kiev of exacerbating the global energy crisis with continued attacks on Russian oil infrastructure.
Russia has historically been the world’s second-largest exporter of diesel fuel, behind only the United States, accounting for roughly 10% of global exports. Disruptions to Russian supplies have tightened the global market, driving up prices even in countries that do not directly import Russian fuel, including the US.
“The volume of diesel exports is so negligible from Russia that it has zero impact on prices in the US. That is totally false information,” the Ukrainian leader claimed during an appearance on Steven Bartlett’s The Diary of a CEO podcast on Thursday.
If Trump cares so much about US energy prices, then “why do American companies export energy?” Zelensky wondered rhetorically. “Well, because how can the president of the United States ban private sector exports?... It sells and money comes in.”
Zelensky accused Trump of unfairly “deflecting the focus away from Iran” and lamented that “everything gets shifted onto us and I’m made the target as the leader of our country.”
According to Zelensky, “the root of the problem” lies in the Strait of Hormuz, where crude exports and other maritime traffic have dwindled to a trickle following the start of the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran in February.
Earlier this month, Zelensky similarly hit out at what he described as a “weak decision” by the Trump administration after Washington temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel exports to ease the global fuel crisis.
Moscow agreed to immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to American and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November, another million tons shortly thereafter, and potentially another 3 million tons, depending on refinery capacity.
Washington struck the deal with Moscow after Zelensky had repeatedly ignored Trump’s requests to stop strikes on Russian refineries. “We said, you can do whatever you want to Russia, don’t hit the refineries, because that’s a world problem that’s caused,” the US president recounted earlier this month.
“And what does he do? He goes and hits the diesel fuel,” Trump lamented, accusing Zelensky of wanting to “make problems for the world.”
Trump also said he found it more difficult to deal with Zelensky than with Russian President Vladimir Putin, suggesting that Ukraine should get a new leader who would not obstruct Washington’s mediation efforts.
Rising fuel prices have become an increasingly pressing domestic issue for Trump ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. US diesel prices surged to record highs above $6.50 per gallon in September, with prices in California exceeding $8 in some areas.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said last week that Zelensky was directly challenging Trump by refusing to accept a deal aimed at easing the global diesel shortage.
In recent months, Ukraine has ramped up long-range strikes on targets inside Russia, including civilian and energy infrastructure, amid continued setbacks at the front. Moscow has denounced the attacks as acts of terrorism and responded with strikes on Ukrainian military-related facilities.

articles.title: Putin claims Russia is ready for new talks with Ukraine, calls occupied land historical Russia
articles.body:
Russia is ready to resume three-way talks with Ukraine and the US, Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed in an interview with Pavel Zarubin of state broadcaster VGTRK, published on 22 October. He said they should settle security for both countries after a final peace deal, not a brief pause.
Putin spoke a day after he hosted US envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he would accept freezing the war along the front line. In May, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov named Ukraine’s withdrawal from Donbas and Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts as the only condition for peace. Any new round would start from that gap: Kyiv offers to stop where the armies stand, while Moscow’s last stated terms demanded more land.
Talks in November
Putin stated that Moscow and Washington had agreed Russia was ready to resume trilateral contacts. He added that he generally agreed with a US point that European security architecture should also be discussed.
On 21 October, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov stated that the sides had settled on mid-November, with Abu Dhabi as the likely venue.
"Historical Russia"
In a 21 October Fox News interview, asked about a freeze leaving Ukraine 75% or more of its land, Zelenskyy answered: “Yes, right now, we have to freeze.”
Trump cannot get Putin to halt strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, so he blames Ukraine instead, Zelenskyy says
Asked about the land Ukraine would give up, Putin replied that the occupied regions were not Ukraine’s but "historical Russia." He claimed their residents had voted for independence and then to join Russia, and called any talk of territorial losses inappropriate.
Putin linked Russia’s readiness to negotiate to Ukrainians being a people very close to Russians. He claimed the latest genetic studies show they are one people. Independent outlet Meduza noted it is unclear which studies he meant. Putin’s 12 July 2021 essay on the historical unity of Russians and Ukrainians made the same case, which Ukraine’s national memory institute rebutted.
He closed that answer by asserting Russia would achieve all the goals of what the Kremlin calls its special military operation. He made a similar vow on 17 December 2025.

articles.title: US has suffered strategic defeats in war with Iran
articles.body:
In remarks published by Iranian media on Friday, Mohebbi said the enemy initially sought to change Iran’s political system and disintegrate the country, before dividing its objectives into 13 smaller goals, none of which it achieved.
He said the war has undermined Washington’s claim that its military presence in the region guaranteed security, noting that despite its large naval fleet and numerous regional bases, the United States had faced challenges in ensuring security and reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
The IRGC spokesman described the situation as a contradiction in US military doctrine, saying bases intended to provide security had instead become sources of insecurity.
He also said the war had called into question Washington’s claims of intelligence superiority and exposed the vulnerabilities of its intelligence centers and bases.
The targeting of US fighter jets, destruction of air defense systems and operations against American naval equipment, he added, had dealt a blow to the country’s claimed technological and military superiority.
Mohebbi further stated that the United States had suffered damage to its international standing, saying its reputation had already been affected by the Jeffrey Epstein case and had been further tarnished by the targeting of the Minab school and the killing of children.
He also pointed to the economic consequences of the war for the United States, citing rising fuel prices and the country’s need for raw materials, including aluminum, as signs of mounting economic difficulties.
Concluding his remarks, the IRGC spokesman praised the Iranian people’s resilience, saying their achievements during the period of resistance had been remarkable and deserved recognition.
