articles.title: Russian forces strike NASAMS air defense systems in Zaporozhye, Dnepropetrovsk Regions
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Russian troops have used Geran drones to strike Norwegian-made mobile NASAMS surface-to-air missile systems in Zaporozhye and Dnepropetrovsk Regions, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"The published footage shows Geran-4 Seeker drone operators from the Rubicon Center striking key military facilities in Ukraine’s rear areas. In particular, precise strikes by Rubicon’s Geran drone operators hit Norwegian-made mobile NASAMS surface-to-air missile systems near the settlements of Shirokoye in Zaporozhye Region and Bashmachka in Dnepropetrovsk Region," the ministry said.
In addition, a previously detected Ukrainian P-18 Malakhit radar station was destroyed near Kotlyarovka in Dnepropetrovsk Region. Real-time footage documenting the strikes confirmed that the designated targets had been successfully hit.

articles.title: The best books from Meduza’s publishing house, according to the people who work here
articles.body:
The best books from Meduza’s publishing house, according to the people who work here
In the three years since Meduza launched its publishing house, we’ve published more than 30 books in Russian. Now, when people ask which we recommend, we have to ask a few questions: Fiction or nonfiction? Or perhaps diaries or autofiction? And on what subject? War, history, politics, film, music, parenting? Yes, we have all of that, and we’re very proud of it. Choosing just one is getting harder. But we gave it a try — and asked our colleagues to write a few sentences about their favorite book from Meduza’s publishing house. Save the list or buy the books as gifts for people you love. Every recommendation here comes straight from the heart.
Galina Timchenko, publisher
Anton Dolin, “Plokhiye russkiye” (“Bad Russians”)
Reading books because it’s all “work — deadlines — got to get it done…” really isn’t as much fun as choosing a book yourself. There’s a story we tell in the newsroom about “Bad Russians”: After the first edit, the manuscript grew by 300,000 characters. And yes, it’s an enormous book, but I found “Bad Russians” as gripping as a detective novel. I even rewatched some of the films I thought I remembered down to the last frame. It was a rare weekend when nothing could get me off the couch. Anton’s extraordinary gift for storytelling is matched by his expertise. I think this is his best book, though he’d surely pick a different one (he’s published 15 already).
Ivan Kolpakov, Meduza’s editor-in-chief
Sergei Lebedev, “Belaya dama” (“The Lady of the Mine”)
Meduza’s publishing house has been around for three years now, and this is still one of my favorite books we’ve published — definitely my favorite work of fiction. The blurb opens with “July 2014, Donbas,” so you might immediately form all kinds of ideas about this book. But unless you already know something about it, I’m sure you won’t guess what it’s like. Anyway, I want to declare my love for this book and its author. Thank you, dear Sergei Lebedev. And to anyone who somehow hasn’t heard of it, I recommend buying it right away.
A. Z., publishing editor
Lana Estemirova, “Pozhaluysta, zhivi” (“Please Live”)
“It mattered to me that this book could be read by a housewife in Ohio, a girl in Germany interested in strong women, and people in Russia who know nothing about Chechnya,” Lana Estemirova says of “Please Live.” For me, the way this book speaks to everyone is perhaps its greatest strength. It brings together hazy childhood memories and wartime chronicles; family stories about how her grandfather survived deportation in 1944 and human rights reports on war crimes in the 1990s; and teenage experiences captured in emails and diaries alongside newspaper articles about the rise of authoritarianism in Chechnya in the 2000s.
The book isn’t detailed enough to be called a biography, isn’t objective enough to claim to be a historical study of Chechnya, and is too painfully true to count as autofiction. But somehow, magically, it weaves together the best of all three genres — more than three, really. A documentary account becomes a sweeping novel about growing up, loss, working through grief, and an immense, incredibly powerful maternal love that even death cannot defeat.
Without false modesty, and with enormous gratitude to the translator who worked under a pseudonym, I’ll say that “Please Live” is equally good in English and Russian.
Dmitry Ivanov, publishing editor
Konstantin Gaaze, “Kuda dreyfuyut diktatury?” (“Where Do Dictatorships Drift?”)
Over these three years, I’ve read quite a few books (and even edited some) devoted to the same question: How did we end up here? Why did Russia attack Ukraine, disregarding the views of its own people, the judgment of the international community, and, finally, historical memory? Different authors offered different answers, but perhaps no one has examined the problem as deeply and systematically as Konstantin Gaaze in “Where Do Dictatorships Drift?” His account doesn’t start in the era of Peter the Great or with Ukraine’s Maidan protests. He aims to show that the current outbreak of Russian aggression was neither predetermined by some historical trajectory nor solely a response to the other side’s actions, as Vladimir Putin’s favorite refrain — “we were left with no choice” — would have it.
Konstantin reconstructs the basic logic of autocracy from Herodotus to the present to show that the Kremlin’s stance toward the West developed along the fairly common “besieged fortress” model. Ukraine became the target of the attack through a whole series of steps taken by Vladimir Putin and his inner circle beginning in 2008. Those steps pulled in different directions and were sometimes independent of one another. Readers will learn how an autocrat’s fears prompt his inner circle to peddle threats, where the “Putin majority” came from and what sustains it, why liberal economists and administrators lost their strategic struggle with officials from the security services and law enforcement, and, finally, how the 2008–09 global financial crisis relates to Putin’s conviction that America could no longer tell him what to do. Where do dictatorships drift? Konstantin Gaaze’s answer: often toward a major war, though with whom and on what terms depends on the particular historical circumstances.
Hi, I’m Vladislav Gorin.
I’m the host of Meduza’s daily Russian-language news podcast. This summer, the Russian authorities opened a criminal case against me — not for committing a crime, but for telling the truth about Russia and its war against Ukraine.
Because the Kremlin has branded me a criminal, I can’t go home. I also can’t safely travel to countries like Turkey — even though it’s a NATO member — because I could be arrested and extradited to Russia. I can’t even renew my passport at the consulate anymore.
None of this is going to stop me. I know there are hundreds of thousands of people in Russia who don’t want this war and who still believe in freedom and democracy, and they deserve access to independent journalism. Please support Meduza so I can keep reaching them.
Sonya, publishing manager
Konstantin Zarubin, “Nashe serdtse byotsya za vsekh” (“Our Heart Beats for Everyone”)
Some books create worlds that, for some inexplicable reason, lodge in your head for good. You’ll be standing in the checkout line at the supermarket, lost in thought, and suddenly find yourself somewhere far, far away without even noticing. Konstantin Zarubin’s novel is one of the books I “jump” into like that. A Selecta cappuccino from a coffee machine in the gray corridors of Iceland’s immigration office, a commuter train car baked by the summer sun on the Riga–Saulkrasti line, the summer cottage community of Medvedkovo, and an awkward portrait drawn in crayon from a VKontakte photo — I remember every house, every street, and every name in “Our Heart.”
I’m mesmerized by this broken, complicated world, so indifferent to the people who live in it. Absolutely anything can happen there — bad or good. I think it’s this unpredictability (sometimes quite cruel), with all its “chance” coincidences and encounters, that puts our humanity to the test and makes life what it is.
Quoting a review, Zarubin calls his novel “a decent light read.” I think that’s an understatement. “Our Heart” is certainly written with a light touch and plenty of wit, and it’s a pleasure to read. But I don’t think just “a light read” (even a decent one) can get so deep inside your head.
Natasha, manager of Meduza’s Magaz shop
Zhenya Berezhnaya, ”(Ne) o voyne” (”(Not) About War”)
”(Not) About War” is a book about the very first days of the full-scale war and being forced to leave. At first, you tense up with anxiety as you read the especially difficult passages. Then, page by page, you begin to relax. By the end, the heaviness gives way to hope: Everything will be all right.
And yet the war never goes away. It’s there the whole time, but even in a world like this, there’s still room for a miracle. I think that’s what the book is about.
The writing helps, too. Before the war, Zhenya Berezhnaya wrote fairy tales, and you can hear echoes of that in the novel: It’s a painful autobiographical story told in wonderfully warm, inviting language.
The book’s design deserves a mention of its own: Yellow symbols are scattered across a green background — they could be spiky anti-tank obstacles or little flowers with petals. Just like the book itself, where a miracle grows alongside the war.
I’m not the only one who liked it: The novel was shortlisted for the Dar literary prize.
Olya V., publishing staff member
Maria Alyokhina, “Politicheskaya. Kak vyzhit v iz Rossii” (“Political Girl: Life and Fate in Russia”)
I didn’t think I’d like Maria Alyokhina’s “Political Girl: Life and Fate in Russia.” But I was wrong. This book is a candid, dramatic diary that never slips into melodrama. Alyokhina feels injustice acutely, and even in the most difficult situations, she doesn’t let hurt and fear get the better of her.
“We don’t choose where we’re born. We don’t choose the color or the lettering on our passports. But we do choose how we live,” Maria writes. The book is her account of that choice. Perhaps “A Political Prisoner” will give you hope and strength — so many people are short of both in these dark days.
And — most importantly — Punkʼs not dead!
Alexander Polivanov, deputy editor-in-chief
Ilya Barabanov and Denis Korotkov, “Nash biznes — smert” (“Our Business Is Death”)
I read Ilya Barabanov and Denis Korotkov’s book about the Wagner private military company roughly two years after Yevgeny Prigozhin’s mutiny and his death. I thought I’d give up halfway through — I mean, what could it tell me about Prigozhin that journalists (including Barabanov and Korotkov themselves) hadn’t already reported?
But “Our Business Is Death” is a book you race through; some of the events feel as if you’re learning about them for the first time. Partly because as soon as something drops out of the news, you forget the details, the things that made it distinctive fade, and all that’s left is a few lines on Wikipedia. From where we stand in 2025–26, Prigozhin’s mutiny seems unimaginable, while his methods of managing people and waging war have, sadly, become commonplace.
A. F., news editor
Sergei Lebedev, “The White Lady” (and more!)
Much of today’s Russian-language publishing abroad focuses on political and social commentary and nonfiction, and that makes sense. It’s really great that Meduza’s publishing house also pays such close attention to contemporary fiction and discovers talented Russian-language authors. Konstantin Zarubin and his novel “Our Heart Beats for Everyone” deserve special mention — it’s a gripping cyberpunk utopia that is, horrifyingly, coming true almost to the letter. Or there’s Natalia Krupenina’s moving young adult book “Ya umeyu padat” (“I Know How to Fall”), a healing balm and a lifeline for teenagers (and adults, too!) in difficult times.
But for now, my top pick is “The Lady of the Mine.”
One setting: a mining settlement in the Donbas. Four characters: Zhanna, Valet, the general, and the engineer. Just five chapters: five days in the summer of 2014. Sergei Lebedev’s novel is compact and full of substance, fewer than 200 pages, but its seemingly simple, self-contained plot quickly expands into a tragedy of universal proportions. The author builds his narrative around the real history of this ill-fated Ukrainian region, closely intertwining events from the current war and a past one: Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17, shot down by pro-Kremlin separatists, and a mine pit that the Nazi occupiers used for executions. The historical parallels really are chilling. It takes your breath away, as great literature does.
P.S. If you do prefer commentary and want more facts about this story, I recommend pairing Lebedev’s novel with “Dom na linii ognya” (“A House in the Line of Fire”), journalist Dmitry Durnev’s true account of the contemporary Donbas.
Katya Abramova, head of communications
Sergei Lebedev, “The Lady of the Mine”
Of course I knew about Sergei’s book: We’d discussed it at work meetings, planned the release, promotional materials, and so on. But I wasn’t in a hurry to read it — I just didn’t have the strength to read any more about war and the Holocaust. Then things didn’t go as planned: My colleagues at the publishing house asked me to help sell books at Sergei’s book event at Berlin’s Panda platforma. I agreed, though without much enthusiasm — it was a Saturday evening. And then… I was spellbound! It was an amazing, fascinating, nuanced discussion that gave me strength without leaving me feeling crushed at all. Despite the difficult subject. I went home and had finished the book by Monday. Now I recommend it to everyone.
From Meduza’s archives
From Meduza’s archives

The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. articles.title: German grocery wholesaler Metro’s Russian operation donates 1 billion rubles to a fund equipping front-line Russian troops, weeks after Putin placed its assets under temporary management
articles.body:
German grocery wholesaler Metro’s Russian operation donates 1 billion rubles to a fund equipping front-line Russian troops, weeks after Putin placed its assets under temporary management
The retail chain Metro, whose Russian assets were placed under temporary management less than a month ago, said it had donated 1 billion rubles to the “People’s Front: Everything for Victory!” fund.
The money will go toward “purchasing equipment needed by the military on the front lines,” the company said in a press release.
The fund said the money would help meet “urgent needs” for vehicles, communications and reconnaissance systems, equipment to counter drones, and “other things needed by troops in the “special military operation.”
“As part of Russia’s economic system, we believe it is important to take part in the state’s strategic initiatives,” said Johannes Tholey, Metro’s chief executive in Russia.
Update: Germany’s Metro said it had not approved the transfer of 1 billion rubles to the Russian military. In a statement to Deutsche Welle, Metro AG said it “distances itself from any support for Russia’s war against Ukraine.” “Financing or supporting military operations runs counter to both our position and our business principles,” the company said.
In late September, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree placing the assets of the German retail chain Metro under temporary management. The company had remained in Russia after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The appointed manager was JSC UK Torg Rus, a company registered three weeks earlier. Its listed owner was Johannes Tholey, who has headed Metro Cash & Carry since 2023.
Le Monde later reported that Metro itself had proposed that the Russian authorities place it under temporary management, deciding to “act preemptively” to avoid the worst-case scenario.

articles.title: First tanker carrying Russian diesel to U.S. heads for New York after Trump-Putin deal, set to arrive after midterm elections
articles.body:
The first tanker carrying Russian diesel to the United States since January 2022 is already on its way across the Atlantic following an agreement between Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump. The Malta-flagged Agioi Fanendes loaded 40,000 metric tons of diesel at the Baltic port of Primorsk on Oct. 22 and set course for New York, Reuters reported, citing LSEG data. The tanker is expected to arrive Nov. 7, four days after the U.S. congressional midterm elections.
According to data from ship tracking platform Starboard Maritime Intelligence reviewed by The Insider, Agioi Fanendes (IMO 9798375) left the Russian port of Primorsk at 10:58 p.m. GMT on Oct. 22. As of the morning of Oct. 23, the vessel was in the Gulf of Finland between the Finnish and Estonian coasts, traveling west at about 12 knots per hour (23 kilometers per hour). The crew listed New York as its destination, with an estimated arrival date of Nov. 7.
Starboard Maritime Intelligence data showed that after leaving Primorsk, the tanker’s reported draft increased from 7.8 meters to 11 meters, consistent with the vessel having taken on cargo. Agioi Fanendes is 183 meters long and 32 meters wide. Its registered owner is Maltatankers Shipping Ltd., and its operator is Greece-based Eastern Mediterranean Maritime Ltd. The tanker is carrying ultra-low-sulfur diesel.
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February of 2022, the United States banned imports of Russian energy products, including refined petroleum products. However, on Oct. 9, Trump announced an agreement with Putin under which Russia would supply 4.8 million metric tons of diesel to the U.S. and global markets.
Under the announced plan, Russia was to export the first 300,000 metric tons in October and another 500,000 metric tons in November, to be followed by larger volumes at later stages. The current 40,000-ton shipment amounts to about 13% of the volume initially promised for October.
The open-source intelligence project TankerTrackers later reported that it had identified three tankers carrying Russian diesel to the United States. According to the project, all three vessels loaded at Russian fuel terminals and openly listed U.S. ports as their destinations.
On the same day Trump announced the agreement, the U.S. Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued General License No. 135, authorizing transactions involving the sale, delivery, unloading, and import of Russian diesel, including direct imports into the United States. The authorization is valid through April 7, 2027. In response, Russian authorities lifted restrictions on diesel exports ahead of schedule. The restrictions had been introduced due to domestic fuel shortages following Ukraine’s sustained campaign of strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Speculation regarding Trump’s motivation for striking the deal has focused on the idea that he is hoping Russian supplies will help reduce domestic diesel prices, thereby providing his Republican party with a popularity boost ahead of the upcoming midterm elections. The first tanker, however, is not expected to reach the U.S. coast until after voting concludes on Nov. 3, and the physical arrival of a cargo does not necessarily coincide with the timing of its effect on futures or wholesale market prices.
As previously reported by Reuters, Russian fuel began returning to other traditional markets after the restrictions were lifted. Tankers leaving Primorsk headed to Turkey and Brazil, and deliveries to Morocco also resumed. Overall Russian diesel exports since the start of 2026, however, have fallen 41% year-on-year — to an average of 345,000 barrels a day.
Sanctions expert George Voloshin previously told The Insider that Russia could realistically meet its initial commitments to export 300,000 to 500,000 metric tons, but that increasing deliveries to between 1 million and 3 million metric tons a month was more doubtful. He said Russian oil companies would have to restore damaged refinery capacity and increase exports at the expense of rebuilding strategic fuel reserves at home.
The Trump-Putin agreement has drawn criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and U.S. lawmakers. Zelensky called Washington’s decision “weak,” while a group of Democratic senators described it as a betrayal of Ukraine and a threat to U.S. national security. They argued that renewed U.S. purchases of Russian energy products would provide Moscow with additional revenue to continue its war.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says restrictions on Starlink remain in force
articles.body:
Zelenskyy says restrictions on Starlink remain in force
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has confirmed that speed restrictions for Starlink satellite communications terminals in Ukraine remain in force.
Source: Zelenskyy during an online meeting at the Hudson Institute on 23 October, as reported by Interfax-Ukraine
Quote: "The speed limits on Starlink and Starshield are still there. The speed has not been restored. And the delivery of interceptors to protect us against Russian ballistic missiles is still delayed.
We are waiting for interceptors that were already agreed on but they are still not coming. Hope that everything is on the way. And this is a real problem for us because the Russians attack almost every day, Russia attacks us massively. So that's where things stand today."
Details: The president said that this is happening while Ukraine continues successful operations on the front line.
Zelenskyy added that he wants relations with America and all other partners to be as strong as possible.
Quote: "Without America, without a strong America and an America that cares about what happens in the world, the world would definitely be a worse place. These days people ask why Ukraine is speaking more openly directly to the world.
The answer is simple. We want people to understand us, and I mean people, societies, nations, as many people as possible. And when people understand what is really going on, political leaders can take a stronger path. The one that can really bring peace closer."
Background:
- The WSJ, citing US and Ukrainian officials familiar with the matter, reported that Trump had called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine.
- On the evening of 22 October, Trump said that Elon Musk has lifted speed restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine but declined to say whether he had personally called Musk about the matter.
- The Ministry of Defence of Ukraine reported that it was continuing to record disruption to Starlink/Starshield services on the front line.

articles.title: Ethiopia's Tigray rebels urged to disarm
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Ethiopia's Tigray rebels urged to disarm as commander vows to fight on
An official in Tigray’s new federal-backed administration urged rebel fighters to lay down their weapons Friday, hours after a rebel commander called for continued resistance despite losing the northern Ethiopian region’s capital.
The calls to surrender and fight on came nearly three weeks after rebels lost control of Mekelle. At a hospital in the city, two wounded men said a drone strike killed four civilians as they loaded goats onto a truck earlier this week.
Redae Halefom Woldeselassie, the caretaker administration’s chief executive for political and public mobilisation, said rebel forces were collapsing and urged fighters to enter a disarmament and reintegration program.
“This is not the time for settling scores, I call upon you to return to your homes and continue your civilian lives,” he said in Mekelle.
He dismissed the prospect of the rebels retaking the city and portrayed the conflict as serving a small group of leaders rather than the people of Tigray.
Hours earlier, Lt. Gen. Fisseha Kidanu, identified in a television broadcast as commander of the Tigray army, pledged to reverse recent military setbacks.
“Local militias across the region — alongside all volunteers joining the resistance — are expected to engage the enemy,” he said Thursday night on Tigray Broadcast Media, a new rebel television station. His location was not disclosed.
Fisseha urged attacks on government-held positions despite his opponents’ advantages in drones and heavy weapons. The Tigray People’s Liberation Front, or TPLF, has also claimed to have inflicted heavy losses on government forces. The Associated Press could not independently verify those claims.
Government-allied fighters entered Mekelle on Oct. 4 after the TPLF withdrew. Ethiopia’s government subsequently established a six-month caretaker administration promising to restore services, help displaced people return and prepare for elections.
The government’s allies include the Tigray Peace Force, comprising former members of the TPLF’s armed wing — a division within Tigrayan forces that has complicated the renewed conflict.
Redae said Ethiopian troops and allied forces were conducting joint security operations, including measures to prevent looting. He promised preparations for displaced residents to return but gave no timetable.
Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, speaking Monday to the Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation, accused the TPLF of acquiring weapons and forcibly recruiting young people instead of disarming under the November 2022 Pretoria peace agreement. He said his government had done everything within its capacity to implement the accord.
Wounded men describe drone strike 
At Ayder Hospital in Mekelle, Luel Berhanu, 22, and Samuel Belay, 20, said they were loading goats onto a truck in Finariwa, about 80 kilometers (49 miles) south of the city, when a strike hit around 9:30 p.m. Tuesday.
They said four civilians were killed and about six people wounded. The AP could not independently verify the casualties or establish who carried out the attack.
Luel said the truck’s headlights were on and a drone was hovering overhead shortly before the explosion. He said the blast severely injured his right eye and right arm, leaving him unable to see through that eye.
Samuel said they were working as day laborers loading the animals.
Hospital footage showed Luel with a bloodstained bandage covering his right eye and dressings around his shoulder and arm. Samuel lay on his side with an intravenous line attached to his arm.
A witness interviewed by the AP reported movements earlier that day by fighters identified as Agew Shengo, a militia that has previously fought alongside Tigrayan forces in neighboring Amhara region. Luel said rebel forces had been in the area several hours before the strike but none were present when it occurred.
Losing Mekelle may not end the war 
The renewed fighting has effectively shattered the Pretoria agreement, which ended the devastating 2020-2022 war.
Magnus Taylor, deputy Horn of Africa director at the International Crisis Group, told the AP last week that controlling towns and roads would not necessarily secure rural areas where Tigrayan fighters regrouped during the previous war.
“We shouldn’t imagine that this conflict is completely over just because the TPLF has lost Mekelle,” he said.

articles.title: New exchange: Ukraine brings back 270 more defenders from Russian captivity – photos
articles.body:
New exchange: Ukraine brings back 270 more defenders from Russian captivity – photos
On Friday 23 October, 270 military personnel returned to Ukraine from Russian captivity as part of a new exchange.
Source: Zelenskyy on social media; Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War
Quote from Zelenskyy: "270 of our people are home. A very important result. National Guard members, including Azov warriors, border guards, warriors of the Territorial Defence Forces, the Navy, the Land Forces, the Airborne Assault Forces, and the State Special Transport Service, as well as nine civilians, are returning home. Most of them had been in captivity since 2022."
Details: According to the president, most of those released are warriors who defended Ukraine in Mariupol. People who defended the Donetsk, Luhansk, Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, Kherson, Kyiv, Mykolaiv, and Chernihiv fronts are also returning.
"Many were illegally convicted in Russia. Among those returning are five people who were believed to have been killed in the Russian terrorist attack in Olenivka in July 2022," Zelenskyy wrote.
Background: Ukraine and Russia held their last prisoner of war exchange in August, when 103 service personnel from the National Guard, the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the Navy, the Territorial Defence Forces and the State Border Guard Service were brought back to Ukraine.

articles.title: Standoff hits Sudanese consumers as Egypt halts cargo trucks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Border standoff hits Sudanese consumers as Egypt halts cargo trucks
Egyptian authorities have suspended cargo truck crossings into Sudan, triggering severe shortages and price hikes that ordinary Sudanese are struggling to absorb.
The decision followed the killing of two Egyptian truck drivers and the injury of a third on 12 October, when a 23-year-old Sudanese gunman opened fire on them in a popular market south of Khartoum.
The incident occurred only a day after scores of artisanal miners, including Sudanese nationals, were killed by Egyptian airstrikes in the border area between Egypt and Sudan.
According to the Egyptian army, the strikes were staged inside Egypt. However, unofficial Sudanese claims to the contrary have caused anger in different parts of Sudan.
Sudanese demonstrators took to the streets, particularly in Nyala—the capital of South Darfur State and a stronghold of the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces which battles the Sudanese Armed Forces for control over Sudan.
Activists also called for a boycott of Egyptian goods, planning to blockade the desert road linking Khartoum to border crossings to halt incoming freight.
Cairo framed the suspension as a protective measure to shield Egyptian drivers from targeted violence.
Regardless of Cairo's rationale, the move has dealt an immediate blow to Sudanese consumers, threatening to trigger widespread inflation at an already precarious moment.
A recent viral video captured a Sudanese shopkeeper gesturing to his fully stocked shelves. Most of the goods, he noted, were either imported directly from Egypt or relied on Egyptian raw materials.
"Do you know what the decision to suspend the entry of cargo trucks from Egypt into Sudan means?" the trader asks. "It means that the prices of all these products will shoot up in the coming days."
Lifeline severed
Egypt serves as a vital gateway for Sudan's access to global markets, particularly as international sanctions continue to cripple Sudanese businesses.
Sudan's civil war, which has been grinding on since April 2023, has also put the brakes on a sizeable portion of the country's industrial and agricultural production, making it more dependent on imports for the needs of its people.
In 2025, bilateral trade reached $1.19 billion, with Egyptian exports accounting for $933.3 million.
In the first half of this year, bilateral trade reached $759 million, up from $570 million in the corresponding period of the previous year, according to the Egyptian government. Egyptian exports amounted to $595 million, almost 40% up from the export figure recorded in the first half of 2025, the government says.
Trade between the two countries partly owes its activity to their ability to develop a barter-style system that helps them avoid stringent international sanctions on Sudanese businesses and foreign currency shortages on both sides, specialists said.
However, cutting off Egyptian goods leaves the war-ravaged nation deeply vulnerable, forcing consumers to endure sudden supply bottlenecks alongside skyrocketing prices, Sudanese specialists said.
"This suspension is having far-reaching economic and human consequences," Sudanese political analyst Osman al-Merghani said.
Speaking to The New Arab, he added that the market has been paralyzed in almost all Sudanese states due to the dramatic rise that happened in commodity prices.
"Some commodities, including sugar and rice, have also completely disappeared, which is causing a lot of suffering to ordinary consumers," al-Merghani said.
Online hostility vs. diplomatic containment
The current disruption to bilateral trade comes at a time when a social media war is raging on between the Egyptians and the Sudanese against the background of the 11 October strikes.
Sudanese nationals commenting on the incident slam Egypt for killing what they describe as "innocent" artisanal miners and allegedly infringing on Sudanese territories, throwing light on growing anti-Egypt sentiments in some parts of the southern neighbouring country.
Egyptian social media users counter by defending their national army, and accusing the Sudanese of mining for gold inside Egypt, hence stealing the country's mineral resources.
The surge in anti-Egyptian rhetoric has heightened anxiety among the estimated 1,000 Egyptian nationals still remaining in Sudan.
Before the war erupted in April 2023, between 10,000 and 15,000 Egyptians lived in Sudan, mostly those married to Sudanese, working in Sudan or investing in the country.
An Egyptian national has recently posted a video where he implored Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi to help him and others return safely to Egypt.
"The Sudanese are lying in wait for us on the road between Khartoum and the Egyptian border," the man said in the video which appeared on social media on October 14.
Most Egyptian nationals present in Sudan are reportedly concentrated in coastal areas under the control of the Sudanese Armed Force, especially Port Sudan where the Egyptian Consulate operates and business activities remain comparatively stable.
The governments of the two countries keep working, meanwhile, to contain fallout from the 11 October strikes.
On 16 October, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and Sudanese Finance Minister Gibril Ibrahim rejected attempts to harm their countries' bilateral relations, noting that those relations are based on shared respect and good neighbourliness.
Meeting the Sudanese minister on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings in Washington DC, the Egyptian foreign minister reaffirmed Cairo's unwavering support for Sudan's unity and territorial integrity.
This meeting came four days after the foreign ministers of the two countries underscored the importance of respecting each other's country's sovereignty, territorial integrity and borders.
Analysts in Cairo view these diplomatic containment efforts as proof of the high strategic value both nations place on bilateral ties.
They call for managing those relations wisely, especially in the presence of persistent attempts by some parties to sabotage them.
"It is clear that some parties work to widen the gap between the two countries and cause a rupture in their relations," Egyptian political analyst Islam Mansi said.
"These parties do their best to incite the Sudanese people against Egypt, a country bound by historical ties and a shared destiny with Sudan," he told TNA.

articles.title: Turkish foreign minister warns new attack on Iran would escalate regional conflict
articles.body:
The Turkish foreign minister warned on Friday that a new attack on Iran would further spread war and conflict across the region, Anadolu reports.
“Military intervention in Iran is by no means a solution. No one supports this at the moment,” Hakan Fidan told reporters after an R4+E3 meeting in Istanbul, the first-ever meeting in this format.
The US and Israel are said to have developed plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the American midterm elections.
The war that began in late February has yet to be settled despite a ceasefire and a memorandum of understanding to finalize a peace deal.
Speaking on the Russia-Ukraine war, Fidan said: “Either the war must stop, or, if it does not, parties must agree to exemptions for energy and grain issues.”
The R4 mechanism was established by Türkiye, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia on the basis of regional ownership, with the aim of supporting lasting stability and strengthening dialogue on regional issues.
The E3 mechanism, made up of Germany, the UK and France, emerged from trilateral diplomatic cooperation on Iran’s nuclear program launched in 2003.

articles.title: Cargo ship sinks off the coast of Romania, local authorities blame Russia
articles.body:
On the morning of Oct. 23, the cargo ship KHORYV (IMO: 8138712) capsized and sank off the coast of Romania, the press service of the country’s Interior Ministry has reported, along with local media. Romanian President Nicușor Dan has placed the blame for the accident on Russia.
At around 10 a.m. local time, the coast guard received a report of a fire on the vessel, which was located approximately 13 nautical miles (roughly 24 km) from the port of Constanța.
The Starboard Maritime Intelligence service map shows several rescue vessels heading toward the ship at the time of the distress signal.
The cargo ship had 13 people on board when the fire broke out. Nine were picked up by another commercial vessel that was in the vicinity (apparently the Norwegian SARTOR). One person was killed, and three are still listed as missing.
The KHORYV was sailing from the Turkish port of Ereğli, also on the Black Sea. Its destination was listed as the Romanian port of Sulina at the mouth of the Danube — the main shipping route that connects the Black Sea with Ukrainian ports on the river. At the end of September, KHORYV had already traveled this route to reach the port of Galați, one of the most important shipment points for exporting Ukrainian grain.
Romanian President Nicușor Dan writes that the vessel was hit by a drone and calls the incident “an example of the tragic consequences of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine.”
In recent weeks, at least six civilian vessels have been attacked off the coast of Romania and neighboring Bulgaria. Against this backdrop, Romania proposed creating a joint command for Black Sea NATO countries to defend against drones. This week, NATO spokesperson Allison Hart said that the alliance will strengthen its grouping of maritime patrol aircraft and drones in the region.

articles.title: Meduza’s sources say prosecution of popular Russian Communist was planned before his election defeat
articles.body:
Moscow’s Basmanny District Court has ordered Oleg Mikhailov, a former State Duma deputy and former head of the Communist Party’s Komi branch, held in pretrial detention. He is charged with justifying terrorism over a post supporting imprisoned political scientist Boris Kagarlitsky and faces up to seven years in prison. Mikhailov built one of the Communist Party’s strongest regional branches, brought together people with different political views, took part in environmental protests, and challenged the republic’s authorities. During his State Duma election campaign, he was also one of the few Communist candidates to campaign for peace. Yet after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began, Mikhailov repeatedly voted for repressive laws.
Warning: This article contains profanity.
Meduza previously reported that the presidential administration was urging the Communist Party’s leadership not to nominate strong regional candidates who had defeated United Russia candidates in single-member districts in the previous election. Among them was Mikhailov, a Communist from the Komi Republic.
The Communist Party partly complied, but its Komi branch leader ran anyway, both in his district and on the federal party list. His original position on the list offered him no prospect of winning a seat.
A Communist Party source told Meduza that the party leadership provided almost no funding for Mikhailov’s district campaign. After his nomination, the source said, Mikhailov and the party began receiving “hints” from the Kremlin: If he did not withdraw, he would face a criminal investigation. Meduza has learned, however, that the authorities planned to launch an investigation regardless, and that the Federal Security Service (FSB) began examining Mikhailov’s social media accounts as early as 2024.
“I told him: Go on vacation after the election, to whatever country you can, and maybe stay a little longer. He agreed to take a vacation, but he ruled out emigrating. He wanted to stay in Russia,” an acquaintance of the former deputy told Meduza, requesting anonymity.
Mikhailov failed to win reelection to the State Duma in September 2026. On October 21, he was detained at Moscow’s Domodedovo Airport as he returned from vacation.
Mikhailov was born in 1987 in Pechora, a district seat in Komi. After studying biology at Syktyvkar State University, he went to graduate school, earned a doctorate, and worked at Komi’s Institute of Biology. He joined the Communist Party in 2007 while still a student and became an activist. At the time, the party’s Komi branch attracted little attention compared with branches in other regions that had prominent local politicians.
“You could’ve called the Komi regional party committee a retirees’ club. They were an opposition group — not very active, but honest,” Pavel Andreyev, founder of the Revolt Center and an acquaintance of Mikhailov’s, told Meduza. “At first, he came across as pretty off-putting — this guy with no sense of fashion, like he’d stepped out of Soviet times. But the older crowd liked that.”
An acquaintance of Mikhailov’s who spoke to Meduza anonymously said he “steadily worked his way up through the party”:
He’d help [the branch leadership] with one thing, lend a hand with another. They promoted him for obvious reasons: He did the things [the branch leadership] didn’t have enough people to do, and [the party leaders] also felt it was time to retire.
And before he knew it, Oleg had become a Syktyvkar city council member, then head of the regional party committee and a member of the regional legislature.
As head of the committee, Mikhailov actively supported protests against the construction of a landfill at Shiyes railway station. The station is in the Arkhangelsk region, practically on the Komi border, and much closer to Syktyvkar than to Arkhangelsk. Mikhailov laid out his position on Shiyes in 2019:
There’s no middle ground on Shiyes: You’re either for it or against it. If you’re for it, you’re an accomplice to the garbage occupiers; if you’re against it, you’re a normal person. There’s no third option.
Another deputy once said to me, “Maybe you should go work in the Arkhangelsk region? It’s their problem, after all.” That tells you something about a deputy who doesn’t understand that administrative and national borders are drawn by people, while nature has no borders. It’s all one ecosystem: Pollution will flow into the Vychegda and Northern Dvina [rivers], then into the White and Barents seas, and we’ll pollute half of Europe.
Speaking to Meduza that same year, Mikhailov called the landfill’s construction “a political issue, rather than an environmental one.” He spoke with considerable emotion in that interview:
The federal government treats Russia’s regions and the people who live in them unfairly. What are we, second-class citizens? Is that why you’re building a dump here? How about we put a dump in your backyard? We’re a region that sends out huge amounts of resources — 151 billion rubles in taxes last year. We send you money, resources, and even our talent. The best of everything goes to Moscow! And we get Moscow’s garbage.
At the time, Mikhailov organized Syktyvkar’s largest protest in several years: The Communists said at least 1,800 people attended. The republic’s authorities authorized the rally at the local “Hyde Park,” a designated protest area, but it turned into a march and continued in the city’s main square.
During the Shiyes protests, the Communist Party’s Komi branch built ties with environmental activists and the Komi national movement. Mikhailov told Meduza that he was half Komi himself and supported compulsory Komi-language instruction in the republic’s schools. It had become voluntary shortly before, in January 2018.
“In places like Vorkuta or Inta, nonindigenous residents openly say, ‘What do we need this language for?’ But if you live here, if you’re staying rather than waiting to move away, then respect the traditions of the local people. If I move to any European country and want to live there, I have to learn the language,” Mikhailov told Meduza indignantly.
In 2019, the Communist Party’s Komi branch actively supported Komi national activists in elections to the interregional civic organization Komi Voityr. For the Communists, that campaign was something of a warm-up for the 2020 elections for the republic’s leader and its State Council. By then, residents saw the Communist Party as the main force for political protest.
Hi, I’m Yulia.
I’m an editor at Meduza, and for almost five years now, I haven’t been sleeping well for one reason: I’m worried about my colleagues in Russia.
I’m often woken up by messages from our freelance reporters inside the country. They sometimes work late at night or early in the morning, and they message me at all hours. I never silence my phone at night in case of an emergency. Every notification jolts me awake. Half-asleep, my first thought is always the same: they’re texting me because the police have come to search their home. In Russia, you can go to prison for working with Meduza. Sometimes I have nightmares about my reporters being interrogated by the FSB. Some of those nightmares have come true.
Meduza’s reporters risk their freedom to tell the world what’s happening inside Russia. They believe their work can help make a better future possible, and they refuse to leave. Please donate so they can keep reporting.
An acquaintance of Mikhailov’s said he had “an ability to build electoral alliances with people of different views.” Previous secretaries of the Communist Party’s regional committee had focused solely on the party and its voters, the acquaintance told Meduza, while Mikhailov worked with “the whole range of civic activists — environmentalists, housing activists, human rights advocates, liberals, and patriots.”
“This guy, who basically never picked fights, hoovered up opposition-minded people and pulled them into his orbit. But the activists didn’t roll over for him. They just understood that Oleg was a reasonable person they could work things out with,” Mikhailov’s acquaintance said.
Opposition to the Kremlin’s appointee, Komi leader Sergey Gaplikov, and his team of “outsiders” was central to the Communists’ 2020 State Council campaign. Gaplikov had had no connection to Komi before his appointment. Mikhailov spoke about him to Meduza in 2019:
Before Gaplikov, the leaders had at least built their careers here. He’s a complete outsider. The State Council meets seven to nine times a year, and the republic’s head shows up exactly once a year, to deliver his report. [During rallies,] people stand on the steps of the republic’s government building, shouting, “Gaplikov must go!” — and he couldn’t care less. The main thing is that everyone who’s more or less politically active understands that these people are just passing through, here for a stint. They’ll leave anyway.
The Communists did well in the republic’s State Council election, winning 14.8% of the vote — nearly twice their share in the previous election, in 2015. Four Communist Party candidates won seats in Komi’s parliament: three through the party list and one in a single-member district. United Russia received 28% of the vote.
Shortly before the election, the republic did get a new leader: Another “outsider,” Vladimir Uiba, replaced Gaplikov. Mikhailov was barred from running for Komi’s top job after the republic’s election commission ruled that he had failed to collect the required endorsements from municipal officials.
Uiba proved a poor choice for the job. The new leader clashed with local residents and with Mikhailov himself. At a State Council meeting in April 2021, Mikhailov told the republic’s head that Uiba had “even run his campaign like a complete coward, picking outright spoiler candidates as his opponents.” Uiba responded by calling Mikhailov a “horse” and threatening to “beat the shit out of” him.
This confrontation only cemented Mikhailov’s position as Komi’s leading opposition politician — and possibly its most popular politician overall. He regularly traveled around the region and met with residents. In the 2021 State Duma election, he won his single-member district, while the Communist Party received 26.9% of the vote in Komi, according to official figures. United Russia had one of its lowest vote shares nationwide in Komi that year: 29.4%, compared with 49% across Russia.
After Mikhailov moved to the federal parliament, libertarian Viktor Vorobyov took over his State Council seat and his position as the party’s caucus leader there.
In the State Duma, Mikhailov did not vote for the 2022 laws recognizing the independence of the self-proclaimed Donetsk and Luhansk people’s republics, or for the law imposing penalties for “discrediting the army.” Nevertheless, the European Union, the United States, and Canada sanctioned him for allegedly supporting the latter law.
Mikhailov did support other measures, including the November 2022 ban on “LGBT propaganda,” the November 2024 ban on adoptions by people in countries that allow “sex changes,” and the July 2025 law allowing the FSB to establish its own pretrial detention centers.
Meanwhile, the Communist Party’s Komi branch continued to oppose Uiba, who remained in office until November 2024 despite his unpopularity. He was replaced by Rostislav Goldstein, the former head of the Jewish Autonomous Region. Goldstein had close ties to Komi: He had run businesses in the republic, served in its State Council, and then represented the region in the federal parliament.
An acquaintance of Mikhailov’s said that, unlike Uiba, Goldstein and his team initially “tried to reach an understanding” with the Communists. “At least an agreement not to fight dirty with each other,” the acquaintance told Meduza. Gradually, however, relations between the republic’s authorities and the Communist Party branch began to deteriorate, he said.
“Goldstein is a pretty tough guy. He also wanted to show the federal leadership that he’d brought everyone to heel in a region known for protest and dealt with the Communist Party problem,” a source close to the presidential administration’s domestic politics team told Meduza.
The confrontation between Goldstein and the republic’s Communists culminated in Mikhailov being barred from the 2025 election for regional leader. As before, the official reason was his alleged failure to collect the required endorsements from municipal officials.
Ahead of the 2026 parliamentary election, Komi’s authorities deliberately worked to keep the “troublesome deputy” out of the State Duma, a political consultant who works with the presidential administration’s domestic politics team told Meduza. To that end, the consultant said, they fielded Stanislav Kochev, who had fought in the war against Ukraine, in the single-member district. “A veteran can’t lose — anything goes to make sure he wins,” the consultant said.
Mikhailov, meanwhile, campaigned on the slogan “For peace,” a rarity among Communist Party candidates. Officially, he lost the State Duma election, but the vote tallies from in-person polling stations where observers were present indicate otherwise. In electronic voting, the United Russia candidate received 2.5 times as many votes as Mikhailov.
An acquaintance of Mikhailov’s said the politician’s arrest could make it harder for the Communist Party’s Komi branch to function and would probably turn it into a typical, largely inactive party branch. “Yeah, he probably could’ve done more. But he could’ve done jack shit, like most politicians,” the acquaintance said of Mikhailov’s work.
The acquaintance still considers Mikhailov one of Komi’s most popular political figures: “His [Telegram] channel is called ‘Voice of the Republic.’ I think that’s how residents see him — as the voice of the people.”
